ARTHUR MELVIN WARREN
Grand Master

ARTHUR MEL VIN WARREN

Grand Master
1952~1953

Arthur M. Warren was born in San Francisco, California, on December 27, 1901. A true native son, he has lived continuously in the
City by the Golden Gate.
He was educated in the San Francisco Public Schools.
At an early age, Brother Warren entered the banking business. After
a successive series of promotions he was appointed Vice President and
Manager of The Bank of California, N.A., Mission Branch, which
position he now holds.
On May 25, 1925, Brother Warren was joined in marriage to Claire
Massey. They have one daughter, Barbara Claire.
As a young man, Arthur Warren came under the influence of many
leaders of Masonry in San Francisco. Their example caused him to
bec~me a charter member of San Francisco Chapter, Order of DeMolay
in January, 1921. He was elected and served as the first Master Councillor of the Chapter, holding office for two terms. In 1922 he was elected
to the office of Scribe, serving in that capacity for one year. He is a member of the DeMolay Legion of Honor, having been invested in 1931.
Arthur Warren's devotion to Blue Lodge Masonry is evidenced by
his more than thirty years continuous service to the Craft. He was
raised in Mount Davidson Lodge No. 481 in San Francisco on May 5,
1923. Progressing through the subordinate stations of the Lodge he was
. elected Master and served as such during 1931. He held the office of
Treasurer of his Lodge from 1933 to 1941. During the year 1932 he
became Secretary of the Masters and Wardens Association of San
Francisco. In 1944 he served as President of the Past Masters Association of San Francisco. Appointed Inspector of the then 40th Masonic
District in 1935, he served until 1939, when he was appointed Assistant
Grand Lecturer. This service continued for seven years. In 1946 he
was elevated to the office of Grand Lecturer. After three years of faithful performance in the duties of that exacting work, he was installed as
Junior Grand Warden on October 14, 1949. He was elected Senior
Grand Warden in 1950, and Deputy Grand Master in 1951. On Ocher 17, 1952, Brother Warren was elected and installed Grand Master
of Masons in California.
He is a 32d 0 member of San Francisco Bodies, No. 1, Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry.
Active in community and civic affairs, Brother Warren is a member
of the following organizations: San F~ancisco Chamber of Commerce,

Mission Optimist Club of San Francisco and the San Francisco Commercial Club.
He was Foreman of the 1948 Grand Jury, City and County of San
Francisco.
During his term as Grand Master, Brother "Art," as he is affectionately known among the rank and file members of the Fraternity, sought
to encourage a greater participation by the Craft in the support of fundamental Grand Lodge programs.
His friendly, gracious and sincere manner struck a responsive chord
in the hearts of his brethren. Inspired by his leadership, California
Masonry achieved new heights in the Public Schools Week Program,
Constitution Month Observance, in the Formation of new lodges, and
in contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
This is Masonry at its best.

DEVOTIONAL SERVICES
The Requirements of God
Very REVEREND ADAM B. MORTON. Grand Chaplain
Most Worshipful Sir,
Members of the Grand Lodge.
Delegates to the 104th Communication of the
Grand Lodge of Masons of California:
It is with humility that I stand before you this morning. and with
a prayer to Almighty God that I may be guided to say something helpful.
Let me first express sincere appreciation for the kindliness I have
encountered everywhere. The year will be one that I shall remember.
The friendliness of the men in every part of the State to which I have
been privileged to go has indeed enriched my own life. For the warm
friendship of the Grand Officers I am most thankful. Truly Masonry
"causes true friendship to exist among those who might otherwise have
remained at a perpetual distance."
This high privilege has been mine through the grace of our honored
Grand Master. When the Grand Lecturer unexpectedly visited my
Lodge on a night when the Master was away and, as Senior Warden,
I had to preside, I felt a little overwhelmed. After I had talked for a
few minutes with Arthur Warren I felt that I had a brother and not ·
a critic present, and all tension disappeared. For the brotherly kindness
he has always shown. and for the high privilege of this office I wish
to say a sincere "thank you" to the Grand Master in this open Grand
Lodge.
Several years ago as I sat in the opening session of this Grand Lodge
listening to a very able address by the Grand Chaplain I found my
mind occupied with thoughts about the audience of which I was one.
I thought of the differences represented in that assembly. We had come
from many occupations. The Governor of the State, many distinguished
judges and attorneys. and at least one humble preacher were present.
There were representatives of most of the trades and professions. We
v:ere men from most of the recognized Churches. Some of us were high
ritualists in religious practice and some of us might have found ritual
and ceremony an impediment to our approach to God. We were polee

10

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

apart in many of our interests and yet we were bound together in the

have indeed been words by which I have lived. A tremendous comfort
in periods of confusion and an ever increasing challenge to higher living.

bond~ of brotherhood. We were united by the cement of brotherly

love into one sacred band or society of friends and brothers. Our conceptions of God might cover a wide field of opinion, but we were all
avowed believers in God and our Grand Chaplain was leading us in a
devotional meditation. I found myself thinking, after all, "What doth
God require of thee but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly
with thy God?"
During ~he past year, as I have participated in many meetings of
our Fraternity throughout the jurisdiction, I have found these words
recurring in my mind, and as I have thought of this service I have been
unable to escape them. The text for our meditation therefore is, "What
doth the Lord require of thee but to do justly, to love mercy, and to
walk humbly with thy God?"
These words come from the writings of the Hebrew prophet Micah
written about the eighth or seventh century B. C. In the lives of many
men there have been times when the experiences of the hour have driven
them to ask, "What are the basic essentials of a religious life?" Micah
had passed through one of those times. On the one hand were many
displays of religious fervor. The people had their ritualistic sacrifices
and kept their Holy Days. On the other hand he found grossness of
life and corrupt practices in the market place. He speaks of "the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure
that is abominable." Of "the man with wicked scales and with a bag
of deceitful weights." He ponders on this conflict of fervor and practice
and asks if God will be pleased with sacrifices? Can we win His favor
by observances and giving of our possessions alone? Then he gives us
his great conclusion, "What doth the Lord require of thee but to do
justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"
I really discovered these words when I was a young theological
student in the second decade of the century. The conflict of so-called
"Fundamentalism" and "Modernism" was then going on. I entered
training with the implicit acceptance of the views of the group in which
I had moved. I soon heard many of the things I believed seriously
challenged. I would go from teacher to teacher and hear different views
propounded. I found myself asking, "What must a man believe?" Many
times I was confused. I had read Micah's words before but at that
time they came to me like a light in the darkness. My beliefs about God
were in a very fluid state but the basic essentials of my duty to God
were quite dear. What did God require of me? Not to accept this or
that belief, but "to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with
Him." These words have remained with me through all the changing
experiences of life. In all the problems of creed and of race. Amidst
the confusions of wars, and the bitter fights over social and economic
systems. I have again and again fallen back on these great words. They

11

There has always been a tendency amongst men to divide life into
the sacred and the secular. To stress the observances of religion--our
worship services, our sacraments, our support of the affairs of a Church
-as the necessary religious duties. As one said a short time ago, "I
must make my monthly communion." I want to say this morning I
believe that life is a whole and cannot be so divided. That God is concerned not only with our acts of formal worship but with our whole lives.
That He is more pleased when we act justly or mercifully than He is
when we make long prayers to be heard of men. Religion is a positive
way of living. To criticise other men's beliefs, or to tear down what they
have built up is not sufficient. Masons are builders and not wreckers.
The message I bring is that "God requires of us to do justly, to love
mercy, and to walk humbly with Him." I invite you to join me for a
few minutes in considering the content of these three requirements.

1. "TO DO JUSTLY"-We are taught that "justice is that standard or boundary of right which enables us to render unto every man his
just due without distinction."
Men often seem to live on different levels of justice or are satisfied
with different measures of being just. Some appear satisfied when they
do not violate the laws of the country. They may even spend time and
money trying to find loopholes or ways of evading the laws-especially
tax laws-but so long as they do not technically violate the laws they
are satisfled .tney are just. While the keeping of the law is incumbent
on all of us that alone is surely inadequate for men who are taught to
act upon the square.
Then there is the man who measures justice by the mores or social
pattern of his group. He keeps the law but he goes a little further and
maintains the standards of the society in which he lives. Many years
ago I had one such in a Church I served. He was a merchant and punctiliously gave sixteen ounces to every pound, but never a shade more.
He did what was required of him for his family even to the extent of
having family prayer yet each member left home when he could legally
do so. He attended Church but his face was not an inspiration to a
preacher. No one questioned his justice but it was hard to find anyone
who loved him. He was just but I do not believe it was the kind of
justice that brings joy to the heart of God. This measure of justice is
not adequate for the man who really sets his heart to do justly.
Many centuries ago a standard was set up which has remained the
ideal of justice for all time. Jesus of Nazareth told his followers that
"all things whatsover ye would that men should do to you, do ye even
so to them." Jesus said this was the teaching of the law and the prophets.

I believe we can say that this too is the teaching of Masonry and the
ideal of justice to which every Mason should aspire. The conduct it
calls for in the different situations and areas of living each man must
decide for himself. Two incidents from the time of my youth have
remained in my thought as exempli.6cations of this standard. One was
in the .6eld of sports. A young Indian prince was a member of an English
County cricket team. They played in a league which was to cricket
what the American or National League is to baseball. The young
Indian had achieved a reputation as a good batsman, a brilliant .Gelder,
and an outstanding sportsman. During an important game he made what
appeared to be a brilliant low catch of a fly ball. The crowd cheered
and the umpire signalled the batsman out. The young Indian spoke to
the umpire, the batsman was called back, and the game proceeded. It
was reported the .Gelder had told the umpire it was not a fair catch.
The ball had touched the ground. I do not know what faith that man
professed. He might have been Buddhist, or Moslem, or Christian.
Regardless of this I believe the heart of the Almighty rejoiced over a
man courageous enough to be fair or just in a difficult situation.
The other incident was in a different .6eld. A business executive was
also an amateur philatelist. He had an extensive stamp collection and
was always gathering more. One day a man brought to him an album
of stamps. He didn't know the value. It had come to him in the personal ·
effects of another and had been lying around for a long time. He wanted
to know if it was of value and if the other man would buy it. After
examining the album for some time the philatelist asked if he would be
satis.6ed with tlie equivalent of twenty-5ve dollars. The other ·said he
would be glad to take it. After a further examination the philatelist
told him that if he would take it to a certain .6rm they would probably
give him closer to one thousand dollars.
Some time ago a man somewhat de.6antly said, "The Golden Rule
is good enough for me." He could not get an argument with me on that
point. My problem has never been whether or not the Golden Rule was
good enough for me. It always has been, and is, for me to have that
internal strength and goodness to measure up to the Golden Rule.
To be a good ritualist and a helpful brother in the affairs of the
Lodge is important, but one of the basic essentials of a good Mason, as
well as of a Godly man, is to do justly in all the affairs of life.
2. "TO LOVE MERCY.'' Shakespeare causes Portia to say:
"The quality of mercy is not strain'd;
It droppeth as the gentle dew from heaven
Upon the place beneath: it is twice bless' d:
It blesses him that gives and him that takes.
It is an attribute of God himself;

13

And earthly power doth then show likest God's
When mercy seasons justice.
"We do pray for mercy:
.
And that same prayer doth teach us all to r.ender
The deeds of mercy."
Jesus said: "Blessed are the merciful for they shall obtain mercy'."
Many a just man has developed a spirit of harshness toward his
brother's failings. Righteousness can soon develop into self-righteousness and a superior scorn toward the weaknesses of one's fellows.
Many just people pray in spirit "Lord I thank thee I am not as other
men," and are indifferent to the unfortunate. God requires a man to be
just, and He also requires him to be kind or "to love mercy." To be
the kind of man whose instinctive re-action will be to help the weak
and unfortunate. Masonry requires us to walk uprightly in our several
stations before God and man. It also teaches us to be ever ready to
stretch forth a helping hand to raise a fallen brother. Acting in brotherly love to relieve the distressed is incumbent upon all of us.
The highest commendation of Jes us was given to a man, not for a
formal religious act, but for a deed of mercy. You will recall the story
of the man who, while going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among
thieves who stripped him, and beat him, and left him by the roadside half
dead. A priest came along the road. He glanced at the man but, pr~b­
ably being busy with important matters, passed by on the other side.
Next came a Levite, a good lay brother, who took one look and passed
by on the o!her side. Then came a Samaritan, an outsider, who, whe?1
he saw the man, had compassion. He stopped, bound up the man s
wounds, set him on his own beast, took him to an inn where he would
be cared for, and paid the bill. As a standa~~ of conduct to hi.s fel~ow;,
men Jesus charges the enquiring lawyer to go thou and do likewise.
Again in his parable of the .6nal judgment Jesus places the basis
of judgment on the mercy one had, or had not, shown to his fellows.
To the approved the Lord says "I was hungry and you gave me food,
I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed
me, I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me,
I was in prison and you came to me. Truly as you did it to one of the
least of these my brethren you did it unto me." Those who were condemned were rejected because of their failure to do these acts of mercy.
They had been indifferent to the needs and failures of their fellows.
Masons in California have been kind to their needy older brethren
and to unfortunate children from a Masonic home. We are all proud
of the magni.6cent work being done at Decota and Covina. This year
this Grand Lodge has paid around six hundred thousand dollars for the
maintainence of these Homes and the Masons of California have contributed three hundred and thirty thousand dollars to the Homes' En-

dowment Fund. We are proud to have been able to do this and I am
sure we all want to see the good work go on.

lives and when something goes wrong with the plan they become <Jngcy
and bitter with God and lose the joy of life. There is a story in the
Bible which we call an Elisha story. It tells about a general in Syria
who was the confidant of his King. He was a great man but he was a
leper. It was told that there was a prophet in Israel who could cure
him of his leprosy and the king sent him to Israel with rich presents and
great hope. He came with his chariots to the door of the prophet. The
prophet did not come out but sent his servant with the message to go
wash seven times in the River Jordan and he would be healed. The
very important person was angry. He thought the prophet would come
out and pass his hands over the spot, and call upon God and heal him.
The rivers of Damascus were cleaner than the Jordan. Could he not
wash in them and be clean? He was going away in anger and bitterness.
If he had not listened to the calmer advice of his servants he would have
missed the big experience-the healing of his leprosy. God doesn't
always work in the way we expect. The tasks given are not those
we wanted to do. The willing acceptance of what He sends: the
cheerful execution of whatever task is ours, and willingness to learn
from all experience is part of walking with God. It brings healing to
our spirits.
Walking with God means trusting in God under all circumstances.
At the core of Masonry is the story of a man who was faithful even unto
death. All Masons put thir trust in God. This means confidence in
God even in adversity. The poem of Job is a classic example. It is
the story of a prosperous man who lost everything and then was himself
grievously afJlicted. His wife told him to curse God and die, and his
friends tried to convince him that he had been very wicked. In response,
and out of his suffering, Job cries, "though He slay me, yet will I trust
in Him." That was the great triumph of Job. His later material success
was incidental. The real richness of his life was that inner resource of
trust and faith in God.

There are brethren present this morning who have given many years
of service to the welfare of the unfortunate. We honor them for it.
One of the greates problems of our age is to help the unfortunate. There
are many in this assembly-line age who are not equipped either mentally
or physically to maintain themselves. Perhaps misfortunte or illness
strikes those who are doing reasonably well and they are soon in dire
need. What are we going to do about it? We can "pass by on the other
side" and allow cancerous growths of need and bitterness to fester in
the body of our society, or, acting in mercy, we can bring our best intelligence to bear to solve these problems and meet these needs. I am not a
Socialist or even a 'welfare stater' and am not especially pleading for
any system. I am pleading that our actions be prompted, not by political
expediency or prejudice, but by mercy toward the unfortunate. Because
many selfish indolent people have exploited our efforts to help we cannot
afford to grow harsh and refuse further efforts to help. There is need
for the finest intelligence to work out methods to help the unfortunate
without encouraging slothfulness. I have a feeling that the security and
welfare of our form of society will depend upon the intelligence and
mercy which we bring to these problems. As individual members of
society and as Masons compassion and justice should guide all our
actions as we live and work together.
3. "TO WALK HUMBLY WITH THY GOD."-This involve~
each individual's relation to his God. It does not set forth any formal
duty or require the acceptance of any creed. What do we mean by
walking with God? We have had many explanations and mystic interpretations which are as mysterious as they are mystic. I do not want
to talk in vague terms which no one will understand, but I do want to
suggest some things I believe are involved in our relationship to God.
Surely walking with God includes a humble recognition of our dependence upon the Almighty. When men were immediately dependent
on annual crops they were conscious that "we plough the fields and
scatter the good seed on the ground, but it is fed and watered by God's
almighty hand". In this age of jet planes, radar, and atomic power we
are apt to forget that we depend upon God. We are in danger of saying
in our hearts "my power and the might of my hands hath gotten me this
wealth". It does us good to remember that we depend upon the unchangeable laws of God in all our enterprises. A humble acknowledgment of our dependence on Him is good for every one of us.
I believe walking with God includes a willing acceptance of God's
will even when it is contrary to our desires. Many want the Almighty
as an ally in their undertakings: they want God on _their side but never
inquire whether they are on God's side. They want to blueprint their

Our own poet Whittier writes:
"Who fathoms the eternal thought?
Who talks of scheme and plan?
The Lord is God, He needeth not
The poor device of man.
And in the maddening maze of things,
When tossed by storm and flood,
To one fixed ground my spirit clings;
I know that God is good!"
The poet walked with God in a great trust and found an inner resource of quiet strength. This inner resource has been enjoyed by many

CONTRIBUTIO NS TO LOCAL CHARITIES

Whereas practically every race, creed and color are represented in
this University. many of whom are friends of Masons or of children and
relatives of Masons.
Now therefore be it resolved that the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
p. & A. M. of California be and is hereby petitioned to consider the establishment of a club house, similar in form and character as those established at Berkeley and Los Angeles, at the campus of the University of
Hawaii in Honolulu, Hawaii.
•
Respectfully submitted, ,

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas our Tuolumne Lodge No. 8, a small Lodge situated in a
community where everyone knows his neighbor, is called upon from time
to time for contributions to various charities such as the American Red
Cross, the Salvation Army, the March of Dimes, the American Cancer
Society, the Tuberculosis Association, our Community Welfare campaign, and many others, and
Whereas our Tuolumne Lodge No. 8 is, we believe, in a similar situation with numerous other lodges, and
·
Whereas it is our desire to be able to make such contributions lawfully, which we are not able to do under present regulations,
Now Therefore, Be It Resolved that Section 159 of the Ordinances
be amended by adding thereto, after the words "fraternal intercourse,"
the following:
"and in its discretion, may expend a portion of said monies authorized by this Section, to make contributions to various local organizations
soliciting funds for charitable, general health and community welfare
purposes."
Done at our Stated Meeting, March 10, 1953.
ELMER R. MERRIHEW, Master

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At a regular Stated meeting of this Lodge held on the above date,

REPEALING TEN MILE RULE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
. ~hereas, It appears that the growth of our State and Grand Jurisdiction has brought about a condition wherein Section 218 of the Ordinances, dealing with our 10 mile law, is causing much confusion some
dissension, and a general misunderstand ing of it, and that the law is
no longer workable or desirable,
And Whereas, A study of Ross Digest will show such confusion and
misunderstand ing in many instances where this Grand Lodge has endeavored to clarify application of the law,
And Whereas, We feel that repeal of the law will be healthy for
Masonry by providing complete jurisdiction for constituent Lodges not
only over members and sojourners, but also over applicants for the degrees as well,
And Whereas, l£ found that repeal would cause hardship in some
isolated instance such could readily be rectified by the Grand Master and
Grand Lodge under the provisions of Section 217,
We therefore propose the following resolution and urge its adoption.
Resolved That: Section 218 of the Ordinances be, and the same is
hereby repealed.
That Section 212 be revised to read as follows: The jurisdiction of
a Lodge includes all its own members, wherever residing, and all
Mason~, and all applicants for the degrees residing nearer to its place
of meeting than to that of any other Lodge in this jurisdiction.
1

FRANK M. HARRINGTON, P.M.
Guy S. HARTS, SR., P .M.
Withdrawn by the sponsors with the consent of the Grand Master.

CONFI RMING IN THE MASON IC HOME S

TO THE PERMA NENT MASON IC HOME S
ENDOW MENT FUND
Whereas in 1909 Grand Lodge adopted the report of a special
committee on the Masonic Homes with a recommendation, among others,
for the creation of a "Perman ent Endowm ent Fund of the Masonic
Homes of Californ ia"; and
Wherea s in 1910 the fund was inaugura ted by the Board of Trustees
of Masonic Homes by combining its "Perman ent Improvement Fund"
with the amount of a bequest received that year from the Estate of
Brother Jacob Hart Neff: and
Whereas in 1919 the Masonic Homes of Californ ia were formed
into a charitabl e corporation with powers to take, receive, hold and
transfer in the name of the Masonic Homes of Californ ia title to real
and personal property howsoever acquired: and
Wherea s by the provisions of Sections 79 and 80 of the Ordinan ces
of Grand Lodge. the Trustees of that corporat ion are declared to be
the successors of the Trustees originally appointe d under the resolutions
adopted in 1892, and subseque ntly thereto; and there is vested in that
corporat ion the "title to all property, real and personal, and all rights
of action belonging to said charity, or to which it may in any way become
entitled" : and
Whereas the Grand Treasure r of Grand Lodge by virtue of his
office is also the treasurer of Masonic Homes of California, a Corpora tion, and as such has the custody of the Endowm ent Fund and all funds
of Masonic Homes of California; and
Wherea s an Endowm ent Board of Grand Lodge was establish ed
in 1933 consisting of 15 members represen ting the various Masonic
districts in Californ ia who are charged with the duty, among others,
of issuing appeals to the lodges and to Masons for contributions to
the Endowm ent Fund for the Masonic Homes of California: and that in
issuing these appeals the Endowm ent Board recommends certain forms
for gifts and bequests , and that in all of them it is suggeste d that the
gift or bequest be made to "Masoni c Homes of California, a Californ ia
corporation, to become a part of its Endowm ent Fund" and gifts and
bequests have been made directly to the Corporat ion, all of which has
resulted in unnecess ary confusion as to the ownersh ip of such funds:
and
Wherea s during the current year a bequest to "Masoni c Endowm ent
Fund of the Grand Lodge of Californ ia" was reported by an Inheritan ce
Tax Appraise r as taxable, as was also, in another case, a bequest to
"Masoni c Homes Endowm ent Board of the State of Californ ia"; and

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 335
( Submitted by Committee on Grievances )

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Resolved: That Section 335 of the Ordinances be amended to read
as follows:

For Fiscal Year Ending July 31, 1953

The penalties which may be inflicted are reprimand in open Lodge,
suspension or expulsion. If the sentence be reprimand, the Master shall
su~~on the adjudged to appear at the next Stated Meeting after the
dec1s1on by Grand Lodge affirming the judgment of the subordinate
~dge. If the sentence be suspension or expulsion, it shall at once go
mto effect, and the Secretary shall immediately notify the person suspended or expelled and the Grand Secretary thereof. If the penalty be
reprimand and the trial of the charges has been transferred by order of
the Grand Master, then the Grand Master may, after the announcement
. of the result of the trial, designate the Lodge in which the reprimand
shall be given; but in any event the Master who presided at the trial,
or such other person as the Grand Master may designate, shall deliver
the reprimand.
·
Approved by Committee on Jurisprudence.
Adopted by 5/6 vote.

. Telegrams and messages of congratulations wer~ received at different times during the Communication from Past Grand Master Samuel
E. Burke; C. A. Carlson, Jr., Past Grand Master of Nevada; the International Order of Jobs Daughters and from the Grand Lodge of Guatemala.
The Grand Secretary reported that by direction of the Grand Master he had forwarded telegrams to those Past Grand Masters of this
jurisdiction who had been prevented from attending the Communication.
The telegram to Past Grand Master. Earl Warren was worded as
follows:
"At its 104th Annual Communication the Grand Lodge of
California directed me to send its congratulations to you on your
appointment as Chief Justice of the United States and to wish
for you a long career of service to the nation in this capacity."

The Assistant Grand Treasurer renders this Annual Report for
and on behalf of the Grand Treasurer, M. W. Francis V. Keesling,
P. G. M., who unfortunately is incapacitated at the present time. Our
sincere and best wishes go out to him for his return to active service to
the Grand Lodge.
Detailed financial statements of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund and the Masonic Homes
of California are included in the Auditor's Reports, to which reference
is hereby made. Also included therein are complete lists of all securities
owned. These securities are all held in safe-keeping by the Trust Department of the Anglo California National Bank, at its main office in
San Francisco.
·
There is also appended at the end of this report as Exhibit AA, a
Consolidated Statement of Total Assets and Liabilities Under the Control of Grand Lodge, as of July 31, 1953.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge is composed of the
Grand Treasurer, the Assistant Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of the
Finance Committee, the President of the Masonic Homes Board of
Trustees or a Trustee of that Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment Boa'rd or a member of that
Board designated by him. The President of the Masonic Homes Board
of Trustees has designated Brother Past Master Ralph H. Head and
the Chairman of the Endowment Board has designated Brother Past
Master Cyril L. Weeks as members of the Committee. It is with deep
regret that we report the passing of Brother Past Master Charles E.
Moore, who was a highly valued member of this Committee, and who
had previously represented the Endowment Board.
Since the adoption of the Prudent Man Rule by Grand Lodge at its
Communication in 1950 the Investment Committee has met regularly
each three months, and between meetings has performed its duties by
mail or telephone. We have now started our fourth year of investments
under the Prudent Man Rule. By Ordinance, under Section 152.1, the
following provisions were established:
GROUP I. At least 40% of the funds available for investment
must be in:
A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions.
D) Such other securities as are legal investments for California
savings banks.
'

GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities
and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
B) Preferred Stocks, which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
GROUP III. Up to 40% may be invested in:
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that this listing
requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance company stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts. ·

At this point it should be mentioned that while the income on investments has risen from $120,598 on November 30, 1950 to $236,590
for the year just closed, a portion of this added income was made possible by contributions made to the principal of the Endowment Fund.
However, one true comparative figure can be used-namely, the percentage income as of November 30, 1950 was 1.97%. whereas as of
July 31, 1953 it was 3.21 % on the total market value, excluding the
$339,850 invested in Masonic Temple stock and the income thereon.
Nor is the income included from $339,675 of Series F bonds of various
maturities, on which interest is paid only at maturity, but these bonds
are included in the total value.
As of July 31, 1953, on the basis of book . value, or cost, the percentage of income on our total investments was 3.22%.

Our investments have continuous supervision by Moody's Investors
Service, and the members of the Committee are well pleased with their
services, represented by Mr. Richard T. Langan, Pacific Coast Manager, who has been faithful in attendance at meetings and most cooperative at all times.
Most Worshipful Arthur M. Warren, Grand Master, favored us
with his presence at the August 3, 1953 meeting of the Investment
Committee. Brother Past Master Ernest G; Bashor, Chairman of the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board, also attended this meeting.
In the past year a larger amount of cash than usual has been kept
in the banks because of the contemplated purchase of real estate for
the Masonic Memorial Temple.
As to Constituent Lodges, we have received the following report
from· Moody's Investors Service covering the period from December 1,
1951throughJuly31,1953:
"Report on Personal Management Service for Constituent Lodges
in California for Period December 1, 1951 to August 1, 1953.
"The volume of activity has increased in our work with the Lodges
on their investment portfolios, especially in the last eight months. In
the time from December 1, 1952 to August 1, 1953 there were 93 periodic reports prepareq reviewing the portfolios and suggesting changes
where advantageous. These periodic reports are those made subsequent to the original report. Since service started in December 1951
we have prepared and mailed 144 such reports. (Periodic after original reports). Of this total it is significant that 93 were in the last 8
months' period indicating a definitely increased volume. These reports include an analysis of the outlook. summary of the portfolio and specific
recommendations. ( 72 Original Reports, 144 Subsequent, Total 216.)
"Since inception of service 96 Lodges have made inquiry of us
concerning investments. The number making original inquiry as time
passes naturally tends to decline. However, in the latest period of 8
months some of the larger lodges have inquired and been reported on.
"The amount of funds supervised for the Lodges amounted to
$2,835,968.22 as of August 1, 1953. This shows an increase of about
$730,000 from a year earlier.
"Our original reports on Lodges resulted in decreased fixed income
items yielding little or no income such as cash and U. S. Savings Bonds
and in increased securities in Groups II and III giving much better
returns. In view of- our expectation as to the business and investment
outlook at the time of the first reports on most of the Lodges we suggested 20% (as against the maximum of 40%) be placed in Group
III. This resulted in increased income. In subsequent reports to the
Lodges we have been suggesting a further small increase in sound income producing stocks to 25%. This will give another bpost to their

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Twelfth Annual Report as your Grand Secretary.
LoDGES UNDER DISPENSATION

Lakewood Lodge U. D. and Verdugo Hills Lodge U. D. were both
instituted shortly before the close of the fiscal year.
Each of these Lodges collected but one month's dues during the
year, and at my suggestion the Grand Master directed they be not required to pay the per capita tax. It is respectfully requested that this be
approved.
SAFE KEEPING OF RECORDS

The Grand Secretary's office continues to microfilm all important
records. which are indexed and stored in the special vault at the Columbia Masonic Temple.
Two sets of the Proceedings of Grand Lodge are also kept in this
vault, as are many other valuable records. Additional records are being
moved there from time to time as circumstances permit.

UNFINISHED BUSINESS

The following matters were continued from the last Annual Communication to the present one:
1. Special Committee on Ceremonies re installation of Grand Lodge
Officers.
2. Discussion of Public Questions, page 319. 1952 Proceedings.
3. Plural Membership, legislation for, page 329, 1952 Proceedings.
4. Mandatory Proficiency, legislation for, page 332, 1952 Proceedings.
COMPENSATION INSURANCE

In accordance with the authorization issued at the last Communica. tion, and in conformity with the report and recommendations of the Special Gommittee, compensation insurance is now provided for all Lodges
and Grand Lodge carries the expense thereof. A detailed report will be
rendered by the Special Committee on Insurance.
. MEMBERSHIP

In presenting the membership totals for the year, I have shown the
years 1949, 1950, 1951, 1952 and 1953 with the thought in mind that our
experiences of these five years might be helpful in considering problems
relating to the proposed Memorial Temple.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The untimely passing of our late Grand Lecturer, Walter von
Konsky, last November, left your Ritual Committee as the youngest
in point of service on the committee since the institution of the present
system of ritual instruction in 1934.
It is only fair to say, however, that the Assistant Gra?d Lecturers
by their efforts and zeal have maintained a record of w~ich they can
justly be proud. They have given me the utmost cooperation and help,
as have the Inspectors throughout the jurisdiction.
Reports have been received from all the Inspectors, and with greater
promptness than ever before. These reports show that o~r lodges,
with a few exceptions, are in good condition, are busy with degree
work, and that their officers are proficient and are seriously concerned
with the work of Masonry.
It was my privilege to attend all of the Division Conferences of
Inspectors conducted by the Assistant Grand Lecturers, as follows:
Divisions 1 and 2, held at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 19.-21, 1953,
conducted by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell and Worshipful Ralph
M. Foote.
Division 3, held at Guerneville, May 1-3, 1953, conducted by Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn.
Division 4, held at Yosemite Valley, June 5-7, 1953, conducted by
Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor.
Division 5, held at Santa Barbara, April 24-26, 1953, conducted
by Worshipful Guy B. Mize.
Division 6, held at Del Mar, March 20-22, 1953, conducted by
Worshipful Augustus H. Allen.
At each of these conferences, the work of the three degrees was
performed by the Inspectors of the division, and the Inspectors and
Assistant Grand Lecturers are to be complimented on the excellent
work they are doing. The Grand Master was present at each of these
conferences, as was the Grand Secretary, and their .talks to the Inspectors
were of great interest. We were pleased to have m attendance at so?1e
of these meetings the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens. Out of a possible 145 Inspectors. only 8 were absent
from the conferences this year. Divisions 1 and 6 had perfect attendance records.
At four of these conferences the Ritual Committee held meeting.s
to consider various matters relating to uniformity of the work. In addition, a special meeting of the Ritual Committee was held in San Francisco on December 6 and 7. 1952, with all of the memb~rs of the
Committee present. The work of the three degrees was reviewed and

performed, and it is probably the first Ritual Committee in our history
to have the Grand Master acting as a candidate.
During the past year, the Monitor has been reprinted to correct
certain errors, and in particular to make corrections in the ceremony
of reception of Grand Lodge officers, which were made necessary by
changes in our law.
The Ritual Committee has received numerous proposals for changes
in the ritual. We have refused to endorse any of them, because we
feel that our present ritual needs no such improvements: and as custodians of the work it is our duty to preserve it as it was given to us;
and that the only changes which may be authorized by Grand Lodge,
under section 248 of the Ordinances, are "for the purpose of having it
remain as it was handed down from time immemorial."
From the reports of the Inspectors, it appears that in about twelve
districts the Inspectors have not made official visits in the manner prescribed by our Constitution. Section 53 provides that the Inspector
on his official visits shall be received with Grand Honors. In 1941 the
Grand Lecturer expressed the opinion that the reception of the Inspector
with Grand Honors is not optional. On the assumption that this requirement has been approved by Grand Lodge, it will be necessary for the
Inspectors to comply with it in all cases.
I have been greatly impressed with the work done by our Inspectors,
and by the countless hours they are devoting to Masonry. From the
reports submitted, I have estimated that in the course of their duties
including att~ndance at the Grand Lodge school of instruction, th~
Inspectors of this jurisdiction annually travel an aggregate of more
than 180,000 miles. This is in addition to some 40,000 miles traveled
by m~mbers of the Ritual Committee.
At the Grand Master's direction I made a two weeks' trip by air
to the Hawaiian Islands, conducting schools of instruction at Honolulu _
and in the lodges on the islands of Kauai, Maui and Hawaii. My findings
as to the situation concerning ritualistic instruction in the Islands have
been reported at length to the Grand Master. Briefly. it was my conclusion that we must provide additional instruction in order to maintain
the same uniformity and standard of ritual in the Islands as on the
mainland. and provide a closer contact between the Ritual Committee
and the Inspectors there. I found that the Inspector in Honolulu, Brother
Potts. was overloaded with administrative matters. The Grand Master
has in part corrected this situation by creating a new lnspectoral District.
numbered 386, to be composed of Kauai Lodge. on the Island of Kauai,
formerly in the 382nd District, and of Honolulu and Schofield Lodges,
formerly in the 384th District, with Robert Edgar presently Junior
Grand Steward, as the Inspector.
I must also state in all truthfulness that the reports as to the hospi.-

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER
ARTHUR M. WARREN, Grand Master

Once more we have assembled in Annual Communication to discuss
our problems and to review the p;ogress of Masonry in this great Jurisdiction. It seems incredible that one year has passed since we last met.
Time moves rapidly in this busy age, much faster than we realize. Since
last October it has been my honor · and privilege to preside over the
Craft in California, and I now present my final report. Whether my
stewardship has been properly discharged will be determined by you,
my brethren. As for me, I have enjoyed the greatest experience of my
life. The opportunity to travel throughout this great empire, to meet and
fraternize with the brethren, and to work with the leaders of our fra.
ternity has given me an education which could not be acquired in the
finest of universities. The fraternal affection displayed and the willing
assistance offered by the brethren will be remembered by me always and
I will be ever grateful for the privilege which has been accorded me.
During the past year I have been able to meet the brethren in practically every district in the Jurisdiction. This has been accomplished by
group district meetings, breakfasts, and other types of gatherings. •
For the record I have had 139 official meetings with a combined
attendance of over 53,000. In traveling about I have covered 42,800
miles: 27,000 by air, 15,000 by car and 800 by rail.

NECROLOGY
V. W. WALTER H. E. VoN KoNsKY

One of the first official acts of my year was the sad duty of conducting the funeral services of my dear friend and brother V. W. Walter
H. E. Von Kansky, Grand Lecturer. We had been friends for over
twenty years and our family ties were very close. Our working together
in Masonry side by side for all of those years made his passing one of
deep sadness. The sei;vices were conducted by Grand Lodge on November 5, 1952. To fill the vacancy made by his demise, I appointed W.
Elbert W. Davis, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 3. Bill, as he is
affectionately called, was also a close friend and confidant of Walter,
and I am certain that there will be no deviation from the high standards
set by our late brother Walter Von Konsky.
To fill the vacancy thus created in Division 3, W. Arthur J. Kahn
was advanced from Inspector of District 344 to Assistant Grand Lecturer.

Southern California Research Lodge reports:
Since the date of the institution of the Lodge on May 20, 1952,
we have held regular quarterly business meetings. No concerted attempt
has been made to recruit new members and the membership by the time
of the next annual Communication will be approximately thirty-five
members.
The interest of the members has seemed to center largely on panel
discussions and the Lodge has been invited to visit other Lodges or

Lodges, in other cases we have opened Lodges ourselves being sponsored by groups of Masons such as Officers Associations.

Northern California Research Lodge reports:
We were constituted on November 12, 1952, and started with 50
members. Since then we have added 21 affiliations and lost one for a
net of 70 members at this time.
While the majority of our members are in the Bay Area, we have
members in Bakersfield, Twain Harte, Nevada City, Sacramento,
Campbell, San Jose, Redding and Weaverville. Also Aptos, Martinez,
and Stockton.
·
We have held 3 stated meetings and attendance is above the usual
percentage.
We have held 5 informal meetings at which the subjects for essays
and papers are discussed and those which are ready are read and commented on.
We have conducted one program for a District meeting, one for
a Lodge, and have sent individual speakers to 7 meetings.
We have received inquiries and invitations for future District and
Lodge meetings for after the vacation month.
This year has been on a course toward gathering material. building
a library as it were, so we have not solicited invitations. Those that
have come were all from the Lodges directly. Our plan has been to
gather material so we would be prepared in future to respond to any
calls that may be received.
·
Following is a list of the essays and papers which we have and
those now being• worked on. A perusal of the subjects will show that
the larger part of them are concerned with factual material as distinguished from interpretation. We consider that for the present we
should avoid discussion of the meaning of our work or parts of it so
as to avoid impinging on the controversial.

Comment:
From the interest and enthusiasm shown thus far, I am persuaded
that the Research Lodges will prove worthy of their i:esponsibility. and
will ultimately fill a most important niche in our educational program.
In reviewing the legislation creating Research Lodges, an oversight
has been discovered. The regulations exempt them from the sections
of the law relating to applications for dispensations and charters. Likewise, their officers are exempt from the requirement of obtaining certificates of ritualistic proficiency, etc. Research Lodges are not required
to pay per capita taxes and by legislation have no responsibility for
the relief of its members or dependents.
In view of the latter, it is apparent that some consideration should
be given to our law relative to minimum dues as applied to them. Because
of the limited financial needs of Research Lodges, they have no reason
for accumulating large reserves.
I. therefore, recommend that section 150 (a) be amended by adding
the following:
17. Research Lodges shall be exempt from the minimum annual dues
requirement imposed by Section 251.

DEDICATIONS

NEW LoDGES INSTITUTED

Masonry is advancing with the growth of population in California,
and it is natural to assume that new settlements will seek to obtain
lodges to satisfy the urge to round out their community life. Masonic
Lodges, as well as Churches and Public Schools, have become a part
and parcel of the American scene and I am happy to state that we are
keeping pace with this trend.
Lodges have been instituted as follows:
December 16. 1952. Geo. E . Tutt Lodge, U.D .• Campbell:
January 16, 1953, Acalanes Lodge. U.D .• Lafayette:
January 16, 1953, San Ramon Valley Lodge, U.D .. Danville:
January 16, 1953, Saint John's Lodge, U.D .• Walnut Creek;
March 16, 1953, Yucaipa Lodge, U.D .• Yucaipa:
June 12. 1953, Verdugo Hills Lodge, U.D., Glendale:
June 20, 1953. Lakewood Lodge, U.D .• Long Beach:
August 7, 1953, Centennial Lodge, U.D .• Compton;
September 4, 1953, Polaris Lodge, U.D., Sacramento;
September 14, 1953, Two Rivers Lodge, U.D., Bell.
The joint institution ceremony on January 16, 1953 was an outstanding event in California Masonry. It is the first time in my memory
that more than one lodge was instituted at the same meeting. The
unusual feature , however, was the novel method of conducting that
' convocation. Eleven hundred and forty Master Masons assembled in

In February. in company with the Deputy Grand Master, the Grand
Secretary. and Past Grand Master John R. Moore, I attended the Grand
Masters' Conference of North America at Washington, D. C .• and
also the George Washington Memorial Association at Alexandria,
Virginia. Both meetings were productive of much good and the services
of Brother Wilson and Brother Moore for the Memorial Association
are proving invaluable to the Craft. In passing, it might be said that
our Grand Secretary is now one of the recognized leaders among the
Grand Secretaries of the United States. and his standing in that group
brings great credit to our own Grand Lodge.
One of the highlights of the Conference was the extension of work
begun at the 1952 Conference. At that meeting, a "Commission on
Information for Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges" was created:
and your Grand Master, who was then Deputy Grand Master, was
elected to a six year term on the Commission. Much valuable information has been collated and is now available to the various Grand Lodges
for their use. At the 1953 meeting, the Commission elected me to the
office of Treasurer, and it will be my pleasure to serve them in that
capacity for the balance of the term.
In addition to the work of the conference, it was the pleasure of
our group to entertain three distinguished Californians, in company
with their wives. On the Monday evening preceding the Conference,
the two Senators from California and the Vice-President of the United
States were our guests at dinner. We found Senator Knowland, Senator Kuchel, and Vice-President Nixon, and their charming wives, to
be truly representative Californians and worthy of their positions of
trust in the Government.

Commission on Revision of Ross Digest
For many' years, we have been using the Ross Digest aa the baaia of
our CaliE.mia Ma80nic Law. Thia monumental work, created by Put
Grand Muter John Stewart Rosa,
given invaluable aufata.nce to
thole who are required to adminiater our MuonJc: Code.
It la appare:nt, however, to many that an Improvement in induhl9,
u well as a clatiftcation and consolidation of edfcta, etc.. should H
made. In recent years, oth~ Grand Lodge! have made great strides in
modernizing the presentation of their Masonic Codes.
·
The law should be considered by practical lawyers as well·as laymen
who are familiar with the continuing problem of Masters and others who
do not have legal training.
Accordingly, I have created a Commission for the purpose of study,
with the objective of presenting to Grand Lodge an acceptable revision
of the Ross Digest. It is, of course, a program which may require several
years of careful and thoughtful attention. I discussed the program with
the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Wardens, and they are in full
accord.
Judge Arthur Paulsen, P.G.M., has agreed to accept t~e Chair~an­
ship, and he is well qualified to undertake the task. He will be assisted
by William Nankervis, Jr., a lawyer and for many years the reporter of
the California State Supreme Court. The third member is P.G.M. Lloyd
E. Wilson, Grand Secretary, who perhaps knows better than any other
Mason in California how complex and confusing our law appears to be
in the minds of our Lodge officers. His daily work and experience makes
him eminently qualified to assume the layman's part of this important
undertaking.
This Commission will make a preliminary report during this Communication, and I heartily recommend the continuance of the Commission
for the ensuing Grand Lodge year.

WoRKMENs COMPENSATION INSURANCE

At the 1952 Communication, the Finance Committee recommended
that the incoming Grand Master appoint a Special Committee on Insurance to investigate the effectiveness and adequacy of Public Liability and
other insurance coverage of Grand Lodge and the Constituent Lodges.
In connection with Workmens Compensation Liability, it suggested
that, should the Special Committee's recommendation meet with the

to purchase such W orkmens Compensation coverage as in their Judgment might be required and desirable.

August 1st, 1953.

RELIEF TO GRAND LoDGE OP THE NETHERLANDS

We are all familiar with the disaster which struck the west coast 0£
Europe and the British Isles with such devastation last January and
February. Upon receipt of the news, the Grand Secretary dispatched
cables to the United Grand LOdge of England and also to the Grand
Lodge of the Netherlands offering our fraternal assistance. Our Brethren in England gratefully acknowledged our offer, but declined to accept
assistance. The Brethren in the Netherlands, however, were not situated
as fortunately and expressed their need for help. After consultation
With the Elective Grand Lodge Officers and the Chairman of our Finance
Committee, I approved the contribution of $2500 for the relief of the
Lodges and brethren of the Grand Lodge of the Netherlands.
HAWAIIAN loDGES

One of the memorable events in a Grand Master's year is his offtclal
trip to the Islands of Hawaii. My experience in this instance was most
pleasant and, of course, educational and informative.
Prom the time Mrs. Warren, myself, and our daughter Barbara
arrived, and until we departed, we were constantly in the hands of
friends who did their utmost to make our stay pleasant and comfortable.

It would be impossible to list everyone who contributed to our happiness. To do so would require the publishing of the entire roster of
membership in the Islands. Special thanks, however, should go to the
two Inspectors, Doug Potts and Gene Jijine, and their delightful wives
who planned every moment for us. Likewise, the Masters of the Lodges
·who, together with their lovely ladies, contributed so much to our joy
and comfort.
Ofllcial meetings were held .as follows:
May 7 Scliofleld Lodge, No. H3

ln addition, we had an opportunity to visit with individual Lodge
groups through the medium of dinner parties and other gatherings.
The Lodges in Hawaii are in excellent condition, the spirit of Masonry is ft.rm, and the leadership· is in good hands.
Attendance at their meetings is above average and the support given
to the various activities of Masonry is remarkable.
The Lodges had just. completed their Public Schools week program
and all reported favorably in that connection. It is interesting to note
that several Island Lodges make the Public Schools observance a continuing one from month to month, climaxing with the ofllcial observance
in April. For this they are to be commended most highly.
Too much praise cannot be given to our Lodges in Hawaii for their
outstanding support of our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. During
my stay, I noted particularly the deep interest of the brethren in the
Homes program. I am happy to report that every Lodge in Hawaii went
over their quota, and will appear on the Honor Roll. This is particularly
gratifying when we consider that perhaps one third of their members
are scattered over the four comers of the globe.
I discussed a number of pertinent subjects during my visit and, as
a result, I make the following recommendations.

Upon his return we considered their problems very carefully, and as a
result, I have appointed an additional Inspector to serve the Islands.
Kauai Lodge No. 589 has been transferred to a new District to be numbered 386 together with Honolulu Lodge No. 409 and Schofield Lodge
No. 443. Brother Robert Edgar, Officers' Coach of Honolulu Lodge No.
409, and who is presently serving as Junior Grand Steward, has been
highly recommended and he has agreed to accept this new responsibility.
. For many years in the past, the Grand Lecturer made a trip to the
Islands to conduct special Schools of Instruction for the Lodges. Since
the death of Thomas J. Baker in 1934, the Grand Lecturer has visited
the Islands only twice. Once in 1946 and again this year. I recommend
that at least once every four years the Grand Lecturer, or an Assistant
Grand Lecturer designated by him, visit the Island Lodges to give
ritualistic instruction to the brethren.
This is a matter which requires proper budgeting and, I request that
the visitations be made a matter of continuing policy and not subject to
a Grand Master's order.
'
Second, Grand Secretary's Visitation
Each year the Grand Secretary. or the Assistant Grand Secretary,
travels about the jurisdiction to discuss with the Lodges, and the Secretaries, matters of Lodge administration and other important business.
The visitations are becoming more valuable as time goes on and it has
become an accepted, as well as a desirable practice. The Lodges in
Hawaii have not had a visitation from the Grand Secretary in over 30
years. I perhaps could have approached the matter in the same way
that I did with the Grand Lecturer. However, I feel that the desirability
of having the Grand Secretary visit the Island Lodges is a matter for
Grand Lodge itself to determine.
I therefore recommend that the Grand Secretary, or at his direction,
the Assistant Grand Secretary, should visit the Island Lodges at least
once every 10 years. Further, that the trip be made at his convenience
and at a time which will not conflict with a visitation of either the Grand
Master or the Grand Lecturer. I likewise suggest that the visitation also
be made a matter of continuing policy and not subject to the order of
the Grand Master.

First, Ritual
The Lodges on the Islands are remotely situated insofar as receiving
ritualistic instruction is concerned. Because of my long association in
this field, I am convinced that we should make a greater effort to assist
the Island brethren in their desire to keep the high ritualistic standards
which our Grand Lodge has always maintained. At my request, V. W.
Elbert W. Davis, Grand Lecturer, made a special visit to the Hawaiian
Islands in August, and conducted a series of Schools · of Instruction.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Hawaii is now, and has been for many years, an integral component
part of our Grand Lodge. Nevertheless, no adequate method has been
devised to administer the Island Lodges.
· A number of ideas have been presented, the latest in 1942, when it
was suggested that a Deputy Grand Lecturer be appointed to ~andle
the ritual and other activities of the Lodges. This was not considered
adequate at the time.
Irrespective of the speed of communication, our Lodges in Hawaii
still feel that they are a long way from the seat of government and that
they have been somewhat neglected.
The Grand Lodge of England, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts,
and ethers, have systems which give a limited amount of home rule, and
yet hold their Lodges closely to home ties. A similar system could be
euily developed and would accomplish the objective.
The majority of our brethren are perhaps not aware of the fact that
on several occasions the brethren of Hawaii have considered forming
their own Grand Lodge. The latest of these meetings to consider such
•
a matter was held on November 20, 1952.
I feel that if we value our ties to Hawaii, we should do something
tQ demonstrate in a concrete manner our affection for them.
The establishment of the office of District Deputy Grand Master
would accomplish such a purpose. The holder of that office could be
a creation of the Grand Master, holding such prerogatives and privileges as might be given to him by the Grand Master. Certain types of
dispensations and other matters ordinarily handled by the Grand Master
or the Grand Secretary could be delegated to him. This will relieve the
Inspectors in the Hawaiian Islands of the heavy administrative work
which accrues to them because of their distance from the Mainland. The
District Deputy Grand Master would have no jurisdiction over the
.ritualistic activities of the Inspectors, who would be entirely responsible
to the Grand Lecturer for that portion of their duties. His work would
still require a review and approval by the Grand Master or the Grand
Ledge at least annually. This would put a proper control over his
activities.
There should be no increase in our ordinary expenses because, up
to this year, we have always appointed a brother from Hawaii to th~
appointive line of officers in the Grand Lodge. The District Deputy
Grand Master could easily take the place of that appointment. This
would keep the mileage payment in line and yet give our brirthren in
.
Hawaii a Grand Lodge Officer worthy of consideration.
Accordingly, I recommend the · addition of the following to our
organic law:
Add Section 52ATbe Grand Master shall appoint, for the Hawaiian Islands, a
District Deputy Grand Master, who shall be a past master of this juris-

diction, resident in the Hawaiian Islands. The District Deputy Grand
Master shall perform such duties appertaining to his office as may be
required of him by the Grand Master, except that he shall have no
supervision over the ritualistic duties of the Inspectors.

USE OF loDGE FUNDS

Public Schools Week
Reports indicate that the 34th Annual Observance of Public Schools
Week was highly successful. It is apparent that there is an increasing
interest in ·t he Public Schools, our great American Heritage. The Committee, of course, will make a full and complete report of its activities
during this Communication.
There is a matter in this connection, however, which in my opinion,
needs adjustment. Each year, successive Grand Masters issue proclamations, proclaiming the week, calling upon the Masons for support,
ftqulring Lodges to remain dark, and to confine their activities to the
Promotion of the Schools Week Program. Lodges are called upon to
IUpport financially the program, and in most instances a very splendid
Job is performed. It seems unreasonable to me to require Lodges to
.lnancially support this work, which is a Grand Lodge activity, and yet
~-be required ay our law to defray the expenses out of refreshment
auuds.

i..To correct this inequity, I recommend the repeal of Section No. 637,
U1cb has to do with the expenditure of Lodge funds in connection

with Public Schools Week. In lieu thereof, I recommend the adoption
of the following amendment to Section No. 157:
Add to Section No. 157The expenditure of funds for any program required by the Grand
Lodge, or the Grand Master, .shall be deemed to be a part of the necessary expenses of the Lodge.

Contributions made in conformity to Section No. 158 are exempt
from Edict No. 718.
This would permit Lodges to contribute to the Homes Endowment
Fund in lieu of flowers, but would still control the contribution of
Lodge Funds in violation of the spirit of Section No. 718.

Proficiency Certificates in Third Degree
All brethren are encouraged to attain proflciency in the Candidates
Lecture of the Master Mason Degree, and in token of such proflciency.
certiflcates are awarded to those who do so. Here again, the Lodge is
required to charge such an expense to the refreshment fund, which is
an imposition upon the Lodge.
I recommend the repeal of Section No. 634 , which requires this
charge.
Trowels to Newly Raised Masons
· This is also a matter which is in keeping .with the highest Masonic
Tradition, and should be encouraged. This item likewise is charged
to the refreshment fund under our law.
I recommend the repeal of Section No. 637, which requires this
charge.
Endowment Fund
The development of our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund is one
of our greatest endeavors. Each year we exert every effort consistent
with Masonic limitations to expand this great Charity.
Many years ago, Grand Master Gist wisely ruled that Lodges
should not contribute to the Endowment Fund, holding that this was
a voluntary effort on the part of the individual. and not on the part of
the Lodge. In this, I heartily .concur.
The passage of time, however, has created a situation which needs
correction. In recent years it has been customary on the part of many,
to make contributions to worthy charities in lieu of floral offerings for
deceased persons. Likewise, many bereft families have made the same
request. There is no rule of reason that should prohibit such a practice
on the part of our Lodges. Under our present regulations, a Lodge is
prohibited from doing so. even if the family makes such a request. I
have reason to believe that contributions are being made in violation
of our regulations. This matter could be easily controlled, and rightfully so, by the adoption of the following addition to Section No. 158.
Add to Section No. 158In lieu of a floral piece for the deceased person, a contribution may
be made to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
To keep Section No. 718 intact, the following Section No. 718a
should be added.
Add Section No. 718a-

COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS

One of our most valuable and active committees is the Committee
on Charters. It was originally created to review the activities and
workings of Lodges operating under dispensation. Since 1947 its
activity has been increased tremendously. Past Grand Master Chester
H. Warlow assigned to the committee the responsibility of accumulating information and other data not ordinarily furnished by the Inspector in connection with requests for Dispensations for new Lodges.
It is true that the procedure outlined in our law does not contemplate
such a program. However, succeeding Grand Masters have found
their work invaluable.
This year with the granting of ten Dispensations, it would have
been a very difficult task to obtain the facts which were compiled by
the committee. The reports presented are comprehensive and cover
population, character and growth of community, Masonic population,
experience of other Lodges in area, composition of new group and other
pertinent data.
It is obvious, with the growth of our State, that new Lodges will
continue to be formed. At least a dozen Masonic Clubs are now functioning with the purpose of eventually applying for Dispensations.
To round out more fully the committee and to lighten its burden,
I suggest the expansion of the committee from seven to nine. In this
way greater geographic distribution of its membership can be obtained.
I therefore recommend the amendment of Section 70 by adding to
line three following the words, "on Lodge Financing," these words,
"on Charters," and deleting from line four following the words, "Pay
of Members," these words, "on Charters."

GRAND LoDGE REPRESENTATIVES

Article II, Section 12 requires the Grand Master to appoint Representatives near other Grand Lodges. and to receive and accept Representatives from them.
This section of our law has not been observed to the extent that it
was originally intended.
In early years. the Grand Representatives were actually ambassadors
who carried- on the work of communicating with other Grand Lodges,
reviewing their proceedings, and performing other assigned duties.
They were received annually at the Grand Lodge, accorded certain
honors, and were required to report as to their activities.
The dianging tempo of time, the rapid system of communication,
the close personal ties of the various Grand Secretaries and Grand
Masters through conferences, and the creation of Committees to review
proceedings, has made this position an appendage which amounts to
a position of honor without duty.
I make no recommendation regarding this section, but request that
our Committee on Policy and General Purposes study the matter in
order that our Grand Lodge may pursue a policy which will be in keep ..
ing with today's requirements and which will enable future Grand
Masters to carry out the will and pleasure of the Grand Lodge.

" ( 1) In investing, reinvesting, purchasing, acquiring, exchanging.

with the power to acquire, mortgage, sell and convey property and to
invest and reinvest its funds; or, it may through trustees provided for
in a standing resolution, iwhc shall always be under its control, hold,
mortgage. sell and othe?Wise. dispose of its property and funds. which
may be invested and reinvested as the Lodge shall direct.
DECISION No. 2

I was asked the following question:
"May there be presented posthumously to the family a Fifty Year
Button?"
The ans~er is "NO."
The Fifty Year Veteran Button is intended for the member by
whom it was earned and not as a memento to the family. Section
658, 658(a) R.D.
DECISION No. 3

I was asked the following question:
"An applicant for affiliation presented to a Lodge his receipt for
dues paid three months in advance, together with a request for a dimit
to his old Lodge. The request for the dimit was lost in transit. A
quarterly period for payment of dues has elapsed in the interim.
"Should the brother be required to bring his dues to date in the old
Lodge before the issuance of a dimit?"
The answer is "YES." (Sec. 250 R._D.)
The applicant would not be entered as a member of the new Lodge
until there was presented a Dimit from the old Lodge. Consequently.
there is no reason why the member should be excused from paying
dues during the intervening period.

"Whether a son of a Past Master who is confined in a mental institution may present a request of a Dimit in order to prevent the accrual
of dues which his father is unable to pay?"
The answer is that the lodge should remit the dues of the Past
Master as one who is unable to pay them. (Section 255, R.D.)

DECISION No. 5

DECISION No. 8

I was asked the following question:
"Whether a lodge on a social occasion may distribute by chance
selection merchandise awards or premiums?"
The answer is "NO."
The circuDlStances presented may be on the legal borderline but
the fact remains that the distribution of the merchandise awards or
premiums is by chance selection rather than by the employment of
skill. Consequently, it appears to be in violation of both civil and
Masonic law, or so nearly so as to call for its elimination as a matter
of policy.
It would be against the spirit, if not the letter, of Section 288 R.D.
See also Section 740 R.D. and Section 319 Penal Code of California.

I was asked the following question:
"Is an applicant who was convicted by general court martial of
desertion in 1930, served a year, and was dishonorably discharged from
the Army, eligible to receive the degrees of Masonry?"
The answer is "NO."
Desertion from the Army may be punished by confinement in a
penitentiary. ( 1928 Manual for Courts-Martial United States Army,
Sec. 90). Such desertion may be punished by confinement in excess of
one year. ( 1928 Manual for Courts-Martial United States Army,
Sec. 104-c). An offense which is punishable by imprisonment for a
term exceeding one year is a felony. (Title 18, U. S. Code Annotated,
Sec. 1 ).
Hence it is apparent that such desertion is similar to a State court
conviction for felony and that the applicant is not under the tongue of
good report and that his petition should not be received. (Sec. 875 R.D.)

DECISION No. 4

DECISION No. 6

I was asked the following question:
"What corrective action may an Inspector take in respect of officers
who fail or refuse to attend meetings of Officers' Associations, or who
do not possess the requisite administrative ability for advancement?"
It is the duty of the Inspector to require attendance of officers at
meetings of the Officers' Associations: likewise, it is part of the duties
of the officers to attend. (Sec. 53, 865 R.D.) If the offending officer
is one who requires a certificate of advancement, then the Inspector
may withhold such certificate. If such officer is one who does not require
a certificate for advancement, the Inspector should request the Master
to remove the offending officer and appoint another in his place. Failure
of a Master to accede to such request of the Inspector, or if the Master
be the offender, would subject the Master to removal by the Grand
Master. (See Sec. 856, R.D.)
Similar action may be taken in respect to officers who are incapable
·of performing efficiently the administrative duties. (Sec. 53, R.D.)

DECISION No. 9

I was asked the following question:
"Does a circular announcement by the Insurance Square Club of
tile East Bay, apparently mailed by first class mail to its members, and
notifying them that an applicant and member was to receive the Third
Degree of Masonry. violate Masonic Law?"
The answer is "YES."
The information thus sent through the mails may well come into
the hands of non-Masons, plus published information which should
be kept within tiled precincts of Lodges. (Sec. 696. 697 R.D.)

DEc1s10N No. 12

"May a Lodge invest more than 20% of its funds in the second
category of permissible investments. prescribed by Section 152.1 R.D .•
if the Lodge has not invested 40% thereof in the third category?"
The answer is "NO.''
The li~itations prescribed for the second and third categories of
permissible investments must be adhered to in all cases. The law does
not, expressly or by reasonable implication, authorize the investment
of.lodge funds in excess of the percentages stated for the second - a~d
third categories even though the Lodge has not invested up to said
prescribed limit in one or the other of the said second and third categories. Of course, with reference to the first category, 4?% of t~e
lodge funds must be so invested and up to 100% may be invested m
the said first category.
DECISION No. 13

I was asked the following question:
"Where a Lodge has invoked Article IV, Section 2, of Section
133 R.D .• in respect of an applicant who has failed to come forth for
initiation or to present himself properly qualified for the Second or
Third Degrees, is this a denial of advancement by action of the Lod~e
so as to require, after proper presentation, a refund of the applicant s
contributions for Masonic Homes of California and for the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial?"
The answer is "YES.''
Section 100 R.D. expressly provides:
"If an applicant shall die before being raised or be elected to membership in another Lodge beyond this jurisdiciton un~er a dimit issued
by his Lodge, or shall be denied advancement by action of the Lodge,
the fact shall be certified to the Grand Secretary by the Secretary of
the Lodge and the Grand Secretary shall thereupon cause the con-

tribution to be returned to the Lodge, which shall thereupon refund
the payment to the widow or representative of the deceased applicant.
or to the applicant himself as the case may be. ( 1950)."
. It will be observed from reading the Section quoted that the obligation on Grand Lodge to return the applicant's said contributions does
not depend upon whether the Lodge has or has not refunded his "fees.''
Hence, when an applicant is denied advancement and the Secretary
of ~he Lodge so certifies to the Grand Secretary. the Grand Lodge is
obligated to return to the Lodge the contributions for refund to the
applicant. This is so whether or not "the Lodge shall otherwise direct"
in respect of the fees retained by the Lodge. Such fees are separate

from such contributions (Sec. 629, 721-A, R.D.)
DEc1s10N No. 14
I was asked the following questions:
" ( 1 ) Does membership in the Communist Party constitute unmasonic
conduct: and
" ( 2 ) May such a member be tried therefor if the Lodge membership was obtained after his Communistic membership had ceased?"

The answer to each question is "YES.''
Membership in the Communist Party is in an organization which
act;vely advocates the overthrow of our Government by force and violence and teaches hatred of God and forms of .religion. There should
l·e no quibbling about this definition. Recent world-wide developments
tnrnish adequjlte demonstration.
Moreover, Past Grand Master, Randolph V. Whiting. in 1935,
with prophetic foresight stated the case against Communism at pages
408, et. seq .• 1935 Grand Lodge proceedings. when he said this in his
annual message:
."The objects and purposes of this organization are so fundamentally
anti-Masonic, and so contrary to the spirit and genius of our government and our religious and social institutions, that I have deemed it not
only a proper subject for presentation in Lodges, but as imposing an
absolute obligation on every Mason in this jurisdiction to advise himself
as fully as possible with reference to it, and to use every legitimate and
lawful means to prevent the spread of its influence and teaching."
Loyalty to the government in whose domain the Mason resides is
an indispensable requisite. See the old York Constitutions of 926,
· Par. 14: the Constitutions of Edward III, Par. 4: the charges approved
in 1722, Part II; Pages 579 and 582 Ross Digest ( 1952).
The said charges approved in 1772, Part II, state that the member
a
of lodge may not be expelled for disloyalty to his government, but
being charges, and not landmarks, that provision is subject to change
