84

and amendment. Under the Masonic law as it exists in our Grand
Jurisdiction, the member is subject to disciplinarian action and expulsion.
For example, declaring an unbelief in God is a Masonic o~ense
and renders the lodge member subject to expulsion. Sections 724, 208.
868-870, Ross Digest.
With respect to the question of whether the membership in the
Communist Party anti-dated the lodge membership (a question dubious
of proof) it is clear under our Masonic law that a Mason may be tried
for offenses committed before initiation. Section 753 Ross Digest.
Moreover, knowing the tactics of Communists, it would seem that you
could not take the word of a person that he had renounced Communism
unless the most cogent proof was abduced.
.
Consequently. for the reasons stated and under the circumstances
presented, the lodge member may be tried and expelled.
DECISION No. 15

I was asked the following question:
"In the event there is a profit on a sale of securities held for life
memberships. should this profit be treated as income for use by the
Lodge as a part of its general fund?"
The answer is "NO."
.
Such a profit is actually an increment of the corpus of the life membership fund, which is a trust, the income only of which may ·be used
for lodge purposes. Sec. 153, R.D.
It should be home in mind that the life membership fund could
decrease as well as increase by the sale of securities. Also, that stock
dividends of such securities are treated as constituting a corpus of the .
trust and not as cash dividends. The "income" referred to Section 153
means interest or cash dividends which may revert to the general fund
of the lodge. The corpus of the life membership fund. or trust, would
include any profit realized on a sale, as being part of the "amounts
paid for life memberships'' and as part of the "original amounts to be
forever kept and maintained as and for a permanent life membership
.fund.'' See · Act. 8696. Sec. 3, Deering General Laws. Principal &
Income Act.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

the brethren of our Lodges scattered throughout our great Jurisdiction
have made my work easy.
My especial thanks go to those brethren who provided for my transportation and comfort during my travels throughout the state. To name
them all would be difficult, and I would dislike to overlook anyone. Consequently. they must remain anonymous.
I would be remiss also if I did not express my appreciation to the
very efficient staff of the Grand Lodge Office, who have been so considerate and thoughtful during the many years that it has been my
privilege to be associated with them. These words are inadequate to
repay them for the fine service which they have given.
During the year just closed I have been privileged to discuss Masonry with a great j!Umber of brethren and on many levels.
Early this year, I had a visit from R. W. W. P. Schetelig, Senior
Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge of the Philippines. We talked
about his experiences in the outer provinces of that great country and
how Masonry has captured the hearts and minds of the people of the
Philippines. We discussed the growth of Masonry in Japan and how,
at last, the leaders of that country were taking the vows of our Craft.
He had a vision of the spread of Masonry through the Islands of the
Pacific, in Indonesia and across to India - that great country just
awakening into a new place in the world: a great ring of Brotherhood
surrounding the. world enclosed by the Iron Curtain of godless Soviet
Russia.
At the Grand Masters' conference, the M. W. Theodore Vogel
told us of the reconstruction of the old Grand Lodges of Germany into
a new Unified Grand Lodge. The M. W. Jaime Granados, Grand
Master of Costa Rica, gave us the story of the craft in his land. We
heard from the representatives of several Mexican Grand Lodges, from
Argentina, and other lands, all testifying to the slow, but constant,
growth of Masonry in countries which are gradually awakening to our
tenets and principles.
For several years it has been my privilege to count as friends my
Masonic brethren who brought into being the Grand Lodge of Chinanot yet recognized by us. Their devotion to Masonry cannot be questioned, because it is genuine.
Last March, at my reception in San Diego, the Grand Master of
Baja California, and his entourage of Grand Officers and Past Grand
Masters, extended to our Grand Lodge the fraternal greetings and
felicitations of our Mexican brethren just south of our border.
I am narrating this to indicate the growing prestige of Masonry
and the unification of all nationals and races into one Great Brotherhood.
The climax w~s reached on August 21. 1953 when an American of
Japanese ancestry was raised to the sublime Degree of Master Mason

in one of our Lodges. The degree was conferred upon the brother by
the Senior Warden of his Lodge-a brother of Chinese ancestry. A
large number of Grand Lodge officers and Inspectors were present, and
it was my privilege to extend to him the Right Hand of Fellowship.
My experiences through the year convince me more vividly than
ever of the Destiny of our Great Fraternity.
Men of faith drawn together in good works by the bonds of Brotherhood, under the Fatherhood of God, can and will lead the world out of
chaos and the morass. which seems to now engulf us. Let us renew our ·
solemn obligations and rededicate ourselves to the great purposes which
bind us together.
May the blessing of Heaven rest upon us all regular Masons! May
1'r<tth.erly Love prevail, and every moral and social virtue cement us!
Amen!

November 20. 1952
EXHIBIT "A"

To the Lodges of this Jurisdiction.
Brethren:
The subject of so..called Masonic Publications caused prolonged
debate and discussion at the last Communication of Grand Lodge.
In view of the intense interest in this question, it becomes necessary
to review certain phases of the matter.
The Committee on Publications presented a factual report which
was received and filed. This report covered the activities of the Com·
mittee and outlined its procedure· and methods.
The Grand Master, in his message. referred to the subject under
Decision and Recommendations No. 44. The Committee on Segregation recommended that this Decision and Recommendation be referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported as follows:
"This ruling contains no decision of law requiring action by the
Committee." This was signed by Brothers Dayton, Moore, Lawler,
Taylor, Jones and Paulsen for the Committee.
In our opinion, the matter is now in the hands of the Grand Master
under the same conditions as existant one year ago.
In light of the temper of the discussion, and the evident interest of
the bre~hren,some modification is desirable without emasculating the law.
It is our opinion (not concurred in by some) that news bulletins or
trestleboards containing dates of meeting and other general information
fall into the category of general news, and no undue harm would come
to Masonry should such information be found in so-called Masonic
periodicals. Likewise, the listing of Lodge officers and places of meeting
occupies a similar position. We all agree, however, that official notices
and matters of information which concern only the Members of the
Lodge should be withheld from public knowledge. The matter of the
use of rosters and Lodge funds is fully covered in our law, and no
relaxation of this condition should prevail.
Another matter which needs consideration is the use of publications
for <:haritable purposes. It seems desirable and proper that publications .
whose entire proceeds are devoted to charity, and which are now banned
under the existing regulations of the Publication Committee, should
have some relief.
After much contemplation, the following rule would seem to be
entirely within the framework of the law.
Publications whose sole purposes are for charitable assistance shall
present to the Grand Master their source of revenue and list all expenses
smd items expended for promotion. The Grand Master may, in such

89

cases. grant sanction upon the condition that the net proceeds of the
publication, after allowing reasonable expense and promotion, shall be
delivered to the charity in who~e name the publication has been published.
This rule would allow certain publications who have always operated
on an ethical basis to continue their very fine contribution to humanity.
Some <:hanges will be noted in the ·personnel of the Committee on
Publications.
M. W. John R. Moore, P.G.M .• who served as Chairman . during
the formative years of the Committee, and who has given immeasurably
of his time, ·has requested to be relieved from further service because of
the press of other Masonic duties. We are indebted to Brother Moore
for his work, and we regret that we must function in this endeavor
without his earnest and truly Masonic guiding spirit.
Likewise. W. Newcomb Condee has asked to be relieved for similar
reasons. Like Brother Moore, Brother Condee has been with this Committee since its inception and his services are, of course. deeply appreciated.
THIS IS A STATEMENT OF GENERAL POLICY ONLY,
and no action whatever is to be taken by the Lodges until after the
Committee on Publications has set out in detail the procedures which
may be followed under it.
I have appointed the following Committee who will put into proper
form the modifications which I have outlined, and which will be in effect
until they are repealed or modified.
James F. Dougan, Chairman, 4210 Linden Ave., Long Beach
Arthur W. Brouillet, 1114 Humboldt Bank Bldg., San Francisco 5
Arthur S. Crites, 1001 Oleander Street, Bakersfield.
Laurence E. Dayton, 1832 Magellan Drive, Oakland 11
J. Everett Houser, 814 Security Bldg., Long Beach 2

February 15, 1953

To the Lodges of this Jurisdiction.
Brethren:
Under date of November 20, 1952, the Most Worshipful Arthur
M. Warren. Grand Master, issued a circular letter containing his statement of general policy on the subject of so-called "Masonic Publications" and appointing the undersigned committee to outline the procedures which will be followed to put the policy into effect.
Pursuant to that authority and with the approval of the Grand
Master the special committee on publications hereby establishes the
following regulations to take effect forthwith:
( 1 ) The express sanctions heretofore granted certain publications
are modified to permit the publication of news bulletins or trestleboards
containing dates of meeting, other general information, lists of Lodge
officers and places of meeting in accordance with the Grand Master's
circular letter of November 20, 1952. and not otherwise.
(2) New regulations have been set up under which the owners.
publishers or sponsors of so-called Masonic Publications may apply for
the express sanction described in Section 127 of the Ordinances under
the modified policy established by the Grand Master. They relate to
periodicals such as monthly magazines and occasional publications such
as programs for charitable purposes. Information will be sent upon
request }:,y the Grand Secretary, 25 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco 2,
California.
( 3) Application for approval under the new regulations must be on
flle with the Grand Secretary on or before June 1, 1953: otherwise any
and all previous sanctions. approvals or statements issued to publications
will on said date expire and terminate without further action.
( 4) Your attention is invited to the fact that neither the Grand
Master's circular nor this letter has altered existing prohibitions on the
acceptance of advertising in Lodge bulletins or trestleboards. the use
of Lodge funds for the assistance or remuneration of Masonic publications. the release of Lodge rosters. official notices of a confidential nature.
or names and addresses of old or new members for solicitation purposes.
( 5) Section 127 of the Ordinances remains in full force and effect.
It provides as follows:
"No Lodge or member of a Lodge. without the express sanction of
Grand Lodge. shall solicit. sponsor. insert. place or print advertising of
any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to be
Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body.
order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to
membership.••

( 6) The general purpose of the new regulations is to permit the
continued operation of those Masonic publications which handle their
advertising and editorial policy in an ethical manner and so as to avoid
scandal or reproach to the Craft. Your Committee is reasonable but
not disposed to leniency toward violators and we will appreciate receiving information on any infractions of the law which may occur.
It is our suggestion that this letter be read at your next Stated
Meeting.
Fraternally yours.
SPECIAL CoMMIITEE oN PUBLICATIONS

James F. Dougan. Chairman
Arthur W. Brouillet
Arthur S. Crites
Laurence E. Dayton
J. Everett Houser

LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary

To the Inspectors of the Jurisdiction:
During the Communication just closed, I bad hoped to have an
opportunity to meet with you at your School of Instruction. Due to the
press of business. I was unable to be present.
I have a few matters which are of common interest to each of us
and upon which I solicit your assistance.

New Lodges

To the Inspectors, Masters, Wardens and Brethren of the Jurisdiction:
An increasing number of violations of Sections 78 and 152 of the
Constitution and. Ordinances of Grand Lodge has been called to my
attention.
AnaThis legislation was adopted after a long series of unfortunate
. ~cial experiences on the part of many Lodges and Temple Assoctations. It is imperative that the provisions of the law be complied
With implicitly.
The Sections read as follows:
Sec. 78. No Lodge, temple association, lodge trustee committee,
~iation, partnership or corporation, representing itself as Masonic
character or operating for the benefit of a Masonic Lodge or Lodges,
asonry or Masons, shall undertake any plan, scheme, project or
whereby real property is to be purchased or leased for more
an three y~s for use as a Masonic Temple or a Masonic Temple
~te, or whereby any Masonic Temple is to be erected or altered and
t expenditure required in any such case will exceed Two ThoUS8Ad,

Five Hundred Dollars ( $2,500.00) without first obtaining the written
approval of the Committee on Lodge Financing.
Sec. 152. A Lodge may invest its funds in securities prescribed as
legal for savings banks by the laws of the State of California or by the
laws of the territory in which the Lodge is located; Provided that after
first obtaining the consent of the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge
Financing, it may invest its funds as follows:
1. (a) In real estate embracing a building suitable for occupancy
or in part by a Masonic Lodge, or
whole
in
( b) In land upon which it is proposed to erect such a building, or
( c) In 'the erection of such a building upon land owned by the Lodge.
2. In memberships or shares, as the case may 'he, of a corporation
(a) which owns real estate embracing a building suitable for the
occupancy in whole or in part by a Masonic Lodge, or
( b) which owns land upon which it is proposed to erect such a
building, provided however, that the Lodge or Lodges shall hold a
controlling interest in any such corporation or shall by such investment
·
acquire a controlling interest therein.
3. By making a loan evidenced by
. (a) A duly executed promissory note amply secured by a first lien
against property of a class described under paragraph 1 above, or
( b) A promissory note duly executed by a corporation in which the
Lodge owns a controlling interest.
Provided, however. that prior to making any such investment mentioned in paragraph 1, 2 and 3 above, there shall first have been submitted to and approved by the Grand . Lodge Committee on Lodge
Financing, such of the following data as circumstances may direct:
(a) An appraisal or other evidence of the value of the land and
building involved,
( b) An appraisal or other evidence of value of the land upon which
the building is to be erected,
( c) Plans and specifications and estimates covering cost of construction for any building,
.
( d) Plans for financing same;
and provided, further, that under no circumstances shall life membership funds of any Lodge be invested in securities other than those prescribed as legal for savings banks by the laws of the State of California
or by the laws of the territory in which the Lodge is located.
In order that there will be no misunderstanding of the responsibility
of Lodge Officers and Inspectors in the matter, this circular is to be read
in full at the next two succeeding stated meetings of your Lodge.

To the Masters. Wardens, Bret.hren of the Jurisdiction:
Each year an increasing number of resolutions are presented to
Grand Lodge for consideration. In order that they may be given proper
attention and -thoughtful processing, it is essential that they be in our
hands as soon as possible.
Section 69 requires that every proposal be referred to a committee
before final enactment . .
It is obvious, therefore, that to properly evaluate these proposals,
they should be given to the proper committee well in ·advance of the
Communication.
I, therefore, request and urge that all Lodges and brethren who have
resolutions or other material to present at the coming Annual Communication have them in the ·h ands of the Grand Secretary not later
·
than July 31, 1953.
In addition, all proponents of measures should be prepared to
appear before the respective committees to discuss their proposals during
the week of Grand Lodge. In this way, we will be assured that the
rights and privileges of every one in the jurisdiction will be guaranteed.
Your cooperation is earnestly solicited.
This must be read at the May, June and July Stated Meetings.
Sincerely and fraternally,

To Masters and Wardens of Lodges in this Jurisdiction:
Brethren:
If your Lodge is planning a week end visit to Columbia Temple and
California's surrounding Mother Lode country this year, we suggest
that you make immediate reservations for use of the Temple through
the Grand Secretary's office. The rental fee is only $25.00.
There are still very desirable open dates, although many Saturday
n(ights have already been reserved by Lodges from all over California
of which yours may be one).

96

Incidentally, it is by no means too early to make your plans now
for 1954 and· to thus assure yourselves of the most favorable date for
your own Lodge.
Columbia and the aunoundfng Sierra foothills are interesting and
beautiful fn every seuon. Right now, the flush of Spring is on the
land and there fa still good skiing fn the Sierra-an easy drive from

Columbia. ·
Early Summer brings the trout season and warm, cloudless days.
Fall presents a variety of autumn color such as is seldom seen in
other parts of California.
Winter finds this region a beautiful gateway to the snow sport
country. Roads are kept in excellent condition the year around.
Thus, at any time of the year, it is an ideal destination for Lodge
pilgrimages.
Excellent accommodations are to be had in Sonora and vicinity.
The Grand Lodge Columbia Temple Committee will gladly assist in
your planning.
We urge you to seriously consider the possibility o1 visiting Columbia Temple and the Mother Lode country-the site of so much of
California's early Masonic history.
Enclosed is an information sheet which you may find of use for
your future planning and guidance.

July 20, 1953

To the Lodges of the Jurisdiction:
The Grand Lodge of California maintains Clubhouses at the Berkeley and Los Angeles campuses of the University of California for the
use of students in regular attendance at these Universities.
Membership is open both to men and women who are closely
related to members of the Masonic Frate~!ty.
The expense of operating and maintaining these facilities is home
entirely by the Grand Lodge. The club organization charges only
nominal dues, which are used to defray the cost of dances, dinners and
social events organized and sponsored by the students.
In addition to the fine association with young people from Masonic
families and with faculty members who belong to the fraternity, there
are many other practical advantages to be derived. Facilities include
a library, study room, typewriters, and adding machines. Many recreational advantages are also provided such as pool and ping pong tables,
ftnl\ dance Boors, stages for the production of amateur theatrical programs, card rooms, television and radio rooms, and kitchen facilities.
It is my desire that every Mason in California be aware of all of our
supported activities, namely, the Covina Home for Children, the Decoto
Home for the Aged, and the Clubhouses for students at our Universities. I, therefore, direct that this communication be read in every
Lodge in the jurisdiction and I further request that suitable publicity
be given through the several Lodge bulletins. I urge that visitations
by the Brethren to these facilities be made at every opportunity. For
information write to: ,
Masonic Club (UC)
2590 Bancroft Way
Berkeley, California

LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary

Masonic Club (UCLA)
10886 Le Conte
Los Angeles 24, California
ARTHUR M. WARREN
Grand Master

In January, 1952, the Board entered into an agreement with the Palo
Alto Clinic for twenty-f our hour medical coverage for any acute or
emergency illness at the Decoto Home. In addition, regular office hours
are held at the Masonic Home daily, Monday through Friday, by a
physician member of the Palo Alto Clinic staff.
The entire facilities of the Palo Alto Clinic, as a diagnostic unit,
have been made available to the residents of the Home, and the services
of the Palo Alto Clinic staff are available and utilized for any indicated
hospitalization or operative procedure. Any patient needing hospital
care uses the facilities of the Palo Alto Hospital.
The plan has continued quite satisfactorily during the year since its
inauguration. The Palo Alto Clinic representatives have been cooperative in endeavoring to reduce hospital expense which; during the past
year, has been considerable.
BUILDING OPERAT IONS-CO VINA

The usual maintenance and rehabilitation program has been carried
out during the year, including painting of some buildings and the resurfaci~g of roads.
MOTION PICTURE

The Masonic Homes Endowment Board have reported that the motion picture "The Extende d Compass" has now been completed, and
prints of it are available for showing by the Lodges througho ut the State.
PENSION PROGRAM

For the past three years the Trustees have made an exhaustive study
of various retirement programs fot the employees of the two Homes.
Surveys have been made as to the desires and wishes of the employees,
and a number of consultations have been held with actuarial ftrms. A
&nal program has been given tentative approval and is expected to be
placed in operation not later than January 1, 1954. The plan provides for
a monthly retirement allowance, based upon longevity and salary, and
coincides with similar programs adopted by private industry.
We re~ommend the continuation of the present 75c per capita tax.

at the end of the year 111 men and 181 women, a total of 2.92. "7'ho are

Report of the Superintendent-Covina Home
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is with a great deal of pleasure and gratitude that I present my
fifth annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children
at Covina, for the year ending July 31, 1953.
HOME MEMBERSHIP

As of July 31, 1953, the population of our Masonic Home Family
numbers sixty-four. Twenty-eight girls and thirty-six boys. An increase
of two over the preceding year. During the ftscal year of 1952-53 seven
boys and one girl have been admitted to the Home, including three boys
who were readmitted. Four boys and two girls left us during the year;
one by graduation: three who returned to re-established homes of their
parents, and one who is now on Outside Relief. Our one graduate,
Lorraine Bowman, will continue her education at the University of
Redlands and will major in sociology. Six boys and five ijirls will enter
High School this year.

Family relationship within the Home consists of the following: One
family of four children, four families of three children each: twelve
families of two thildren each: twenty-four families of one child. Of
the sixty-four children, twenty-five are in Covina High School, thirtynine in Charter Oak and Covina Grammar Schools. Eleven children,
representing seven families, are in the Home under membership of the
grandparent. Total number of Lodges having wards in the Home-thirty-nine, from forty-one families.
HOME, SCHOOL, AND COMMUNITY ACTMTIES

Children of the Covina Home presented a program at the May
meeting of the Los Angeles Board of Relief. Our older girls and boys
are active members of Bethel No. 98, Order of Job's Daughters and
George Washington Chapter, Order of DeMolay. Patricia Allison,
class of '54, is Senior Princess of Bethel No. 98. The children have
participated .fully in activities of Covina High School and Charter Oak
and Covina Grammar Schools. They have successfully represented
the Home in social and service clubs, athletic competition, and scholastic

109

honors. The senior boys have enjoyed week-ends camping and fishing
expeditions, while the younger camping enthusiasts have "campouts"
whenever they request them. Children's Guest Days are popular among
the members of our Home Family and children of the community: picnics;
barbecues, swim parties, and dances _are planned for the children and
by the children themselves; they are encouraged to invite their school
friends to visit for a day, a night, or a week-end. Each child is given
the opportunity of receiving instruction in piano, group singing, ceramics,
ballet, or woodcraft. A well equipped woodshop is in operation, where
our. boys learn "to do by doing" ·under- a competent instructor. The
above, in conjunction with our all-around, supervised recreational program, occupies most of the children's free time, and as a result, our boys
and girls are busy and ·happy young people. As has always been our
policy, the members of our Home Family attend the church and Sunday
school of their choice.
IMPROVEMENT PROGRA_M

Several acres of waste land have been reclaimed as permanent pasture and the installment of a sprinkler system now makes possible green
feed for our livestock throughout the year. The old pigpens have been
replaced by modern structures, making the work of our 4-H Club easier
and far more efficient. Part of our long range plan for resurfacing the
roads has been achieved. The barbecue area equipment has been increased to provide picnic facilities for approximately four hundred
Visitors, and two rest rooms, with complete facilities, were built adjacent
to the picnic grounds. In the basement of the Junior Boys' Buildfng, a
storeroom was converted into a Woodworking Hobby Shop, with the
installment of essential machinery and tools. This is a supervised activity
in our boys' program. The Intermediate Boys' entire dormitory has been
painted and a new dormitory opened for the care of our smallest ·boys.
During the coming fiscal year. we ·hope to complete the Junior Boys'
Gymnasium, which is already well under way.
SUMMER PROGRAM

Our program of activities for the children's summer· vacation included four camping periods from July 1 to August 21. A special feature
of the Senior Boys' camping experience in the Yosemite Valley was a
~-da~ saddle trip into the High Sierra, camping one night each at
osem1te Valley, May Lake, Glen Aulin, Tuolumne Meadows, Vogellang, and Merced Lake. The Junior boys and girls camped for two weeks ,
11t Wrightwood, California. This area provided a mountain setting, with
a supervised, privately owned lake. Hiking, swimming, and handicrafts
Mere part of the daily program: This camp was under the supervision of
rs. Robert M. Henry, assisted by a trained and competent staff. InterDlediate and Junior Intermediate boys joumeyed to Lake Tahoe, using

Bay View Park, in U. S. Forest Departme nt, as a base camp. The boys
"packed in" above Emerald Bay to the Velma Lake Region in the
Desolated Valley Area. Hunting, swimming, .fishing, and nature study,
were among the camp activities. A camping trip consisting of a tour of
State and National Parks and other points of interest was enjoyed by
our Senior and Intermedi ate girls. Two nights and one day were spent
at the following stops: Hoover Dam, Salt Lake, Tipanoga s Caves, Zion
National Park, Bryce National Park, Grand Canyon, and visits were
made to Montezum a Castle, Cliff Dwellers of Arizona, and the Indian
Ceremonials held at Flagstaff, Arizona. Providing an entirely new
atmospher e in camping periods pays big dividends in renewed health
and vigor. The children learn to live harmoniously with one another
und~ conditions essentially different from their Home routine, and to
accept camping responsibilities with good sportsman ship. Thete tripa
are formulated primarily on their educational value and secondarily on
the recreation al aspect.
HEALTH AND WELFARE PROGRAM

This has been a good year for our health and welfare program. We
report for surgery, eight tonsillectomies and one appendectomy. In
childhood diseases we have had twenty-tw o cases of measles, nine cases
of chickenpox, and ten cases of mumps. Dr. W . P. Magan and his
associates have been untiring in their help and guidance toward maintaining, as nearly as possible, the perfect health of every child. At six
months' intervals each child received a complete physical examination:
the results of these examinations were carefully recorded to serve as a
guide toward the attainmen t and maintenan ce of good health. Dr.
Ellwood Laine, our visiting dentist for several years, was recalled to
the Armed Services, but were were fortunate indeed in securing the
services of Dr. Elmer King, an alumnus of the Covina Home. Periodic
dental examinations and subsequen t correction and treatment, are an
important part of our health program. Eleven children received orthodontia treatment s from Dr. Townsend Paul, Pasadena. One hundred
and twenty orthodont ia treatments for these children are recorded.
Thirty-on e children under the care of Dr. Wayne D. Kuetell, Optometri~t. were given opthalmic examinati ons and visual training treatments .
Every child received booster shots twice during the year, giving immunization against smallpox, diphtheria , tetanus, and pertussis. Three
hundred and seventy-fo ur children were admitted to our Home hospital.
with a total of seven hundred and forty-four hospital days. Three
thousand, one hundred, seventeen Home Hospital Clinic treatments
were administered. To Dr. W. P. Magan and ·his associate doctors, to
Dr. Elmer King, to Mrs. Hetty Fair6eld, our nurse, and to our staff of
housepare nts, we tender our most sincere gratitude and appreciation for
their constant vigilance in behalf of our children's health and welfare.

METHODS
Your Endowment Board has continued to follow the educational
pattern that was set many years ago. Our aim has been to educate the
Brethern. and give them an opportunity to participate in this, our one
over all Charity. The use of the written word continues to be very help~
ful. This year, we have distributed the amazing number of 96,9~0 P.a~~
phlets·, telling the story of our two great H~mes. Letters and 1nqumes
have been answered promptly, and all possrble means have been used
to give the Brethem interested all possible info.rmation about our Pro~
gram. Every member of the Board has the responsibility of a certain
number of Inspectorial Districts. These areas have their special tel>-'
resentatives, either the lnspecior, or one duly appointed or suggested by
him to ·represent that area. Such a Program has made it possible for ua
to get more personal touch with the members of the Craft. Perhaps the
greatest accomplishment during the past year. has been the release of
our new 16mm. Kodachrome sound picture. This tells the story of the
Homes in a vivid and appealing manner. Sufficient Masonic history is
revealed in the picture, to make it particularly interesting to all Masons
in California. Although we have a liinited number of copies of the pie~
ture, we are distributing it by request, and complying with such requests in a most satisfactory manner. We urge all Lodges to take advantage of this picture.

FIVE MILLION DOLLARS, PLUS
It seems like a dream come true. It was only a few years ago until
the members of your Endowment Board were dreaming about an En,
dowment Fund of .6.ve million dollars. It is now a reality. There were
those who felt such a fund would be adequate for our needs.
Such is not the case. Since only the income from this fund is used,
and since the increase of expenses for the upkeep of our Homes has kept
pace with the general economic situation, we are still far short of our
goal. This situation is not disheartening, but still remains the challenge
for the Craft.
Since the adoption of the Prudent Man Rule by Grand Lodge, the
in~ome from our Endowment Fund has increased remarkably, but even
with such an increase, it will be necessary that a much greater sum be
secured before we attain the satisfactory status of knowing that we have
ample Endowment, the income from which will care for our upkeep of
Covina and Decoto.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
BOARDS OP RELIEF

In this jurisdiction we maintain eighteen ( 18) Boards of Relief. All
of these boards have placed on file with the Board of Control a complete
record of the activities of their offices for the Masonic year just closed,
as required by the ordinances. These reports have been audited by quali~
fled accountants and have been carefully analyzed by the Board of
Control.
During the past year their reports show as follo~s:
Advanced for Relief.................................................. $55,267

Many of our Boards of Relief maintain Blood Banks for the benefit
of our Masonic Brethren and their families. During the past year these
boards report as follows:
Units of Blood Donated...........·--··········-···-····-··-···-·-· 2256
Units of Blood Withdrawn...................................... 2040
Actual Cost saved our Brethren.............................. $53,045
REIMBURSEMENTS

The Board of Control is pleased to announce that the efficient management of our Boards of Relief has again resulted in a year wherein
there are no requests for reimbursements from Grand Lodge.
Our California Grand Lodge has long ago established the policy that
it is incumbent upon us to render relief in all worthy cases, and Grand
Lodge has reimbursed lodges and Boards of Relief for relief extended
where foreign Jurisdictions have refused to relieve their own brethren
and the lodges and Boards of Relief have applied for reimbursement
from Grand Lodge.
To relieve the distressed, our Boards of Relief have advanced over
$55,000.00 during the past Masonic year. These advances have been so
managed by our offices that all foreign jurisdictions have recognized their
obligation and our Boards of Relief have been made whole.

REpORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is the third year I have been privileged to render a report to this
Grand Lodge on Memorial Temple.
In rendering this report. even at the risk of repeating that which is already known to some of the brethern here in attendance, your Committee believes a brief review of the history of the activities of thi~ C.ommittee is significant and most important, particularly for you Masters and
Wardens who may be in attendance for the first time and who are not as
familiar with the work that has been done as some of the rest of us.
1947

It was during the 1947 Annual Communication that Past Grand
Master John R. Moore made the following suggestion:
"l. That a committee of nine members of this Grand Lodge be appointed by the incoming Grand Master, to be known as the Committee
on Memorial Temple: that said committee be empowered to purchase
and acquire land for a temple site in the name of this Grand Lodge in the
city of San Francisco and to erect a Grand Lodge Temple thereon of
such size and type as it shall decide: that said committee be further empowered to make, sign, and enter into all documents, contracts, and
agreements in the name of this Grand Lodge, which may be required or
necessary to erect and complete said temple: that said committee be
definitely enjoined to complete said temple and have it ready for occupancy on or before September l , 1950: and that said temple, when
completed, be called "Masonic Memorial Temple" and bear an appropriate inscription to the memory of the Masons from California Lodges
who served and died in World War 11. as determined by said committee.
2. That the War Relief Fund, amounting to approximately $155.574.94, be transferred to. and set up as, a special account and entitled
"Memorial Temple Fund."
3. That a levy of $6 be made upon every member of Lodges in this
jurisdiction. payable on or before July 31, 1950, but in no case less than

1951

By 1951 your Committee and its predece ssor committees had surveyed every known available parcel of real estate in the City of San
Francis co that might fulfill our requirements. Those that were adequa te
were not available at the time. Your Committee ··lien turned to older
structur es, and through Brother James Hurst, Past Master of Californ ia
Lodge No. 1, and Brother Henry J. Brunnier, Past Master of Mt. Davidson Lodge No. 481, we began to survey many structur es with the
thought of possibly remodeling a structur e already in existence.
In reportin g on the "Mason ic Memor ial Temple " Commi ttee's recommendations, the Finance Committee reporte d as follows:
"This Committee has labored diligently but to date has not been able
to submit a proposa l worthy of conside ration by this Grand Lodge. In
its current report, the Commi ttee states that due to building restrictions,
it now has under conside ration several improved propert ies which might
be suitably remodeled for our purpose but that it is not in a position to
make a definite recommendation at this Communication. , Howeve r, it
does recommend that the Committee be continued, and we concur in this.
"The Committee also recognizes that we are experiencing great difficulty in accommodating the members of Grand Lodge at the Annual
Communications, hence the recommendation to hold the Annual Communications in the San Francis co Civic Auditorium for five years beginning in 1952, subject to the approva l of the Grand Master. The
Committee also recognizes that moving to the Civic Center cannot be a
perman ent arrange ment but that eventua lly some provision must be made
for a perman ent Grand Lodge headqu arters and meeting place. However, no provision has heen made for the financing of such a project,
and before any material progres s can be made some attentio n must be
given to this importa nt phase. Therefo re, it proposes the levying of a
fifty-cent per capita tax for the purpose of creating a building fund.
"Your Commi ttee on Finance concurs in both of these recommendations. Every member of the Grand Lodge has a right to attend all of its
sessions, particul arly the opening session, and those who desire to do so
should be accorde d by that right the provision of more commodious
quarters : The proposa l to create a building fund with the assessm ent of
a per capita tax of 50c is sound. Our capital funds are not sufficient to
enable us to engage in a building enterpri se. Outside of the War Relief Fund, capital funds of this Grand Lodge have increase d at the rate
of approxi mately $26,000 a year for the past ten years. A fifty-cent per
capita tax would yield approxi mately $100,000.09 per annum, and if

GRAND LODGE OP CAiJPOR NIA

131

carried over for a number of years ' would create a very substanti'al
building fund."

1953
Since our last Annual Communication, at the request of the Chairman of your Committee, we have added two new members to our Com"ttee They are Past Master John Bovey of Excelsior Lodge No. 166
:; S~ Francisco. and Past Master Otto H. Fischer of Oak Grove
Lodge No. 215 of Alameda. Brother Bovey is a banker and ~rather
Fischer a manufacture r. The change in Committee representati on was
occasioned by the fact that Brother Henry Brunnier was out of the city
for the entire year and Brother James Hurst acted as our real estate
agent. your Chairman recommended and the Grand Master concurred
in the recommendation.
Following past practice this Committee continued to invite other
brethren. when available. to sit in on meetings. Those who attended
most of ou~ meetings giving us the advantage of their coun~el were Past
Grand Masters Francis V. Keesling and Lloyd E. Wilson, all the
elected Grand Lodge Officers when in the area, and other brethren.
your Chairman has also endeavored to keep all el~ted Grand ~dge
officers not in the vicinity and the Chairman of the Finance Committee
currently advised of our progress.
Early in 1953, and shortly after the Stock Exchange deal fell through.
your Committee. together with the Grand Master. the Grand Treas~rer.
the Grand Secretary and P.M. James Hurst, held a number of meeting~

133

affirming its continuance each year since 1948 and by the most unselfish
display of complete confidence vested in the Committee and the elected
Grand Lodge Officers at the last Annual Communication, we all felt that
we ~hould continue our efforts and either find that which we sought, if
available, or return to Grand Lodge at this Communication and acknowledge that the Committee had failed and recommend that it be discon-·
tinued. The mandate was clear, the solution not so easy. Functioning
under the 1951 authority. page 292 of Proceedings heretofore referred
to, we renewed our efforts.
This re-survey unfolded to the Committee very dramatically and
clearly several conclusions: Namely. that of the 15 principal sites heretofore surveyed we picked out the five most likely ones. We received
the file on each of these and made a personal inspection. Some had
structures on them. We concluded (a) that to try to remodel any of
these would defeat our purpose, namely-th at the memorial feature of
our new home could not be readily obtained: ( b) locations were not the
locations we would have picked had the properties not been offered for
s~le:. ( c) the _neighborhood in most locations was not in keeping with the
dignity of this Grand Lodge: ( d) the seating capacity in most instances
would be inadequate for future expansion and ( e) after remodeling most
of these old buildings v.:e realized they left much to be desired from the
functional standpoint of Grand Lodge.
Our next move was to again definitely determine if 25 Van Ness
A venue could be remodeled to be made adequate for our purpose. I wish
to quote from l3rother Albert Roller's letter of March 18, 1953. He reported in, part: "The building code in San Francisco now stipulates as
follows: A_ssembly halls are permitted on any floor in a building of Type
1 construction but they are limited to a maximum seating capacity of 300
on any one floor above the second floor.' " With these limitations it was
concluded that to try to remodel 25 Van Ness Avenue would not be the
answer to our problem. A similar conclusion was reached in 1948.
Our next move seemed to have· been directed by divine guidance because about the time your Committee decided that Nob Hill would be
the id~al locatio_n our real estate specialist reported that a parcel of land.
a portion of which had previously been considered for our use but which
was purchased by others before the Committee could get authority to
act, li,ad again been placed on the market because the owners were in
lnancial difficulties and had to abandon their plans for a substantial
apartment hotel.
After careful and prayerful consideration, and with full consent of
all elec~ed Grand Lodge officers and this Committee, an option was taken
on Apnl 27, 1953 on a piece of property located on Nob Hill which was
pbsequently purchased for $730,000.00.

LOCATION OP PROPERTY

PARKING PROBLEM ON NOB HILL

The site is located on the south side of California Street on Nob Hill
between Taylor and Jones Streets, just across the street from Grace
Cathedral and diagonally across the street from Huntington Park (Municipal) and Pacific Union Club. This makes the site just one block
west of the Mark Hopkins and the Fairmont Hotels.

IMPROVEMENTS

It is occupied by a Standard Oil Station on the corner of Taylor and
California Streets, and a four story apartment on the California
Street frontage. All leases are subject to cancellation on not less than
120 days' notice. With present occupancy the property is not carrying
itself. We have adopted a policy of giving all_ tenants a one year lease
with a month's free rent if we cancel within 12 months.

OPTION TAKEN AND REZONING

On April 27, 1953, after many meetings, much checking ~nd r~­
checking, and after having unanimous consent of all those mentioned m
the 1951 resolution in addition to those mentioned in the 1952 resolution, it was decided to take an option on the property.
Our first offer-$700,000 with $10,000 down payment. , This offer
was rejected with advice to us that a similar offer had already been rejected.
Our final offer of $740,000 (about $14.84 per square foot) with a
$50,000 deposit was the best we were able to do. This was made subject
to our ability to obtain satisfactory rezoning from second residential to
commercial. The rezoning has been accomplished as of July 9, 1953.
On September 25th we exercised our option and took title to the
property, our incentive being a $10,000 discount fordosing rather than
waiting till October 20, 1953. This brought our cost to $14.61 per square
foot. Since we obtained our option the adjoining property sold for
$15.86 per square foot, according to reports. Your committee now asks
that by the adoption of this report that that action be ratified, affirmed
and approved.

135

Nob Hill area has been declared critical from a parking standpoint
which has given rise to providing for a public parking garage.
Current i)arking rates on Nob Hill range from $26.00 per month to
$1.50 per day. Some monthly rates are as low as $19.00, but one of the
problems on the Hill is the great number of cars ,p arked on the streets
because there are no off-street parking facilities available. Day Rates
range from 50c for 2 hours to 75c for night parking, and $1.50 for
over night parking when space is available.
A survey made for the Committee by Standard Oil Company of
California shows real need for parking facilities. They estimate an
annual net income, of $90,842 out of estimated gross of $159,101 from
parking revenue.
The Committee feels a parking garage is in order since it may be
included without excessive cost per car area for excavation since the
property drops about 22 feet from the west to east on California Street
and 62 feet from California Street south on Taylor Street.
The Standard Oil survey also shows that there are 3,HO apartments
and 205 rooms in 185 units or buildings in the 4 x 6 square block area
with 1,297 parking spaces. Of the 1,297 parking spaces 957 are open
lots or in public garages and/or service stations, leaving 340 for residents of the area in competition with transients.
Your Committee, while grateful to the Standard Oil Company of
California for its survey, feels that it may be too optimistic and has requested the San Francisco Parking Authority to make a survey for comparative purposes. This survey should be available to tis in the next few
weeks.

GROWTH OP GRAND LODGE

Since 1920 we have had an annual increase in membership of over
4,070 net per year.
Population has increased from 3,426,861 in 1920 to 12,075,000 in
1953. It is estimated by official sources that by 1975 the population of
California will be at or near the 20,000,000 mark.
During the period 1920-1953 inclusive, we have had an average of
1.165 new applicants per year. For the year ended July 31, 1953 we had
10,003 initiates and a net gain in membership of 5,807. This
represents an increase of 751 new applicants and 475 new members over
the previous year. In 1920 we had 395 lodges with 76,783 members.
As of July 31, 1953, the end of the current fiscal year, we had 624 lodges
and 213,639 members.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE o,, CALIFORNIA

in operative, but speculative Masonry alone. After one hundred years
of Masonry in California, during which· time the pioneers of our great
Fraternity labored long and hard with determination and vision. of which
we may all be proud, yet there is still no visible monument. To the credit
of these valiant workers not only Masons, but all citizens of California,
are deeply indebted, but more particularly the members of the Craft may
have a feeling of personal pride and interest in their accomplishments.
We are now confronted with the desire and deep determination that a
real monument may be established, not only for their memory and their
accomplishments, but one that will be useful for present day activities,
and one that will stand the ravages of time and forever be for our children and our children's children, a commanding landmark, and an inspiration to all Masons and the public at large.
With such a thought in mind, it would seem that every able bodied
Mason in California would want-yes, even demand-the privilege of
participating in something so meaningful. This is possible, feasible, and
practical. and yet with so little effort on· the part of each of us. Let us all
be a part of this great Temple. Let us put something of ourselves in it.
Let us suggest that all of us participate to the extent of ONE DA Y'S
WORK in operative Masonry. For one day, and for one day only, we
abandon speculative. and unite as one great organization in one day's
work of operative, Masonry. Not a day in a week, a month or a year,
but one day in the balance of our lifetime. One day's work or it's equivalent, for each and everyone of us, would build this momentous, immortal Temple. Such would not involve a huge debt that implies interest and principal payments. In a sense, it is not a gift or contribution,
but represents our participation; it is of ourselves, and we, in a sense,
remain in the Temple forever. To a great degree, it relieves our Grand
Lodge Officers and Committeemen of an immense burden. something that
is not theirs to carry. but it comes from the many for the benefit of all.
It carries with it the spirit of the Craft, recorded in the Halls. Beyond
the corridors would be recorded all the participants. More important
would be the personal satisfaction that everyone had a part in making
this one day's work their participation in a great Temple that will stand
on for decade upon decade, and never can be removed.

Your Committee is most grateful for the suggestion by Brother
Ernest Bashor. This is one of many constructive suggestions received
since our August 2nd meeting. We urge that you at this Communication, or after you leave, if an idea strikes you, to drop the Committee a
line. Your idea may be part of the answer to a difficult problem the
Co.mmittee is struggling with. After all, what we give of material wealth
is important, but all can't contribute material wealth. What we give of
ourselves is irreplaceable. Engineers and architects can draw plans for
bridges and buildings but behind that planning is much individual thinking. With the continued co-operation of all Masons of this great, grand
Jurisdiction we will build for the future a memorial to our war dead that
will be a distinct credit to all Californians. The Grand Lodge of California and the Golden State of the West have paralleled each other in
age, in growth, in leadership and in progress. Masonry must continue
to keep pace for it is destined to exert a potent influence for the good of
all mankind in the marvelous future.
Your Committee recommends for your adoption the following:

"So Faith, Love, Hope abide; these three,
but the greatest of these is Love."
"We could demonstrate our faith in our great organization, we could
see the fulfillment of our hopes, but above all, we would demonstrate our
love for free Masonry which has meant so much to our great country.
the State of California, to our families, and to ourselves.
DR. ERNEST G. BASHOR, Chai~man

1. That this Grand Lodge adopt the official name for our Memorial
Temple to be "California Masonic Memorial Temple".
2. Since it is the unanimous belief of your Temple Committee that
any program of financing should contemplate long-term borrowing that
this Grand Lodge adopt in principal the following general ideas:
(a) That through the cooperation with the Memorial Temple Committee the Grand Master be authorized to appoint a sufficient number of
sub-chairmen and sub-committees to impliment the proposal suggested
by Brother Ernest G. Bashor above referred to. (The details and refinements to be worked out in committee.)
( b) That our goal be set at a minimum average contribution from
each lodge, based on the equivalent of a day's labor, to be not less than
an average of $10.00 per member.
( c) That when a lodge reaches that goal its name (the name of
the lodge) be inscribed as a permanent memorial in the "California
Masonic Memorial Temple" to those California Masons who gave
their lives in any war and a particular memorial to the Masons of the
respective lodges. (Note: Our architect has indicated that such a program is practical and would add substantially to the decoration of the
building and can be worked out to great advantage. It is recommended
that a special sub-committee be appointed to cooperate with the Grand
Master and the architect to work out all the details to properly carry
out this idea.
( d) Your Committee suggests $10.00 average per member because
that amount, together with other sources of revenue hereafter recommended for adoption, will beyond any reasonable doubt be sufficient to
aceomplish this objective.

3. That the Memorial idea be so developed that new lodges in the
future may participate, and have their names properly inscribed. so long
as there is any unpaid debt on the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
4. That this Grand Lodge again re-affirm the $1.00 per annum per
capita tax, that it be made a constitutional provision and that it be fixed
not to exceed $1.00 per year per member. It is our belief that such a
provision will be helpful in arranging long term financing as soon as
the "day's labor" program is well on its way. By making this a constitutional provision, and fixing it at $1.00, it would give adequate assurance that your Committee entertains no idea of ever levying. at
some future time, a large assessment or assessments. Once this is
fixed at $1.00 it would take a 5/6ths vote of this Grand Lodge to amend
the ordinance. It also follows that the more money raised by the "day's
labor" program, the less will be the borrowing. It is entirely conceivable
that at subsequent sessions of Grand Lodge the per capita could be fixed
at something under $1.00. Incidentally, this is not a new .tax or an increase; it is only retaining in effect that which was voted last year.

there be added Section 100 ( b) to our ordinances to read substantially ,

My Brethren, this has been a busy year, a difficult year and an interesting year for your Committee. Every week seemed to bring a neVI
challenge. Each challenge inspired and stimulated new thought.
In 1947 it was suggested that a Memorial Temple be built and completed in time for our Ct;ntennial. Obviously, that was not possible due
to conditions and restrictions beyond our con~ol.
This Committee has had but one motto "Make Haste Slowly". With
reasonable breaks and not too many unavoidable road blocks we should
be able to dedicate the new "California Masonic Memorial Temple"
during the 1955 Annual Communication.'
Your Committee feels that we have a splendid start. The proposed
Temple is in keeping with the dignity and high purpose of California
Masonry.
Much is expected of us in California. It has been said that some day
in the not too distant future California.will be at the top in size measured
in terms of numbers. Even greater is our responsibility in leadership.
The enterprising spirit of Masonry abhors the word "can't". This project is a challenge to every Mason in California. We dare not fail.
EDWARD H. SIEMS

AFTERNOON SESSION-Tuesday, October 13, 1953

HE IS "IN TRUTH" A MASTER MASON
Lovs T. NEWTON, Grand Orator
Most Worshipful Sir, our honored Past Grand Masters, distinguished guests and visitors, and members of the Grand Lodge of California; AU MY brethren in Freemasonry:
In accordance with the Ancient Charges of Freemasonry and the Law
of this Grand Lodge, it becomes my duty. and it is a pleasant one, to
deliver at this time, an address on matters pertaining to the Craft.
I would feel remiss in that duty if I did not pay a just and well earned
tribute to the brethren who have labored so well to make of this an outstanding year in the annals of Freemasonry: the Grand Lodge Officers
and Committee Men who have given unsparingly of their time and
ability in the performance of their respective duties.
•
Too much credit cannot be given these brethren, and in particular
our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Arthur M. Warren. Through his
many. many visitations to all sections of our vast Jurisdiction, participating in Masonic functions of every nature, kind and description he
has in his kindly and friendly manner carried the principles of Freemasonry to the brethren, not by precept alone but more so by example.
His contribution to the cause of Freemasonry will long endure; and the
fruits of his labors will be gathered in all the years to come, for the good
deeds a man performs live long after he has gone to that bourne from
which no traveler returns. May I say to him, for you, "Well done, thou
good and faithful servant of Freemasonry."
At each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California
we review and evaluate in full the collective results of our individual
labors during the Masonic year just passed and prepare for the new
year to come.
In keeping with that custom I shall review Freemasonry itself.
Masonry's personal obligation to each initiate, the Master Mason's duty
to the Fraternity, the principles we have espoused, the doctrine we
teach and our potential power to influence the lives and destiny of all
mankind.
There will be nothing new, perhaps, in what I say here; but is it not
well that we should be reminded, at our Annual Communication, of the
great heritage we possess, our duty to preserve it unimpaired and to resolve, each man individually. to labor unceasingly in its behalf?
Here the leaders of Freemasonry are met in solemn conclave: the
Officers of the Grand Lodge, the Masters and Wardens and Past Masters from practically every Master's Lodge in California; the men upon
whose shoulders rests the responsibility for the continued success or the

143

failure of Freemasonry in our day, for without strong and devoted leadership we fail.
Freemasonry is a brotherhood of free men; men of good reputation
and therefore presumably of good character; men with a firm belief in a
Supreme Being, a kind and beneficent father of all mankind, who wisely
and justly governs the universe and the lives of men: men who believe
He has endued each of us with a spiritual entity which will never, never,
never die. These four qualifications are basic, fundamental. and a necessity in all Freemasons. He who does not possess them can never be a
Master Mason though he be regularly invested with that ancient and
honorable title. He is, on the contrary, a cheat and a fraud unworthy of
the title bestowed upon him, for he has declared himself to be such a man
and accepted on that premise.
There are, as you well know, no religious qualifications for membership in the Masonic Fraternity other than a declaration of a belief in a
Supreme Power and a future existence. Those who declare that we deny
men membership in Freemasonry because of their affiliation with any
specific church are both ignorant and uninformed and they bear false
witness. It is not true now: it never has been. No where in our Masters
Lodges, or in our Masonic Law, is there any mention of church or creed
as a qualification or disqualification for membership. To the contrary.
communicants of some churches cannot become Freemasons because the
Canon Law of their church prohibits their uniting with us in the great
work to which we are dedicated. These men are not free men and are
more to be pitied than censored. A man can be held in spiritual bondage
just as sure as he can be held in bodily bondage. To be a free man in
the true sense of the word men must be free both spiritually and materially.
For him who is held in material bondage through forces beyond his
power to overcome, there is always hope of acquiring freedom, if he be
spiritually free: but for him who lives in spiritual bondage through the
powers of ignorance and bigotry, and fear of eternal damnation if he
disobey the Canon Law in matters social, civil, political or religious,
there is little hope: and so he lives in bondage in a free country.
Our founding fathers knew about this from the lessons of history
and their own bitter experience in the old countries, when they wrote in
Article I of Amendments to the Constitution, "Congress shall make no
law respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." That basic law is Masonic. Let us ever defend it to the
utmost, for we are free men in a free country and from a free church,
or we could not be here today.
Freemasonry is most certainly not a political institution despite continuous false reports to the contrary. We know that politics and political
discussions of every nature, kind and description are prohibited in our
Lodge rooms and in our Temples. And yet, one of the fundamental
Principles of our fraternity, the right to freedom of all men, ittust of

144

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

necessity be the basic doctrine of any political party which declares that
it stands for free men under a free government.
Our sole political duty is to so inculcate our initiates, each one individually. with the doctrine of Freemasonry that they shall never be
deceived or misled by the false doctrines or irresponsible political philosophies of misguided leaders, self-anointed saviours of the people, or
blatant demagogues who seek to obtain power over men for their own
selfish ends.
The primary purpose of Freemasonry, therefore, is to make Master
Masons of men whom we believe possess the necessary qualiflcations and
who come to our door of their own free will and accord. It most surely is
not just to invest them with the title that we labor in our lodges but
rather to make them 'Master Masons in fact as well as in name. This is
Masonry's personal obligation to each novitiate. This is a labor for
Freemasonry that can only be performed in the Masters Lodge.
It matters not how strong nor how efficient the Grand Lodge of California may be, it can only suggest and direct in a general.way. The final
answer as to whether the candidate becomes just another member or a
Master Mason in fact, as in name, is the responsibility of the Masters
Lodges, for there, of necessity, he must receive all the understanding of
Freemasonry that can be conferred upon him. Once again upon the
leadership of the men who are assembled here today depends the fulfillment of that most important Masonic duty.
When one labors in the Masters Lodge. the vineyard of Freemasonry,
he devotes himself not only to the building of the Temple of Masonry
but more so to the ultimate moral. spiritual and political welfare of all
mankind.
He who lives and labors only for his own selfish desires is indeed
poor and without honor among men.
To. strive to make men better and wiser in the "truth" is the noblest .
of virtues; and when one labors in the Masters Lodge he exercises that
virtue in the fullest measure, for he is working in the service of the
greatest institution eve~ conceived for the enlightment of mankind.
. .To enlighten men is to bestow upon them mental. moral and spiritual
"light" and this is in "truth" the avowed purpose of Freemasonry. for
"light" as all Master Masons know symbolizes knowledge and wisdom
_and understanding of the "truth".
To impart "light" one must first acquire "light". Let the "light" ·be
diffused in every Masters Lodge that it may shine in the hearts of all
Master Masons and thus enlighten the world.
We have stressed the great importance of our labors in the Masters
Lodge: the diffusion of "the light", which ever shines in our Lodge
· rooms, and of the vital necessity to make of each initiate a Master Mason
·in ·fact as in name. It is well, therefore, that we should define the title

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

145

that only we can bestow; determine what constitutes a true Master
Mason and evaluate the results of thus attaining our desired objective.
That ancient and honorable title itself is the key to the answer.
In the Operative Craft a Master Mason is one who has perfected
himself as an artisan in the building of Temples and great buildings of
stone and brick and other material substances, and who controls and
directs the workmen in their labors thereon.
At this point you will remember that we no longer labor in Operative Masonry but in Speculative only, using the tools of an Operative
Craft to depict the great moral and spiritual lessons of a Speculative art
-a symbolic system, of teaching, as old as the recorded history of mankind.
A Master, therefore, is one who rules or commands, who subdues,
overcomes and conqu_ers something by physical, mental or moral force.
A Mason is one who builds. in the Operative Craft a building perchance:
but in the Speculative art in which we engage he builds a man.
Through his acceptance and deep study of our beautiful ritual with
its explanatory lectures, and with a full understanding of the ancient
symbols of Freemasonry, and most important of all, of the full and true
significance of the legend of the Third Degree, the initiate has acquired
the necessary moral and spiritual strength to conquer and overcome the
sensual and material passions of hatred and envy and greed and avarice,
love of power over men, pride of opinion and intolerance ·toward and
hatred of men because of their race or their political or religious opinions
and ·beliefs, and all of the kindred evils which beset men from the cradle
to the grave in their journey along the rough and rugged highway of
life.
Having attained the victory in that battle he is in fact a Master
Mason-master and ruler over himself: and as the Master Craftsmen
of King Solomon's time erected a beautiful material temple with the tools
of their craft, he has used the tools of a speculative art-wisdom and
knowledge and understanding-to build within himself, within his material. earthly body, a beautiful spiritual temple.
He is master of himself, he has builded his temple: and through his
knowledge and understanding of the "truth" he has become worthy of
the title we conferred upon him.
The "truth" is that immutable or never changing law laid down in
the beginning by the Supreme Grand Master of us all for the guidance
of all mankind. It is just' as certain in its operation and in its cause and
effect as the law which governs the sun, the moon and all the planets in
their course in the firmament above.
Serene and confident in his understanding of the "truth" the Master
Mason walks uprightly before his God and his fellow man. He neither
·bows his head nor bends his knee in obeisance to any man for he pays
that homage only to Him in whom he put his trust, for the "light" from

147

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

the "truth" shines within him and he is spiritually a free man-a Master
Mason.
Through his knowledge of this divine attribute, "the truth", one of
the three principal tenets of Freemasonr y, he has developed his power
of understand ing-that power with which men think and ponder and
reason, and thus arrive at just and honest opinions on all subjects pertaining to life here an earth and on that future existence which Freemasonry proclaims and teaches. All animals possess the five powers of
seeing, hearing, feeling, smelling and tasting; but man, alone, of all the
creatures on this earth, ascending the seven steps, possesses the sixth
power of understandi ng; and through the seventh power of speech which,
also, he alone possesses, he conveys to future generations his knowledge
and his understandi ng for their welfare and advancemen t.
Through his knowledge of "the truth" he denies the divine right of
any ecclesiastical power, of whatever denomination, to dictate what
men shall think, and thus to proscribe all religions and faiths except their
own man-created doctrine which may or may not contain the "truth".
He demands the right to worship the God of his faith, in tlie church of his
choice, and in accord with the dictates o.f his own conscience; and he
grants this same right to all men, and defends it to the utmost.
He also denies the divine right of king, prince, potentate, ·dictator,
or tyrant by whatever title, to rule and govern men without the consent
of the governed, and proclaims and demands the right of men to a voice
in the enactment of all laws under which they must live.
From the Master Mason's knowledge of the sad record of education,
or rather lack o.f education o.f the people WMn undertaken under the
domination of private institutions in the centuries passed, he recognizes
that free public schools maintained by public funds are a vital and necessary factor in the successful continuance of any free government, for
from the schools of today come the citizens o.f tomorrow; and only in the
free public schools, uninfluenced by any ulterior motive, can students and
pupils learn to think, free and untrammeled by the insertion in the curriculum of teachings and doctrines which are not democratic and which
have as their objective the perpetuation of a religious doctrine above
the true doctrine o.f free men. He knows that the free public schools are
Masonic, and that as such they should ever be protected and defended
from those subversive elements that would destroy them.
The true Master Mason knows from his interpretatio n of the ritual
and the legend o.f the Third Degree that the Great Architect o.f the
U~iverse create~ man spiritually free, that though despots and tyrants
might enslave his corporeal being, place him in chains, cast him in the
darkest dung~n, or .t.o~ture his body with the whip or on the rack, yet
man would still be spmtually free-free to think and to reason and decide, and to commune with his Creator through that spark of the divine
wisdom with which all men, sons of a common Father, are endued and

who willed it thus. Even in the dungeons and the chains o.f tryanny he
reasoned through his power of understandi ng that if his God made him
spiritually free, he must have of necessity willed that men should be
materially free.
From that divine truth comes the great doctrine of the Fatherhood
of God, the brotherhood of man and the right to freedom of all mankind which we teach in our Lodge rooms now. Upon that doctrine rests
all that has been declared previously in this address, for without spiritual
and material freedom man is devoid of the power of free speech: he has
lost the right to act in accordance with the dictates of his own heart,
and his power to reason has been destroyed. He is indeed as an animal
with no conception of God, no feelings of brotherhood and no ideals of
freedom.
Men lived in terror and bondage and ignorance, century upon century, and only because men who believed in the truth were willing to
suffer untold tortures and the agonies of a living death, and to die upon
the field of battle by the hundreds of thousands, are we meeting here
today as free men and as free Masons.
The lamp of freedom burned dimly in some of the Grecian states
about 500 B.C., the days of the great philosophers, but it was extinguished and destroyed by the tyrants of the Grecian and Roman Empires. Darkness then prevailed for over a thousand years principally
because men were held in spiritual and material bondage through an
unholy alliance o.f church and state.
The lamp of liberty, the light from the "truth", was lighted again in
the 13th century on the British Isles. It came to us through the men who
learned it there, and here it has grown and grown until its light illumines
the world. It is a priceless heritage; and in a dosing paragraph, I like
to describe it thus:
From the knowledge acquired-of the "truth" in the ages past, we live
in the present: and in living as free men in the present, we
freedom
in
build for the future and for generations as yet unborn.
It is a sacred heritage given by God to man.
In this day and age it is ours, but only so long as we have the will and
the courage to defend and retain it.
Its destiny is in our hands. Let it not be written on the pages of history that this priceless gift from our Heavenly Father to His children,
and which means so much to us and to the ages yet to come, was
abridged or destroyed in our time.

PROCLAMATIO NS
"The Public Schools -

I

A.n A.me,rican Heritage"

Most Worshipful Arthur M. Warren Grand Master proclaimed:
"In our troubled world today the struggle between the forces of
darkness and light, slavery and freedom has reached a critical point.
And as this struggle grows in scope we can all be truly grateful for
the depth of enlightenment that prevails among our people. Only in
free men and women is there to be found true courage, wisdom and
understanding, for they are free because they willed it so.
"The Public School which our forefathers founded so wisely and
made an integral part of our national life, is the very lamp of this
freedom. Like all lamps it required tending and Masonry again will
provide this care in its own inspired 34th annual Public Schools
Week observance."
Governor Earl Warren's proclamation emphasized the importance
of public interest, understanding and cooperation in the sol1Jtion of problems of California's tremendou.sly increased population in the schools.
Governor Warren said in part:
"The public school system in California goes back literally to the
very beginnings of our State. California's first constitution-draw n
by a convention meeting in Monterey only a few months after the
discovery of gold-made provision for a system of public education.
"The progress of our public schools from that small beginning
to the vast educational system we have today has not been easy. It
has required the cooperative efforts of State and local officials, the
active int-erest of parents and of citizens generally, and the energy
and devotion of public-spirited men and women who have been willing to devote th~ir lives to the teaching profession._
"In recent years we have had to face tremendous problems in
the administration of our schools, as in many other activities of government, because of California's unprecedented increases in population. We have learned that the solution of these problems is only
possible when there is public interest, understanding and cooperation. Such public support is likewise essential to encourage those in
the teaching profession.
"The best demonstration of such support is for each citizen to
become familiar with the public school system and to keep in touch
with it."
Proclamations were issued by mayors of cities and towns throughout
the State.
The three heads of the York Rite Bodies sent proclamations to the
subordinate bodies requesting no meetings to be held during the week
that would conflict with the Observance. They state in part:

153

''Let us not forget that if we are to preserve and perpetuate this .
heritage of a non-partisan, non-sectarian, efficient and democratic
system for the children of all people, inculcating patriotism with an
undying loyalty to the Constitution of the United States of America,
respect for law and order and the entire separation of church and
state, we must support that institution which is the foundation upon
which this country has grown-our 'Public Schools'."
Grand Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star, sent a letter to its members, asking them to individually cooperate with local committees in
charge of Public Schools Week programs, and give every effort to make
the Observance a success.
Official civic individuals and groups, industries, state-wide and local
organizations recognized the Observance by formal resolutions.
Both Houses of the California Legislature formally recognized the
Observance by the following Resolution introduced into the Senate on
April 15, 1953, and adopted by the Assembly and Senate on April 20, '
1953.
Senate Concurrent Resolution No 59-Relative to the observance of
Public Schools Week.
"WHEREAS, our forefathers in their wisdom at the time of the
Constitutional Convention, held in Monterey 1849, provided for
the establishment of a Public School System in Article IX of that
historic document: and
WHEREAS, The public school in the United States has always
been a living symbol of our life since earliest Colonial times: and
WHEREAS, Public education has been recognized since pioneer times as an imperative preparation for the responsibilities of
citizenship in our free and democratic Country: and
WHEREAS, The complexity of local, state, national and international responsibilities of citizenship make grave demands today
on our people: and
WHEREAS, The thirty-fourth annual Public Schools Week
which will be held April 27th to May 2nd will be presented for
the purpose of bringing the public and the schools into a closer
understanding of the functions and problems of the schools today:
now, therefore, be it
Resolved by the Senate of the State of California, the Assembly
thereof concurring, That this Legislature does hereby endorse the
purposes of Public Schools Week and urges on our citizens the
\risiting of one or more schools during the week of April 27th to
May 2nd for the purpose of seeing what the schools are doing in
preparing our youth for the responsibilities of intelligent and use·
ful citizenship."
