Exceptional results have again been achieved by lodges organizing
within districts, some of them capitalizing on successes of many years
experience with united effort, others reporting outstanding results o.n
"8.rst tries" in combining several lodges, or districts. The scope of this
integrated effort can only be fully recognized. by a study of their large
volume reports. (On display at Annual Meeting of Grand Lodge.)
Many of the lodge combinations broke down into committees to
cover various phases of the Observance, and obt~ined unusu~lly. fine end
results. Rosters of civic, business, and professional orgamzations and
leaders were evolved, personal contact enlisted their aid to create a
community..wide spirit of observance for the 1953 Public Schools Week.
Lapel badges, posters, street banners and sidewalk stencil~, car..window
stickers, car bumper strips, store window placards and displays, essay
and poster contests in the schools, production of school calendars of
events, radio..TV coverage, and complete newspaper presentations, were
some of the promotional ideas initiated and followed through in metic.-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

159

ulous detail. A breakdown of one committee went something like this:
clippings, posters, speakers, newspapers, window displays, open house
committee.
At the close of Public Schools Week, committees conscientio~ly
sent letters of congratulation s and "thank you's" to all community groups,
and individuals who cooperated in the success of the event, and have
thus established a firm foundation of cooperation and rapport with these
organizations for future years.
One lodge reported that in contacting their newspaper, there was
such enthusiasm that a "Back to School" coverage took place, with a
photographer in every school during Public Schools Week.
An outstanding example of community-wide spirit and cooperation
was shown by one lodge whose city devoted an entire edition of its
newspaper to Public Schools Week. Each advertiser plugged the pub..
lic schools, and every phase of the paper had something of constructive
value to say regarding the public schools. The local committee sparked
the idea with its copy of "The Press Book."
Another lodge attempted a "school survey" for the first time, achiev..
ing a high standard of success. Each school visited was surveyed for
personnel. physical conditions, number of teachers, bonding, condition
of buildings, enrollment in relation to available space, transporatation
systems, etc.. and reported on a survey form. The survey forms were
then compiled into a general report of the area facilities. This gave a
clear picture of school conditions, and alerted the membership and com ..
munity to needs of their local public schools.
The sponsorship of poster, essay, and window display contests stimu..
lated community interest to the utmost. An increasing number of lodges
employed this method of promotion for the first time, and "old..timers"
report even bigger and more successful events of this nature.
Movie trailers held the spotlight in several areas, and met with ex ..
ceptional success.
The publishing of school "calendars of events," highlighting all
programs during Public Schools Week in the community, was another
type of promotional device utilized by many lodges. These were dis ..
tributed among the membership and civic organizations of the 'area.
Everyone knew just what was going on, and as a result an excellent
turn..out for Public Schools Week ensued.

163

City-wide coordination of certain aspects of the program are
most effective: newspaper promotion, window displays, car
bumper strips, tags, tie-in ads, pamphlets, posters, window placards, street banners, radio-TV coverage, etc.
This affords the advantage of large quantity printing at low
cost, and uniformity in an area. Joint steering committees from
the several Lodges can take care of these particular aspects more
effectively and efficiently than can individual Lodges.
Masters and Wardens Asso~iations serving as clearing houses
in the large cities, are effective devices for coordinating joint activities.
Lodge sponsorship of schools, and general community and school
contacts and support can best be accomplished on an individual
Lodge basis.

Follow-through •••
Immediately following the close of the 1953 Observance, school authorities throughout the jurisdiction received information regarding next
year's dates, in order to make early provision for the event in their school
calendars-Grand Lodge Committee letter, dated June 1, 1953.
Acknowledgement of appreciation for this early data has already
been overwhelmingly noted from several school district officials.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In accordance with the motion adopted at the annual communication
in 1950, Grand Master Paulsen appointed a special committee on ceremonies in 1951 and the committee reported to the 1951 communication
relative to the ceremony for the laying of a cornerstone, the ceremony
of instituting a new lodge, the ceremony of coristituting a lodge, the ceremony of dedicating a Masonic hall and that of presenting a fifty year
button.
Approximately five hundred changes, ranging from single words to
paragraphs, were recommended and adopted. The revised ceremonies
have been in use for two years and considerable favorable comment has
been made to the members of the committee relative to the changes effected. These comments have come from the officers performing the ceremonies. inspectors and brethren on the side lines. One change has been suggested to the committee, in the closing words of the presentation of a
fifty year button. The committee itself has reexamined all of these ceremonies and desires to recommend the change of one phrase in the ceremony for the laying of a cornerstone, add the new Master as an escort
of the Grand Master in the ceremony of institution, change one word in
the ceremony of constitution, add one word and change two others in
the dedication ceremony. change a preposition and one sentence in the
presentation of fifty year button and the brother who leads the salute.
We are refommending these changes at this time because the revised
ceremonies have not been printed as yet and we judge the time for printing to be at hand.
In the ceremony for the laying of a cornerstone, we recommend that
the words of the Deputy Grand Master, spoken after he has poured the
corn upon the stone, "May the Great Architect of the Universe ... "
(Proceedings, 1951, p. 148) be changed to: May our Heavenly Father
• , . This change is recommended because the architect appellation is
used by the Grand Master approximately one minute later and we believe
a difference will be more pleasing.
In the ceremony for instituting a new lodge we recommend that the
direction: " . . . the Grand Master shall enter without escort .•. "
(Proceedings, 1951, p. 150) be changed to: ... the Grand Master enters,
escorted by the Master named in the dispensation ... A further direction
should then be added: The Master takes a seat in the north east with
the two wardens.
In the ceremony of constituting a new lodge, we recommend that the
words of the .Grand Master: "The grand officers will repair to their stations ... " (Proceedings, 1951, p. 160) be changed to: The grand officers will return to their stations and places ...

In the ceremony for the dedication of a Masonic hall, we recommend
that the word "reverently" be added in the statement of the Grand Master (Proceedings, 1951, p. 161 ) so that the Grand Master shall say: We
shall, therefore, reverently unite with our Grand Chaplain ... We further recommend that the direction of the Grand Master to the Grand
Marshal ( p. 162) be changed from: " ... you will uncover the emblem
... "to: ... you will prepare the emblem ... and" ... to their proper
places ... " be changed to: ... to their respective places . . .
.
Relative to the ceremony for the presentation of a fifty year button,
we recommend that the statement of the Master to the recipient (Proceedings. 1951, p. 166) use the word "fraternal" rather than "brotherly"
and the phrase will then be: ... this visible token of the fraternal love
and appreciation of your brethren. We further recommend that one
"from" be changed to "of" and the last sentence of the Master's said
statement be altered. This portion would then be: ..• This button is
made of the pure gold from the hills of California. It is emblematical of
that purity of life and conduct which should be displayed by Masons
whithersoever dispersed. It is also an emblem of the esteem with which
you are regarded and the affection in which you are held.
Finally. in this same ceremony we recommend that the direction that
the brethren will salute the recipient under the direction of the Marshal
be changed to: Master: Brethren, you will join with me in saluting our
brother by the battery of three times three.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

The regulations which we have tested and found satisfactory are
attached to this report as "Exhibit A"/ We think it will benefit the
entire Fraternity if they are enacted into law so that all may know what
Grand Lodge expects.
2--0CCASIONAL PUBLICATIONS

By this term we refer to publications put out for special occasions
only, such as the programs used at Shrine football games. We have
developed a different set of regulations adapted to the needs of occasional publications. A copy is attached hereto marked "Exhibit B"
and is likewise recommended for enactment into law at this Communication.
The general purpose of these regulations was to permit sponsors of
publications whose sole purposes are for charitable assistance to apply
for the aforementioned sanction. · In the words of the Grand Master
"this would allow certain publications who have always operated on an
ethical basis to continue their very 6.ne contribution to hiJmanity."
Applications from the following organizations were approved:
Islam Temple, A.A.O.N.M.S., San Francisco.
Al Bahr Temple, A.A.O.N.M.S., San Diego.
Al Malaikah Temple, A.A.O.N.M.S., Los Angeles.
Aloha Temple, A.A.O.N.M.S., Honolulu, T. H.
3---oPPICIAL BULLETINS

Before the enactment of the Publications Law it was the practice in
some of our Lodges to sell advertising space in their official monthly bulletins. We believe that without exception this was for the purpose of
defraying the cost of publication and circulation but such activities have
necessarily been suspended until ·there is a change in our law.
The practice was even more wide spread among the appendant
Masonic Bodies such as the Eastern Star. We have had a host of inquires from such Bodies as to why they cannot accept financial assistance
for a publication which is exclusively under their control and which is
necessary to their successful operation and while we have been unable
to give them any assistance or encouragement under the present law we
have reached the conclusion that a change in our law is desirable.
We are living in a day when there is sharp competition for the time
and attention of the members of any organization. A simple post card
announcement of a meeting is not sufficient to arouse the member's
interest and secure his attendance. The announcement of the meeting
has to he presented in an attractive manner and in some detail. A sales
talk is needed. If the member is advised of the advantages he will gain
from attendance he will make an appearance more often.
Another great advantage to be gained from an adequate "house

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

171

organ" which corresponds to our official bulletin is that space is available
for personal items concerning members. We are all human and the
mention of a person's name in print is a recognition to which he is entitled and which invariably stimulates his interest in the organization.
The publication of an attractive official bulletin involves expense
which some Bodies and perhaps some Lodges are not able to assume
unless they are allowed to sell advertising space. We think, however,
that any solicitation for the purchase of advertising space should be
limited to the cost of printing and circulating, provided that the nature
and contents of the advertising shall conform to Grand Lodge regulations and that with this safeguard such activities can be carried on without any harm to Masonry and with some probable benefit.
For these reasons we have become convinced that the publication of
such official bulletins should be made possible by an appropriate amendment to our laws. A suggested amendment is attached hereto marked
"Exhibit C" and will no doubt he referred to the proper committee for
consideration and report.
4-RESTRICTED INFORMATI<ON

We find it necessary to report to Grand Lodge on a matter which is
really collateral to our main concern hut which has caused your committee a great deal of trouble. We refer to the right of Lodges to release
for publication their news bulletins or trestleboards containing dates of
· meeting, other general information, lists of Lodge officers and places of
meeting.
The Publication Law as enacted in 1951 related only to the soliciting,
placing or printing of advertisements. It has not been repealed or
amended. It says nothing about the release of information which should
be, and in our opinion, is an entirely different subject.
Grand Master Drapeau was the 6.rst to administer the Publication
Law. He appointed a committee to assist him just like the present committee. Some of us are hold-overs from that committee. The committee
appointed by Grand Master Drapeau drew up regulations governing
publications and the then· Grand Master so approved them. Among
them were the bans on the release of information which I am discussing.
They may have been eminently proper and necessary at the time. I suppose I should take some responsibility for them as a member of the
Drapeau committee but I can say with equal positiveness that, as far as
I am concerned, they were never intended as permanent fixtures of
California Masonry or to work any change in our established practice
under which such items have been published. They were the means
employed by last year's committee and Grand Master Drapeau to enforce the law on advertising.
When our present Grand Master took office he had different ideas
on enforcement and on November 20, 1952 issued a circular letter an-

EXHIBIT B
Certificate of Sponsor of Occasional Publication .
The undersigned has bee.n authorized by................................................
.•.............................................. to be in charge of the publication described
in the attached letter and the solicitation of advertising to appear
therein. With the knowledge and permission of said sponsor and in
its behalf as well as my own, 1 certify and agree as follows:
1. The net proceeds derived from the project will be devoted to the
charitable purpose described in the accompanying letter of application.
2. No advertising will be printed for alcoholic beverages, patent
medicines, horse racing or other gaming, or for political candidates.
3. Lodge mailing lists or rosters or Grand Lodge rosters will not be
used.
4. No money will be solicited or received from Lodges for subscriptions or otherwise. No representations will be made to Masons that it
is their duty to subscribe or advertise.
5. Donations for charity or otherwise will not be solicited or accepted
by advertising solicitors. No advertisements will be accepted of a
congratulatory or greeting nature.
6. No printed or oral representation will be made that the publication is an official publication or is sponsored, authorized or controlled
by Grand Lodge, any constituent Lodge or Masonry in general or that
any such Masonic body will receive any benefit or advantage, financial
or otherwise, from subscriptions or advertising.
·
7. No business of this publication will be conducted in a Masonic
Temple or Lodge Hall.
8. If approval is granted hereunder, the same shall not printed in
the publication but prospective advertisers may be informed that application for sanction to solicit and publish advertising has been approved by Grand Lodge and such approval may, but need not be displayed to the prospective advertiser.
9. Two copies of the publication will be forwarded to the office of
the Grand Secretary, 25 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco 2, within
10 days after printing.
10. I agree to furnish such additional information concerning the
publication as may be requested and I understand that any approval
granted may be withdrawn .at the pleasure of the Grand Master.
11. Within 30 days after the event for which the publication is
designed a financial statement in duplicate will be filed with said Grand
Secretary itemizing the expenses, gross and net proceeds of the pub-

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON CORRES PONDEN CE
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee completed its review of the 1952 proceedings of
our sister jurisdictions on Septembe r 1st so that the printer might have
copies ready for those attending our 1953 Communication. Much valuable information is collected in this Review and it is hoped that it will
be widely read by members of our Grand Lodge.
Considera tion has been given to issuing the Review quarterly instead of once a year. The usefulness of the Correspon dence Committee Report is lessened because it comes out during Grand Lodge week
when the attention of the brethren is centered on immediate problems.
If the material was divided into separate parts and distributed during
the year, its value would be enhanced. ·If a copy is mailed to each
officer and Committeeman of Grand Lodge, to the Masters and Wardens
of the Lodges and several copies sent in bulk to each Lodge Secretary

REPORT OF COMMI SSION ON REVISIO N OF
ROSS DIGEST
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge of California:
Your _Commissi~~· recently appointed by the Grand Master, to study
the question of rev1smg the Ross Digest, reports as follows:
More than twenty-tw o years have elapsed since Most Worshipf ul
John Stewart Ross presented the Ross Digest to Grand Lodge for approval. It is unnecessa ry for us to dwell at length on the great service
he performed . This wo_rk has been our constant companion for many
Y~ars. On many occasions the Craft has recognize d its value and it
wdl always stand as a monument to this great and loyal Mason.
However, all law is in a constant state of change and the books that
record it must keep pace with these changes so that they may be found
and understoo d by those who need them. New questions arise that bring
forth amendmen ts and new problems result in far-reachi ng decisions and
interpretat ions. And this is as true of Masonic Law and Masonic Law
Books as of all others. No law book is of enduring value unless it is
r~ised from time to time and adapted to existing needs. The present
Digest has served its purposes during a period when the State has
·doubled in population and when Masonry has developed at a corresponding pace. If the author of the Digest were here today, he would
be among the first to recognize the need for revision at the present time.
. Since Brother Ross became ill several years ago, no one has been
directly charged with the duty to see that the book was kept up to date,
SO that new material could be readily found and understoo d, and
it has now reached the state where nothing short of a complete revision
\Vould be adequate.

178

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

During the past twenty years: the publishers of law books generally,
have greatly improved them both as to form and as to the methods of
keeping them up to date. Better indexing techniques have been developed, and in our opinion, these should all be used in our own statement of Masonic Law to the end that the Craft may find the law more
easily and be able to understand it when it is found. We should, to
the extent possible, have a law book written for laymen rather than for
lawyers. By re-writing many provisions, incorporating the gist of decisions in the text, and by the aid of comments and illustrations, we
believe that this can be accomplished.
The suggestion has been made from time to time that a partial revision would be sufficient if a more adequate index were supplied. We
do not share that view. If the work is to be done at all, it should be
done well, and a complete and thorough revision should be undertaken.
It will require time and some expense. but in the end it should lead to
clarifications that will prevent costly mistakes and the excessive expense
of re-printing should be reduced. Men are available within the Craft
to get this work done. and to keep the resulting product up-to-date in
the years that follow.
We therefore recommend:
( 1 ) That a permanent comm1ss1on on Masonic Law be
created, the members to be appointed by and serve at
the pleasure of the Grand Master;
( 2 ) That the commission, with such assistance as it may
secure from the brethren, undertake a thorough revision
of our law as herein suggested; and
( 3) That the sum of $1,200.00 be appropriated for the use
of the commission to cover material and stenographic
expenses.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws has carefully examined and considered
the one hundred sixteen Amendments to By-Laws submitted by constituent Lodges for approval during the past year.
Forty-three of these Amendments increase the initiation fee and
twenty-nine of the Amendments increase the annual dues. This procedure is all in keeping with the increasing costs of today. Likewise nine
Lodges increased and adopted a reasonable initiation fee.
To the brother who values his Masonic membership and the worthwhile interested applicant, there can be no serious objection to these
changes. An unreasonable increase of dues will result in a loss of
membership.
For various reasons, certain Lodges decided it was rtecessary to
amend their By-Laws to provide for changing date of Stated Meeting
and also providing for the postponement allowed because of certain
holidays.

We further urge Secretaries to sign and place the Lodge seal on the
official communication of the atcion to Grand Lodge. Only a few of
these omissions appeared, but they raise technical questions. We urge
th'e Secretary to see that all blanks in the Uniform Code of By-Laws
express a meaninq. True a blank does not mean anything, but it is Just
as easy to insert "no," or "nil." When a provision is not used it should
be stricken out. then surplusage cannot cause any confusion of interpJ"etation.
One Amendment increasing dues was rejected by the Grand Master
and Grand Secretary because it attempted to be retroactive. Their action
was completely sound. This Amendment was reconsidered by the Lodge,
and provided that the increase take effect at the beginning of the next
quarter, following the action of the Lodqe. It was approved by the
Grand Secretary as to form, and by the Grand Master as to Masonic
law. We call attention to it here for information only.
We ask the Grand Secretary to insert into his prepared form for
Amendment of By-Laws, a blank for the address and location of the
Lodge. Also a blank for when the proposed Amendment of By-Laws is
to become effective.
.One unusual Amendment provided for a reduction of the annual
Lodge dues, but the Amendment was noticed, voted on and adopted by
the Lodge in 1936. Amendments to By-Laws do not become effective
until approved by the Grand Master and Grand Secretary; their action
is then considered and confirmed by Grand Lodge upon the report and
recommendation of the By-Laws CommiUee, at the next Annual Communication. There is an interesting question here as to the amount of
the annual diRs for the last sixteen or seventeen years. However, the
Amendment as to the action of our Committee is in proper form and we
approved it. We have allowed the Secretaries where necessary to correct
errors or omissions, for the chief objective is to avoid duplications and
yet keep the Lodge record legally sound and complete.
We recommend that incoming Masters look over the By-Laws with
the Secretary at the beginning of the term, and that Amendments be
checked by them together as to notice thereof, adoption and date to
take effect.
All the Amend.ments as finally submitted have received the approval
of the Grand Master and the Grand Secretary. We approve them and
recommend the adoption of this report approving the Amendments set
forth therein by Grand Lodge.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Canby Cross Lodge No. 679, Tulelake; San Marino Lodge No. 685,
San Marino. Financing of these buildings, with one exception, will
require no fixed debt, aside from the non-interest bearing loans made
by the lodges to their own temple associations. Consent has been granted
to commence construction of these new Masonic temples with the
stipulation that no liabilities, either for labor or materials, be incurred
beyond those currently approved by your. Committee. As in previous
years, cooperation of the respective Masonic inspectors has been sought
and letters from them certifying the proposed Lodge rooms are suitable
for proper tiling, have been requested.
Your Committee has approved the purchase of eleven Masonic
temple building sites this year which sets another record. In addition
twenty-four Lodges have received permission to incorporate Masonic
temple associations under the non-profit laws of the State of California.
These associations have for their purpose the acquisition and operation
of Lodge prope~y.
Your Committee on Lodge Financing held its regular semi-annual
meeting at the Marines Memorial Club, in San Francisco, Sunday,
February 22, 1953. The following members were present: Chairman,
E. J. Blickfeldt; E. Herbert Phillips; Walter Pybon; Darrell R. Purcell;
Harold R. Richards; Glen C. Holbert; William D. Verbarg; Mark A.
Green. The meeting lasted from 10:00 A. M. until 4:10 P. M. and
much good work was accomplished. Representatives from Sotoyome
Lodge No. 123 and Salinas Lodge No. 204 presented themselves for
Committee advice and cooperation on their Lodge Financing problems.

"That the incoming Grand Master, the chairman of the Committee on
Finance, together with the Chairman of the Committee on Lodge
Financing be hereby authorized to expend such monies of Grand Lodge
to relieve the unfortunate condition of the Tehachapi and Maricopa
Lodges in their rebuilding projects as may he collectively decided upon,"
the Committee on Lodge Financing at its February meeting voted unanimously to recommend a grant from Grand Lodge funds of $10,000.00
to Tehachapi Lodge and $10,000.00 to Mariposa Lodge to assist in
the rebuilding of their earthquake destroyed temples. This recommendation was made after several meetings had been held with representatives of the respective Lodges, after much discussion between members
of the Committee on Lodge Financing and the Committee on Finance,
and much prayerful consideration and study by all concerned.

a fe~~i:ddition to the few such specific sugg~stions. there seemed to be

questi~~abve attlt~de is th~ true Masonic method of approach to the
of Masonic education and information, it leaves the Lodges and

9:

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

membership to provide their own source of information, or else remain
in complete ignorance of the Masonic world, except only the Ritual and
the Ordinances of Grand Lodge.
There is one source from which the brethren might receive some
light, viz., the so-called Masonic Magazines, but these, in the judgment
of your Committee, do not attain an average grad~ of more than 5.0%
in the accuracy of their statements. Grand Lodge ts now engaged m a
program of cleaning up the advertising policies of the so-called Masonic
magazines, but it appears unable to correct the errors of. the ~ther pages
for, as we are informed, even the Grand Lodge of Cahforma does not
know what is right. ·
It is the reflection of your Committee that, if the same attitude of
absolute accuracy were insisted upon in the public schools, classes would
have to be restricted to such subjects as mathematics, which contain
internal methods of proving their own verity.
It seems to your Committee, therefore, that the choice which m~st
be made by Grand Lodge lies between giving the brethr~n the best mformation which Grand Lodge can compile through well informed,
though not infallible Committees, or else abandoning all effort to give
the Craft any Masonic Information at all.
Out of 707 Questions and Answers, certainly there must be many,
probably several hundred, that are . so nearly correct that the most
meticulous critics could find no fault m them. If even half of 707 were
salvaged, a big step would be taken by publishing those and leaving
the rest to be settled later.
The Grand Lodge of California ·is just a little over 100 years old, but
it is not generally realized that for approxim~tely the last one-third. of
its life, that is, since 1915, it has been attemptmg to carry on some kmd
of Masonic educational program. It has accomplished very little, because it has never adhered to any program for very long. During the
past thirty-seven years which have witne~sed the ~incere efforts ~f a
number of different Committees on Masonic Education or Information,
your present Committee is the only one that has succeeded in establishing a permanent program, small as it is. We refer to the four booklets
that are handed to the candidate as he passes through the degrees. The
707 Questions and Answers would supplement those books and provide an inexhaustible supply of material for lodge programs of a variety
which would permit a considerable choice of different subjects. T~e
following are the eighteen headings: Origin of Freemasonr y, Gothic
Operative Era, The Transition, Foundation of Grand Lodg~s, European Masonry, The Ancients and the Moderns, Freemasonr y m America Freemasonr y and the Negro, Masonic Literature. Masonic Rituals
in General, Ritual of the Entered Apprentice Degree, Ritual of the Fellow Craft Degree, Ritual of the Master Mason's Degree, Rites of Freemasonry, Masonic Jurisprudence, Freemasonr y and Religion, Free-

masonry Roman Catholicism and Mormonism, and Miscellaneous. Each
of these heads has an average of thirty-five or forty questions on that
particular subject.
Your Committee recommends :
1. That the sum of $5,000 be added to the Grand Secretary's printing appropriatio n for the publication of this book; that three copies
thereof be distributed free to each lodge and that additional copies be
sold to lodges or members at approximate ly the cost of publication to
be estimated by the Grand Secretary.
2. That your Committee be continued, and that there be appropriated for the general expense of your Committee during the ensuing
year the sum of $500.
Respectfully submitted,

YucAIPA LoDGE U.D.
Yucaipa Lodge was instituted March 16, 1953, and is the outgrowth
of a Masonic Club which was formed in 1946.
The Lodge began its existence with 27 charter members, has gained
26 by affiliation and 11 applicants have been accepted, of whom 3 have
been raised.
The meeting place is adequate, its finances are satisfactory, and the
progress already noted justifies the prediction that this Lodge will fill a
real Masonic need in Yucaipa Valley.
We, therefore, recommend that a charter be granted to Yucaipa
Lodge No. 726 in the County of San Bernardino.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CONSTITUTION
MONTH OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
As we approached our seventeenth annual observance of the signing
of the Constitution of the United States of America in September, in
accordance with our custom, it occurred to your committee that while we
could and should pay homage to those great and good men and women
of the past who, by their efforts, made the Freedoms which we enjoy
possible, it was even more important that we as Masons, because of our
heritage, should develop a program which would emphasize the opening
words of that great document, "WE THE PEOPLE," and place emphasis upon what we, as Citizens, could and should be doing to preserve,
protect and defend the Liberties which, as the years come and go, we
are all more and more inclined to take for granted.
In an address by W. G. Vollmer, President of the Texas and Pacific
Railway Company, we found thoughts expressed which provided a basis
upon which to suggest a rededication of ourselves to the "Spirit that
built our Country" by reaffirming the "Four Great Faiths" of our founding fathers. A program was developed on this theme and offered to the
Constituent Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction in the hope that as we
reaffirmed our Faiths we would thoughtfully remember that down
through the years, because of them:
We have been free to dream, to explore, to invent.
We have been free to work, to achieve, to accumulate.
We have been free to venture, and failing, to venture again.
We have been free to spend our money or to save it.
We have been free to rise from rags to riches.
We have been free to enjoy the fruits of our labors.
The faith of our pioneering ancestors was a living, vital force. It
was what sustained and guided them as they toiled and fought to lay

REPORT ON OVERSIZE LODGES
NOTE:
The Committee on Oversize Lodges spent several months on the subject, and, as a
reaul!, p;ese~ed a most i~eresting refX!ri. _the complete text of which is too long for
publication in the Proceedings. The highlights of its findings and the conclusion are
presented herewith. The entire report is on file for study by anyone wishing to do so.
Grand Secretary.
REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON OVERSIZE LODGES

Interested in knowing what other Grand Jurisdictions were doing in
this field, the Committee sent a questionnaire to all Grand Lodges as
follows:
"1. Does your Grand Lodge restrict the size of membership in its
constituent lodges?
2. Do you limit the number of candidates or degrees which a lodge
may have in a year?
·
3. If you have such restrictions, what are the laws or rules concerning same?
4. Has your Grand Lodge given consideration, by committee study
or otherwise, to these questions? If so, what was done?
5. What, if anything, do you do toward sponsoring or fostering the
formation of new lodges?"
Replies were received from 50 Grand Lodges in the United States
and Canada. All answered Question No. 1 in the negative. Only 2
(Pennsylvania and New York) answered Question No. 2 in the affirmafl'le. In reply to Question No. 5, all Grand Lodges advised that they
l*\couraged the formation of new lodges-with the single exception of
Missouri. Montana recently chartered a lodge with 230 chartered
members.
New York's solution on the limitation of candidates for degrees is
as follows:
"Except upon dispensation from the Grand Master providing
otherwise, no lodge shall confer any degree on more than five ( 5 )
candidates at a time or more than one degree within any seven
( 7) consecutive days.
"A lodge shall not confer the Second Degree or the Third
Degree on the same candidate at a less interval than two weeks
from the time of conferring the preceding degree."
Pennsylvania's law on the same subject is as follows:
"Lodges under 600 members are unlimited as far as the number of their initiations are concerned: Lodges between 600 and
700 members may receive 10 petitions monthly: if 700 members,
only 9 petitions monthly: if 800 members, only 8 petitions monthly: if 900 members, only 7 petitions monthly: if 1000 members,
only 6 petitions monthly: and if 1100 or more members, only 5
petitions monthly."
Examining the California situation, your Committee found 613

any one year since 1933. According to size, the 613 lodges fall into the

Therefore, taking the figure of 500 as a desirable maximum membership, our problem affects only 134 lodges, or a little more than one-fifth
of the lodges in the jurisdiction. In the group with over 1000 members,
the venue of the "offenders" is as follows: San Diego, 3; Los Angeles,

1 each. However, this picture as of July 31, 1952 was not too black. The
largest lodge in the State had a membership of only 1240.
As early as March 27, 1953, the members of your Committee, by
correspondence, considered a suggestion for limiting the yearly net gain
of all large lodges. We felt that it was unwise to decrease their present
sizes and we would allow replacements for the yearly loss by deaths,
demits and suspensions, which reach a considerable figure. For instance,
the lodge of your Chairman loses an average of 25 to 30 members a year.
Suppose that we limit a lodge with over 1000 members to an annual net
gain of 1 %: a lodge with 751 to 1000 members to an annual net gain of
2%: and a lodge of 501 to 750 members to an annual net gain of 3%.
After being informed of the Pennsylvania law, we compared our own
ideas with it, and we have up to date continued our analysis. We consider that our proposed plan is preferable to the Pennsylvania rule for
the following reasons:
1. A check-up on each lodge on a yearly basis, rather than monthly,
gives a better overall plan, and would be simpler to administer,
both by Grand Lodge and the constituent lodges.
2. Since it is based on net increase, it allows for replacements for
losses by death. demit and suspensions.
3. It would not result in the rejection or postponement of desirable
applicants.
4. It would check the growth of large lodges because the net percentage gain is less than the current gross growth of many of
such lodges, whereas under the Pennsylvania rule, the large
lodges may continue their growth by a rather large rate.
Your Committee, after completing their study of all suggestions
which we have been able to obtain, have reached the conclusion that a
limitation of the annual net gain of all lodges with over 500 membe_rs is.
desirable; and we therefore recommend it to you for your consideration.
Our recommendations and suggestions are as follow:
1. We endorse the proposed legislation for plural membership and
urge you to vote in favor of it.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At the 1952 Convocation of Grand Lodge, the then Grand Master.
himself a judge, reported with praise upon the services rendered during
the year by the Junior Grand Warden in doing the necessary research
and preparing the text for most of the Grand Master's legal rulings
(Proceedings 1952, page 21).
As a result of the invaluable assistance to this Grand Master in this
respect, he recommended that a Special Committee be appointed to
report at the next annual communication of Grand Lodge upon the
advisability of this Grand Lodge establishing an office to be designated
as Judge Advocate (Proceedings 1952, page 26 ).
This recommendation was referred to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes, which recommended favorably upon the appointment
of such a committee. The recommendation was adopted by the Grand
Lodge (Proceedings 1952, page 304) and such a committee was ap#
pointed. (Proceedings, Grand Lodge. 1952, page 435).
Your committee deemed it advisable to seek the views of the six
most recent Past Grand Masters upon the subject and accordingly did so.
With a degree of unanimity surprising among Past Grand Masters,
each of the six approved and recommended the creation of such an office.
There can be no doubt but that a heavy burden rests upon the
shoulders of our Grand Master. As our fraternity grows, its problems
increase in number. The Grand Master is called upon to supervise the
general administration of Grand Lodge affairs. His travel. visitation,
and ceremonial duties are heavy and time#consuming. He is called upon
to make decisions and rulings on a wide variety of matters. Many of
these require extensive study of the provisions of our Constitution and
Ordinances and frequently a studious research of former rulings and
decisions of Grand Lodge, and, in some instances, an examination of
Masonic literature. Some Grand Masters, by virtue of legal training,
are peculiarly adapted to such a type of work. Others, not members of
the legal profession, may not possess such ability in a marked degree.
In any event, it appears that the Grand Master merits and deserves
such assistance as Grand Lodge can provide for him in relieving against
these heavy duties.
It would be a privilege of the Grand Master to utilize the services
of a judge advocate as much or as little as he chooses. It should, how#

It has also been suggested, and the suggestion seems to have merit,
that if the judge advocate was a skilled parilamentarian, he might be
of great assistance to the Grand Master in passing upon some of the
knotty problems of parliamentary law which arise with some frequency
during our sessions of Grand Lodge.
It appears that the Grand Lodge of New York has an officer known
as judge advocate and that the use of such an officer has met with sin#
gular success in that Grand Lodge.
Based upon its study of the problems and the opinions of the Past
Grand Masters consulted thereon, your committee believes it to be
desirable that this Grand Lodge should add to its list of officers that
of judge advocate; such officer to be a Master or Past Master in good
standing who shall act as the legal advisor of the Grand Master with
such duties as the Grand Master may prescribe.
Accordingly, we so recommend.
To accomplish this end, it appears that Article II of Section 3 of the
Constitution, dealing with the composition of Grand Lodge, should be
amended by inserting in the list of officers a judge advocate and that a
new section, numbered 50#a, should be added to the Ordinances pre#
scribing the qualifications and duties of such judge advocate.
We therefore further re~ommend that, after study by the appro#
priate committees of Grand Lodge, Article II, Section 3, of the Con#
stitution be amended to read as follows:
"Sec. 3. The Grand Lodge shall be composed of a Grand Master,
(whose address shall be Most Worshipful), a Deputy Grand Master,
a Senior Grand Warden, and a Junior Grand Warden (whose addresses
shall severally be ,Right Worshipful), a Grand Treasurer, a Grand
Secretary, a Grand Lecturer, and a judge advocate (whose addresses
shall severally be Very Worshipful). a Grand Chaplain (whose address
shall be Very Reverend), the Assistant Grand Lecturer, a Grand Orator,
an Assistant Grand Treasurer, an Assistant Grand Secretary, a Grand
Marshal. a Grand Standard Bearer, a Grand Sword Bearer, a Grand
Bible Bearer, a Senior Grand Deacon, a Junior Grand Deacon, two
Grand Stewards, a Grand Pursuivant, a Grand Organist, and a Grand
Tiler (whose addresses shall severally be Worshipful): together with
all Past Grand Officers and Past Masters of this jurisdiction, and the
Masters and Wardens of the several chartered and duly constituted
Lodges, or the representatives thereof duly elected.":
and that a new section numbered 50#a be added to the Ordinances
of G.rand Lodge, reading as follows:

"Sec. 50-a. The Judge Advocate shall be a Master or Past Master

The movement to erect a Masonic memorial to George Washington
began February 22, 1910, at a meeting of the representatives of 18
Grand Lodges, in the Lodge Room of Alexandria-Washington Lodge
at Alexandria, Virginia. Our representative was Oscar Lawler, Senior
Past Grand Master, who was then Junior Past Grand Master. Brother
Lawler suggested that a fireproof replica of the Lodge hall as a memorial
building-to cost around $50,000.00-be erected to house and safeguard
the Washington Masonic relics. With the passing of 43 years and the
expenditure of more than $5,668,000.00, the Memorial is now near
completion.
American Freemasons have labored to create this Memorial, this
majestic temple, to the memory of the Father of our country. The great
aim was not to add to the enduring luster of his name but to hand down
to coming generations a monument to one who was an ornament to
Freemasonry.
As above indicated, this Grand Lodge, at its Annual Communication
in 1947, flxed its proportion of the full cost of the Memorial, including

THE GRAND LODGE OF P1Am (GRANDE LoJA Do P1Aur), BRAZIL.
This Grand Lodge is located at Teresina, the capital city of the
State of Piaui in northeast Brazil. It was organized by three regular
Lodges on November 13, 1948, and constituted on December 9, 1948,
under the sponsorship of the Grand Lodge of the State of Rio de Janeiro,
which was recognized by our Grand Lodge last year and with which
we are still in fraternal accord.

Lodges.

organization, having exclusive, dogmatic Masonic authority over resident Masons and the three symbolic degrees in the State of Piaui.

requires a belief in the existence of God, the Great Architect of the

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY

WALTER HANS EMIL voN KoNSKY

"We sta~d between the barren peaks of two eternities; we seek to
pierce beyond the veil: but have no answer from the darkness, save the
echo of our cry."
All existence has its beginning and ending in birth and death: it is
God's immutable law. We rejoice in birth, we sorrow in death. We
sorrow in death only in proportion to its closeness to us. It has been
estimated that two people die in this world every second. That is 120
every minute, 7,200 every hour, 172,800 every day~ 63,072,000 every
year. More people have been buried on the banks of the Nile than there
are people living in this world today.
Such staggering figures make little or no impression upon us. We
may be shocked, but we do not grieve nor lament the loss of three
million by starvation in far off India, nor the destruction of hundreds of
thousands in the floods of the Yangtze, nor when whole communities
are destroyed by earthquake in some distant land.
. It is when death beckons those with whom we have been closely
associated: those whom we have known well, admired greatly and loved
much, the members of our own family. Then we grieve and mourn and

Death, as it must to all men, came to the Very Worshipful Walter
H. E. van Kansky, Grand Lecturer, November 3, 1952, and in his passing we lost a helpful friend, a sincere and constructive Mason, and an
esteemed citizen.
The son of Harry and Caroline Wilhelmina van Kansky, Walter was
born in Cincinnati, Ohio, May 28, 1892. His parents brought him to
San Francisco at an early age and with a few intervals he lived the
balance of his life in that city.
In his business career he followed in the footsteps of his father, who
was a journalist and editor, having published for many years the "California Democrat", an early San Francisco newspaper. Following the
earthquake and fire of 1906 Walter was indentured as apprentice in the
composing room of the San Francisco Evening Post. After completing
his apprenticeship he became a member of the International Typographical Union, and in the capacity of journeyman worked in the composing rooms of many newspapers and commercial and publication
printers, both in San Francisco and in some of the larger cities of the
middle west. In 1923 he acquired the sole proprietorship of the Elite

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Printing Company, which he owned and operated until his death. His
activities in the affairs of the San Francisco Typographical Union were
so outstanding that he was elected President of the San Francisco Printing Trades Council, and served two terms in that office.
Walter was a man of great energy and enthusiasm. When he was
initiated in Mount Vernon Lodge No. 517 in 1922 he found something
worthy of his energy and his talents, and for the succeeding thirty years
he was most active working energetically for its success and its happiness. He dimitted from Mount Vernon Lodge to become a Charter
Member of Seaport Lodge No. 550, which was instituted February 22.
1923. He held all offices in the line from Junior Steward in 1923 to
Master in 1929. He served as Secretary and later as President of the
San Francisco Masters and Wardens Association. also served as President of the San Francisco Past Masters Association.
He first became an officer in the Grand Lodge on January 1, 1935
when Grand Master Earl Warren appointed him Inspector of District
No. 41. He served in this office until October 18, 1946. when he was
appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer, and was re-appointed in 194 7-48.
He was elected Grand Lecturer October 14, 1949.
·
Walter was deeply interested in the activities of his daughter Viola,
and when she became an officer of the International Order of Job's
Daughters he became Associate Guardian and worked in that position
for several years. In 1944 he was Patron of Seaport Chapter No. 427
Order of Eastern Star, when his daughter was Worthy Matron. He
joined Mission Chapter Royal Arch Masons but later dimitted to San
Francisco Chapter No. 1.
In the City of San Francisco on March 25, 1916 Walter was married
to Miss Clara Scherr. Of this union three children were born, Viola
Martha, Arthur Walter and Bertram Carl, all of whom survive him.
In 1950 he conferred the three degrees of Masonry on his two sons.
and in all probability the meeting of Seaport Lodge on September 19,
1950 gave him greater happiness than any other meeting he had ever
attended, for on that evening he raised his sons to the Sublime Degree.
Walter von Konsky is gone, we will see him here no more. but we
offer loving testimonial to him in whom all proper elements united and
worked together for the making of a truly great man.

Wednesday. February 25, 1953. was a sad day for California Masonry. for at three o'clock that morning Leonard Gross died in Mission
Hospital, Huntington Park. The services were held in the Little Church
Around the Corner in Inglewood. Past Grand Master Louis Drapeau
officiating. The eulogy was delivered by Myron E. Smith, member of
the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes. Brethren were in attendance from all parts of Southern California and many came from as
far north as San Francisco. The chapel was not large enough to hold
all those who came to pay him tribute.
Leonard Gross was the son of Charles and Emma Gross. Born in
Saint Louis, Missouri. August 28, 1893. he attended grammar and high
schools in that city, later attended business college training for purchasing, production and traffic management. Coming to Los Angeles in 19.23
he became associated with the Southern Glass Company, and later with
the Verno~ Kilns of Vernon. and spent the balance of his life in the employ of that company.
He married Miss Mae Stahl in Saint Louis July 19, 1919. She survives him.
On January 14, 1915, at 22 years of age he petitioned Meridian
Lodge No. 2, Saint Louis, Missouri. Elected February 11, was initiated,
passed and raised and stood his proficiency examination in the Third
Degree October 28 the same year. Meridian Lodge issued him a dimit
June 28, 1928 and he was elected to membership in Jordan Lodge No.
654 of California the following July 3. Appointed Junior Steward of
Jordan Lodge in 1930 he progressed annually until he filled the Master's
Chair in 1937.
His love and steady attachment to the Fraternity came to the attention of Leon 0. Whitsell, Grand Master, and on December 17, 1938 he
was appointed Inspector of District No. 96A. His accomplishments in
that important office were outstanding and on June 27. 1948 Gran.d
Master, Chester H. Warlow, appointed him a Trustee .of the Masonic
Homes of California. October 14, 1949 he was elected Vice President
of the Board and was serving in that office at the time of his death.
At the meeting of the Homes Board March 14. 1953 a resolution was
adopted expressing the deep sense of loss in the passing of Brother
Gross. The resolution was entered upon the Minutes of the Board of
Trustees and a copy properly engrossed was sent to his widow.
Leonard Gross was quiet, modest and retiring. He was taciturn by
nature and tributes to him seem to grow in relation to the closeness of
his associates. Those who knew him best loved him most. Masonry
was close to a religion with him, and in his passing we have lost a great
and good man.

DR. WILLSIE MANNING MARTIN

Dr. Willsie Martin, clergyman and civic leader, died June 7, 1953
in his 75th year, in New London, Connecticut. Death came while he
and Mrs. Martin were visiting their eldest daughter, Mrs. John M. Ide
of Quaker Hill, Connecticut.
Born in Johnville, Quebec, Canada, Dr. Martin came to California
at the age of eleven. He attended Santa Ana High School and was
graduated from the University of California at Berkeley with the class
of 1900.
In that same year he was ordained to the ministry at Pacific Grove
and joined the California Methodist Conference. After a pastorate at
Oak Park and Sacramento he became assistant pa5tor at First Church
of Oakland. Following a study course at Drake Theological Seminary
he served as assistant pastor at Madison Avenue Methodist Church in
New York City, before he returned to California and married Miss
Muriel Eastman.
Dr. Martin held pastorates at Chico for two years, Alameda for
seven years, Boise, Idaho for seven years, and then at Hollywood First
Methodist Church before taking his post at Wilshire Methodist Church,
serving that organization until his retirement twenty years later.
He was chosen 6.rst president of the' Church Federation of Los Angeles after the reorganization of the Protestant group in 1938, and was
again elected to the post ten years later. He also served as Chairman
of the Los Angeles County C~mmittee for Church and Community
Co-operation.
Each individual is given 24 hours a day by the Great Architect of
the Universe. The multiudinous accomplishments of some with this
allotment of time are beyond the comprehension of most of us. Dr.
Martin was such a man, and in civic affairs his work was outstanding.
He was one of the founders of the Hollywood Bowl Association, serving that group as a director and vice president, and was a director of the
Southern California Symphony Association.
In 1939 he was appointed to the City Board of Park Commissioners,
was elected president of that body in 1945 and re-elected in 1946. In
1947 Governor Warren appointed him to the advisory committee of the
California Centennials Commission.
He was president and a director of the International Institute, a
member of the board of Scripps College, president of the Family Welfare Board, and a member of the Elks, Rotary and Lions clubs.
On many occasions Dr. Martin was called upon to serve on citizens'
committees appointed to deal with community problems, such as the
harbor labor disputes of 1937, and the "zoot suit" riots of 1943.
During World War I he served overseas with the YMCA. and in
World War ll he was a member of the Labor Conciliation Board. Dur-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

223

ing his pastorate at Boise he served as Chaplain of the National Guard
unit there.
His Masonic career is equally impressive. He was initiated in Oak
Grove Lodge No. 215 of Alameda, California, and affiliated with Boise
Lodge No. 2 in Boise, Idaho, on May 5, 1914. Dimitted from Boise
Lodge No. 2 and joined Hollywood Lodge No. 355 of California on
Feburay 3, 1920. He was a member of Hollywood Chapter Royal Arch
Masons, Hollywood, Council Royal and Select Masters and Hollywood
Commandary. He served a term as State Chaplain of the Knights
Templar. In October, 1949 Grand Master Ellsworth Meyer appointed
him Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge of California. His duties
were discharged with distinction and honor.
We mourn the passing of this great and good .man, and on this day
we salute him with our most exalted love.
ALVIN E. MELIM

The Worshipful Alvin E. Melim, Junior Grand Steward of the
Grand Lodge of California, died April 18, 1953 in the City of Honolulu,
Hawaiian Islands.
Alvin, the son of Theodore P. and Mary A. Melim, was born at
Honolulu, Island of Oahu, July 27, 1899. He received his education in
the public schools of that city, graduating from Mt:Kinley High School.
He later attended Merkins Business College, San Francisco, California.
His entire business career was connected with Adjusters Ltd. He
was president and general manager of the company at the time of his
death.
Brother Melim was enthusiastically patriotic. In World War I he
became a member of the United States Engineer Corps. In World War
ll, in addition to serving as a Block Warden, he organized. trained and
assisted in equipping an emergency ambulance crew to serve in case of
~ttack on the civilian population. He was deeply interested in veterans'
8ffairs, and in the Veterans of Foreign Wars he filled the office of Commander of his Post, Commander of his Department, and at the time of
his passing was Adjutant Service Officer.
Alvin Melim entered Masonry in 1927, being initiated in Justice
Lodge No. 549 in San Francisco; December 14, 1942 he affiliated with
Honolulu Lodge No. 409, and seven years later was elected and installed
its Master.
His Masonic interest extended to other bodies and he was a member
of Honolulu Chapter No. 1 Royal Arch Masons, Honolulu Council No.
1 Royal and Select Masters, the Scottish Rite Bodies of the Valley of
Honolulu, Aloha Temple, Ancient Arabic Order of Nobles of the
Mystic Shrine, and a Past Patron of Leilani Chapter Order of Eastern
Star.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The ardor and enthusiasm which he had shown in other activities
soon manifested itself in Masonry, and in recognition of his contribution
to the Craft, Grand Master Arthur Warren, in October 1952 appointed
him an officer of the Grand Lodge of California.
On July 22, 1922 Alvin was married to Miss Evelyn C. Correiro.
He is survived by his widow. his only son, Robert D. Melim. and two
grandchildre n.
To our brethren in the Islands we extend our deepest sympathy in
their grievous loss.
WILLIAM L. DAVIS

When the Supreme Being in his infinite wisdom saw fit to call Bill
Davis to his heavenly home on October 9, 1952, He removed from our
midst not only a brother but a man who had witnessed and also made
much of the history of the community in which he lived.
Bill Davis was b<nn in Azusa, California, March 12, 1874. Whe;
22 years of age he moved to Owens Valley and for some years there~
after drove the stage from Mojave to Darwin. As stage driver he had
intimate contact with many of the men whose exploits in the Death
Valley area are now the history and legends of that fascinating n~tional
monument. Later, as a mule skinner and cow puncher, he experienced
the thrills and excitement which now hold the attention of the young
through the medium of motion pictures, radio and television.
In 1908 Bill moved to Big Pine, married Mary Albers of Manzanar.
built the home in which they lived until his death. He was a carpenter
and builder and did contract work in Owens Valley, Bakersfield and
Miami, Arizona.
His Masonic career began in Waucoba Lodge No. 413 at Big Pine,
where he was initiated October 30, 1910, passed November 5, and raised
November 12, the same year. He served three terms as Master of the
Lodge, 1924. 1925 and 1932. This lodge surrendered its charte~ in 194_5
and consolidated with Inyo Lodge at Independen ce. In 1934 Bill Davis
was appointed Inspector of the then 60th Masoni~ District by Gran_d
Master Gist and served until April 1952, when ill health forced his
resignation.
He was instrumenta l in the formation of Trona Lodge No. 684. The
only building available was an old pump house at Valley Wells. some
five miles from the town. With other members of the Craft he gave
much of his time, knowledge and resources, to the conversion of this old
building into a suitable lodge room. Bill affiliated with Trona Lodge
May 18, 1944, and demitted to Alta Lodge No. 333 at Bridgeport F~b~
ruary 14, 1945. Much credit is also due him for the formation of Indian
Wells Valley Lodge No. 691 at Ridgecrest.
Bill is survived by ·his wife and two children; a son. Albert S. Davis

225

of June Lake, a member and Past Master of Alta Lodge No. 333, and a
daughter, Mrs. Vada E. Buck of Bishop.
· Brother Bill Davis was one of the few remaining links between the
old and the new West, a loyal citizen and a conscientious Mason. We
leave him in the hands of our Heavenly Father, firm in the belief that
his rewards will be many.
HARRY STANLEY CLARK

The faithful and loyal attachment for our Fraternity by so many men
in high position is a never ending mystery to the profane. Those of us
fortunate enough to be selected for office understand and deeply appre~
date our good fortune. We grieve when a good and efficient brother is
removed from our midst. Such a man was Harry Stanley Clark of San
Diego who died of a heart attack at the corner of State and Cedar
Streets, that city, December 26, 1951.
Born in Spring Valley May 16, 1891, a third generation Californian,
he was educated in the public schools of San Diego. After graduation
from Russ High School, new San Diego High School, he attended the
University of California. He was a past president of the South Border
District of the University of California Alumni Association. Also Past
Commander of the American Legion and Veterans of Foreign Wars
Posts. He was connected with the City Attorney's office for more than
25 years.
On November 1, 1919 Brother Clark petitioned Coronado Lodge
No. 441. Raised January 22. 1920 he was appointed a line officer in
1921, and filled the Oriental Chair in 1925. A member of numerous
Masonic organization s he was appointed Inspector in 1932, and filled
that office for 20 years, being Inspector of District No. 644 at the time
of his death.
Harry Clark is survived by his widow, Maxine, three sons, Monroe
Clark of San Diego, Harry S. Clark, Jr. of Oak Ridge, Oregon, Donald
L. Clark, United States Army, stationed at Fort Lee, Virginia, and a
brother, Charles T. Clark of Los Angeles.
Harry Clark was a model citizen and a true friend; honest and sincere
in his dealings with all men; unostentatious, charitable, always looking
for the good and not the evil in men. He is sorely missed by this Grand
Lodge.
CHARLES E. MOORE

That death is no respecter of persons was clearly demonstrate d on
the night of June 19, 1953 near La Honda when Charles E. Moore,
prominent San Francisco industrialist and Masonic leader died of a
heart attack while on a trial ride with the San Mateo County Sheriff's
posse. Brother Moore was 59 years of age.
Head of a socially prominent San Francisco family. he was a member

226

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the Bohemian Club, and president of the Moore Machinery Company.
He also headed the Moore Industrial Company, and was formerly
president of the Joshua Hendy Iron Works, which he sold to the California Shipbuilding Corporation in 1945.
Highly active in business circles he was ever willing and anxious to
give of his time and services to the Federal Government, and in 1941
participated in a government mission to Moscow regarding trade in
machine tools. He figured prominently in Federal Government activities
during World War II and in 1946 was Chief of the ECA in Italy.
His activities in Masonry covered a wide field and he rendered valuable service as Master of Ingleside Lodge No. 630, and as a member
of the Committee on the Memorial Temple. At the time of his death
he. was on the Investment Committee of the Endowment Board.
Brother Moore is survived by his widow, Ann Whittier Moore, two
daughters, Mrs. Elizabeth M. Dostal and Mrs. Mary Ann Hayes, and
two sons, John Moore and Charles E. Moore Jr.
Charles E. Moore was a gentleman, a faithful friend, a loving husband and father, a true and zealous Mason. As such he lived and as
such his memory will be cherished in the hearts of his family, his associates, his friends and his brethren.

Commandery No. 16 Knights Templar, a Past Commander of the Grand

General Mathewson is survived by his wife, Katherine; a son,

Brother Mathewson was a man of exemplary character, possessed

Not only our Fraternity but California has suffered a grievous loss in
his passing.

HENRY GEORGE MATHEWSON

March 21, 1953 at Letterman Army Hospital death claimed Brigadier
General Henry G. Mathewson, in his 77th year.
Born in Gilroy, California, iµ 1876, he moved to the Bay Area and
was a long-time resident of 869 Walnut Street, Alameda.
For more than twenty years General Mathewson was secretary of
the California Railroad Commission. He was a past president of the
Lincoln Gramm~r School Association, and a member of Alumni Association of the University of California.
A soldier by nature he enlisted in the California National Guard in
1896 and gained rapid promotion attaining the rank of Colonel in the
Coast Artillery, and with his unit served in World War I. He was promoted to Brigadier General by Governor Culbert L. Olson in 1939.
Things of patriotic and military importance claimed his interest and
he became a national first vice president of the Sons of the American
Revolution; a founder of the San Francisco post of the American Legion:
Society of American Legion Founders, Barnet Camp No. 29 U.S.W.V.
Freemasonry exerted a strong influence upon him from his first entrance into the lodge room. For the balance of his life he gav~ bounteously of his time and substance to further its interests. He was one of
the founders of Argonne Lodge No. 514, was its first Senior Warden
and its second Master. His other Masonic affiliations were the Scottish
Rite, Golden State Chapter No. 121 Royal Arch Masons, California
Council Royal and Select Masters, a Past Comma.nder of Golden Gate

Few men have given more to an organization than have our departed
brethren given to Freemasonry. Their experience in this world gave

contact with the realities of life and its vicissitudes gave exceptional

Our brethren are safe in our Father's House and there wait patiently

He had an unusual ability for clear and concise statement and was
an able speaker on any forum.
On July 7, 1901. he was married to Harriet Brown Lumley. The
union was blessed with two children, a daughter Rachel, now Rachel
Pursel living in Berkeley, and a son Robert B. Jr., who lives in Oakland
and was associated with his father in his law practice. There are three
grandchildren-Linda, Anne and Susan Gaylord. His wife Harriet
survives him.
His Masonic career was long and honorable.
He was raised a Master Mason in Oakland Lodge No. 188 and
served his lodge as Worshipful Master in 1906.
He served the Grand Lodge of California as Grand Orator in 1917
and again in 1925.
He was Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Grievances in
1924; was elected Junior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge of California at its annual communication in 1928 and was elected Grand
Master of Masons of California in 1931. He devoted the entire year
to the duties and responsibilities of his office. It was due to his ruling
that the law was placed on our statute books forbidding the use of
lotteries or gambling devices for the raising of funds by any Maso?ic
organization. He also presented the resolution which brought into being
Constitution Month Observance as a policy of Grand Lodge.
After retiring as Grand Master he was appointed on the Jurisprudence Committee and continued to serve until 1949.
He was a member ofOakland Chapter No. 36, Royal Arch Masons
Oakland Council No. 12, Royal and Select Masters
Oakland Commandery No. 11, Knights Templar
and served as its Eminent Commander in 1913, and as Right Eminent
Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of Knights Templar of
California in 1929.
He was a member of Oakland Scottish Rite Bodies, having received
the Thirty-second Degree, Master of the Royal Secret, on June 14, 1909,
and was elected Knight Commander of the Court of Honour, October
22, 1929, and was coroneted a Thirty-third Degree Inspector General
Honorary, on January 19, 1952.
He was a member of Islam Temple, Nobles of the Mystic Shrine,
of San Francisco, and also San Francisco Court No. 4, Royal Order of
Jesters.
Bob was also a member of Saint Philip Conclave No. 23 of
Oakland, of the Order of Red Cross of Constantine and served as
Sovereign in 1929.
He was appointed Grand Standard Bearer of the c;;rand ~ncampme.nt
of Knights Templar of the United States of Amenca at its Tr1enmal
Encampment in San Francisco in 1934.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

233

He continued by regular progression through the Grand Official
Line and was elected and installed as Most Eminent Grand Master of
the Grand Encampment of Knights Templar on September 23, 1949.
He displayed his great fidelity to every trust by faithfully performing all the duties and responsibilities that the position entailed.
It was noticeable that these heavy responsibilities were drafting upon
his physical well being. Many times he expressed the hope that he would
be permitted to carry through until the end. This wish was granted
him and he presided, with ability and distinction, at the Triennial
Encampment in New Orleans in September 1952. After the session
was over he often expressed profound gratitude that he had been given
his wish and had been allowed to preside, with all his faculties intact,
at the Triennial Session.
Shortly after retiring as Grand Master it was noticed that his health
commenced to fail. He began the long journey from which no traveler
ever returns on August 4 of this year. His friends paid their final
respects to him on August 6, 1953 at the Chapel of the Chimes in
Oakland. The tribute was most fitting. The floral offerings were exceptionally beautiful.
The Masonic funeral ceremony was used and was impressively
performed by William H. Owens, a Past Master of his own Lodge. His
final resting place is in Mount View Cemetery in Oakland.
This is a brief story of the life of Robert B. Gaylord, a faithful and
devoted Mason, an eminent member of the bar, an exemplary citizen
and a good an~ noble man. The World is the better that he has passed
by this way.

EULOGY
WILL H. FISCHER

By CLAUDE H. MORRISON, Past Grand Master
The death of Will H. Fischer on October 4, 1953 came as a distinct
shock. The fifth of our Past Grand Masters to leave us during this
year, his passing on the eve of our Annual Communication when he was
expected to assume his duties as Chairman of the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes makes it hard for us to realize that he will be with
us no more. Funeral services were held October 7, a week ago today,
in the Scottish Rite Cathedral in Los Angeles. They were conducted
by Wilshire Lodge No. 445 together with Rev. Dr. George Davidson,
who had served Brother Fischer as Grand Chaplain.
Will H. Fischer, our sixty-first Grand Master, was born in Yolo
County, California, on September 11, 1875. At that time his father was
a farmer. Later the family moved to Woodland and the father, Peter
Fischer, became Justice of the Peace.
He was educated in the public schools of Woodland and received

235

In 1922 he served as Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge.
He received his 32nd Degree on November 27, 1920 in the Los
Angeles Bodies of the Scottish Rite and in 1949 received the rank and
decoration of a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor.
In 1924 he was elected Junior Grand Warden and in 1927 was
elected and installed Grand Master of Masons in California.
At Coloma, June 2 and 3, 1928, during his year as Grand Master,
he sponsored a great historical observance at the site of Marshall's
Mill where gold was discovered January 19, 1848. A vast concourse
of Masons from all parts of California gathered there to honor the 75th
anniversary of all lodges chartered in 1853. The program of the observ..
ance was based upon the influence of pioneer Masons preceding statehood, the events and customs of the days of the gold rush, the establishment of the early lodges, and of the Grand Lodge. It was followed by
special observances at San Diego, Sacramento, Grass Valley, Mariposa
and Fresno, together with a dedicatory service at the vault in which
was stored the records of Western Star Lodge No. 2 in the old lodge
buildings at Shasta City.
It was upon his recommendation that Grand Lodge adopted the
beautiful custom of presenting 50 year Masons with buttons made from
native gold from the hills of California.
Another activity of his year as Grand Master, and to which he
applied his energy was the financing of the Masonic Clubhouse for
students at the University of California at Los Angeles. Every year
the use and appreciation by hundreds of stud~nts of this beautiful
edifice are testiiil.ony to his wisdom and leadership.
In these brief phrases, we review the events and accomplishments
of a lifetime of seventy-eight years. But the real Will Fischer cannot
be described in words and phrases. Probably his many friends will
remember him for many different things. Those of us who served with
him on the Committee on Policy and General Purposes will remember
him as a man of common sense, always seeking to preserve the basic
character of Masonry. The older members of Grand Lodge will remember him as one who was always master of the situation.
There were many times when a quick quip or a witty anecdote from
him relieved what might have otherwise developed into a tense situation
in our sessions. Those who were younger Masons will remember his
kindliness and thoughtfulness to those who were less experienced, and
many will remember his patriotism and his genuine concern for the
welfare of his country. And these memories will keep the kindly spirit
and the winning personality of Will Fischer alive through many future
Communications of our Grand Lodge. May the faith that is in all of
us sustain us and may our pride in Masonry rise high as we record the
passing of this kind friend and wise leader.

REPORT OF THE HISTORY COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report:
It seems proper that the History Committee should keep a record of
the last resting places of our deceased Past Grand Masters and to report
the supplemental list to Grand Lodge every year, so that it may be properly recorded in the proceedings of Grand Lodge.
Five Past Grand Masters have passe<i away this year, and their
resting places are as follows:
JAMES THOMAS FRASER, Section N, Grave No. 97, Ocean
·
View Cemetery, Eureka.
WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, Lot 150, Sequoia Plot, Inglewood
Memorial Park.
ROBERT N. GAYLORD, Plot 33, Lot 124, West Half, Mountain
View Cemetery, Oakland.
ARTHUR W. BROUILLET, Plot 166, Section D. Urn Garden,
.
Woodlawn Cemetery, Colma.
W1LL F. F1scHER, Lot 25, Block 8, Grave 3, Woodland
.
Cemetery, Woodland.
As far as your History Committee is informed, six instances have
occurred in California where a Past Master has presented a fifty year
button to a candidate he had raised 50 years before. They are as follows:
On June 5, 1930, Past Master John Mclnich, of Eureka Lodge No. 16
.
at Auburn, presented a fifty year button to George McAuley.
On August 16, 1953, Past Master Louis Muller, of Herman Lodge
No. 127 at San Francisco, presented a fifty year button to Charles H.
Hildebrandt.
On May 22, 1945, Past Master Daniel McFadzan, of Visalia Lodge
No. 128, presented a fifty year button to John L. Rhode.
On January 25, 1953, Past Master J. H. Runckel. of Rising Star
Lodge No. 83 at Forest Hill, presented a fifty year button to John. Alexander Ferguson. The presentation was in Eureka Lodge No. 16 m Auburn.

249

On April 6, 1953, Past Master Carl Phillipi, of Granite Lodge No. 222
at Roseville, presented a fifty year button to Edward L. Layton. The
presentation was in Roseville Lodge No. 222 in Roseville.
William Rhodes Hervey was Master of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202
of Los Angeles in 1899, and while Master, conferred the Third Degree
upon James Black Gist. On the First of November, 1949, Past Grand
Master William Rhodes Hervey presented a fifty year button tp Past
Grand Master James Black Gist, in Pentalpha Lodge No. 202 in Los
Angeles. This was an event of unusual interest, the first time in California where a Past Grand Master had the distinction of presenting a fifty
year emblem to a Past Grand Master he had raised.
The presentation of a fifty year button to John Alexander Ferguson
in Eureka Lodge No. 16 is also a notable event, for it is the second similar
presentation in Eureka Lodge No. 16.
Arden E. Turner of the National Sojourners, Chairman of the Committee on Honor Roll of Masonic ·Patriots, addressed a communication
to our Grand Master which has been turned over to your History Committee for a reply. The names to be included on the Honor Roll are
Masons who have distinguished themselves in the Naval or Military
forces, or who have contributed to the establishment or growth of America. The list is to include only California Masons who have been dead for
twenty-five years or more.
We have carefully prepared and sent the requested list, as follows:
General Nelson A. Miles, U. S. Military Force, Southern
California Lodge No. 278.
Rear ~dmiral Joseph Bullock Coghlan, Battle of Manila,
Spanish-American War, Solano Lodge No. 229.
Admiral George W. Baird, famous on all seven seas, Lodge
No. 87.
Commodore John Mills Browne, Civil War surgeon at the
Battle of the Merrimac and the Monitor off Hampton Roads, retired as Commodore in 1893, Naval Lodge No. 87.

Regiment, New. York Volunteers, California - Mexican War,
California Lodge No. 1.
General Homer Lea, distinguished military authority who
rendered yeoman service on behalf of the Chinese Republic, and
was Military Adviser to President Sun Y at Sen of the Chinese
Republic, Pentalpha Lodge No. 202.
