Thomas Starr King, distinguishe d minister and orator, who
was responsible for the success of the Sanitary Commission Fund
during the Civil War, Oriental Lodge No. 144.
Leland Stanford, president of the Central Pacific Railroad,
was Governor of California, U. 'S. Senator from California and
founder of Stanford University, Michigan City Lodge No. 47.
Something new is happening in Masonry every day. Proper records
should be kept of current events in the Lodges and of activities of Masons
in the respective communities. From our experience, we know that in
many instances records have not been kept of human interest stories
proper to be written. OWmes we do not regard happenings in the Lodge
room as history, unless they are unusual. highly spectacular or startling.
What may appear as an isolated event may be a part of, or result in,
something of greater moment. What appears of little consequence today
may, in the light of ·subsequent events. prove to be of major importance.
In our efforts to obtain from Lodges facts which properly reflect
Masonic events, we frequently receive the reply. "There is no history
worth relating in our Lodge." Several times further investigation has revealed that incidents vitally important had occurred in Lodges and to
Masons which, at first blush, brought the stereotyped reply, "No history."
It might be highly interesting and profitable if each Lodge in the
State would maintain a History Committee of one or more members,
which would write up these records and keep available interesting Masonic events.
Your Committee again respectfully urges all Lodges to keep a scrapbook in which may be pasted published accounts as to activities of the
Lodge or its members, so that future historians or new members may be
able to acquaint themselves with what has been published in papers or
magazines about the Lodge or its members. Lodges which have maintained scrapbooks for any considerable time report that new members
fully appreciate the information thus made accessible to them.
The various members of your History Committee have, upon invitation, appeared before Lodges, High Twelve Clubs and other meetings
sponsored by Masons and have discussed various phases of California
Masonic History. We are perfectly willing to thus accommoda~e the
Lodges and clubs, if dates are arranged at convenient times. If you desire this service, call upon members of the Committee living closest to
your Lodge or Club.
On the evening of January 16, 1953, in the gymnasium of Acalanes
High School. between Lafayette and Walnut Creek in Contra Costa
County, there occurred an event of unusual interest in California Masonic history. Grand Master Arthur Warren, in the presence of eleven
hundred forty Master Masons therein assembled, in addition to many

others turned away at the doors, instituted three new lodges! They were:
Acalanes Lodge, St. John's Lodge and San Ramon Valley Lodge. The
halls of these three new Lodges were in Lafayette ( Acalanes), Walnut
Creek (St. John's) and Danville (San Ramon Valley). Anticipating a
large attendance, and knowing that no ordinary hall would hold the
crowd, it was wisely decided to move over to the high school gymnasium
for the occasion. The attendance warranted the decision, and there were
many who claimed never in their lives to have seen so large a crowd at
a Blue Lodge meeting.
The Master of Acalanes Lodge presided in calling the brethren to
attention when the Grand Master was escorted into the Lodge room.
The Masters of the two sister Lodges occupied seats in the East. After
the Lodges were instituted by the Grand Master each of the three Lodges
repaired to its respective hall and separately opened the initial meetings
of their respective Lodges for the purpose of adopting their By-Laws, in
due form.
At this writing, it is contemplated that these· three Contra Costa
County Lodges will be constituted together in the same high school gymnasium in October or November, should all three be granted charters by
the Grand Lodge.
The background history which led to the establishment of Acalanes,
St. John's and San Ramon Valley Lodges is as follows:
Alamo Lodge No. 122 at Walnut Creek was for nearly ninety years
the only Masonic Lodge between Concord and Oakland. With the tremendous influx of population during the war years of 1941-45, and the
post-war years following, petitions in Alamo Lodge poured in upon the
Lodge in never-ceasin g numbers. From approximate ly 165 members in
1945, the Lodge grew to 450 members in January of 1953. The officers of
Alamo Lodge conferred nearly 900 degrees during the eight years!
When, finally, it appeared there would be no slackening of petitions,
the call went out to a group of sojourning brethren to afford the only relief possible by forming new Lodges. The call was answered by three
groups forming simultaneously. Each group sought signatures of sojourning brethren and tendered petitions for dispensations to the Grand
Lodge bearing approximate ly fifty signatures on each. Of these 150
charter members, only thirty were from Alamo Lodge.
Immediately following the granting of the dispensations, the Lodges
went to work in earnest. Many petitions came in from men who either
were waiting to join the n~w Lodges, or who were inspired to petition
through the excitement and publicity aroused over the unusual event. At
the last Stated Meeting of each Lodge under dispensation before the
1953 Grand Lodge Communication, they reported that during the intervening eight months, Acalanes Lodge had received nineteen petitions for
the degrees and four for affiliation. St. John's Lodge had accepted

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

twenty-one petitions for the degrees and ten for affiliation. San Ramon
Valley Lodge had accepted twenty-one petitions for the degrees and
sixteen for affiliation. Total petitions for the degrees was sixty-one and
for affiliation-thirty. Total petitions received was ninety-one. In addition to these. Alamo Lodge, the mother Lodge, received fifteen petitions
for the degrees, and eight for affiliation. The grand total of petitions for
degrees and for affiliation by the mother Lodge and her three offspring
was 11 O! The total number of petitions that Alamo Lodge ever received
during the rush of petitions following the influx was about forty.
Orinda Lodge No. 704 was instituted on September 28, 1949, in the
hall of Alamo Lodge. and received its charter at the Annual Communication in 1950. This lodge continues to grow in a creditable manner. and
also received a number of petitions during this eight-month period in
1953. However, the actual number was not obtainable in time for this
report.
In conclusion, it · should be stated for the record that the Mother
Lodge, Alamo, gave to her offspring unstinting support. Three Past
Masters of Alamo were asked to serve as Ritual Coaches for each of the
three new Lodges. They taught every officer his required work. Alamo
also provided St. John's Lodge with their meeting place at very nominal
rent, and the use of some of the Lodge room furnishings. Various officers
and consecrated members of Alamo Lodge gave continued support and
encouragement during the formative stages of organization when it
seemed that some of the three would never effect a lodge organization.
In conclusion, the Secretary of Alamo Lodge reports that as of the Septembers Stated Meeting before the 1953 Grand Lodge Communication,
through petitions for the degrees and for affiliation, the Lodge had recovered in membership 24 of the 30 lost by dimit since January 16, 1953,
and that by January 1, 1954, it appeared there would be sufficient petitions to make up the whole loss.
Your Committee recommends that the History Committee be continued for the following Masonic year, and that the SUJil of $100.00 be
appropriated and set aside for its use.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON

LEON 0. WHITSELL, For the Committee

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In accordance with the understanding of the Committee that we were
to study and recommend the proposed revision of Section 295 of the Ross
Digest, we submit the following report. The suggested procedure is for
the purpose of simplifying the proceedings where a plea of guilty to a
Masonic offense is to be offered.
We recommend that Section 295 be amended to read as follows:
"Sec. 295. Upon the presentation of such charges, the Master shall
carefully examine the charge and specifications, and, if they are evidently
frivolous, or if the act or acts with which the accused is charged, is or
are clearly such as to not constitute a Masonic offense, he may refuse
to entertain them. But, should it appear otherwise, and it is known to
him that the accuser is a Master Mason in ·good standing, he shall" ...
cause to be served upon the accused, by the filer or some other member
of the Lodge authorized by the Master for that purpose, or mailed to
the accused at his last known address by registered mail. postage prepaid, a copy of the charges and specifications and notice to the accused
that unless the accused intends to make any defense to the charges, the
Master and Wardens will proceed to hear the matter summarily and fix
the penalty. The notice of int~ntion to make a defense by the accused
shall be mailed by accused within 15 days after service or receipt of
the charges and notice by the accused. The notice to the accused shall
be substantially in the following form:
.
Brother......... ~............................... :
There is attached hereto a copy of charges and specifications filed
with the undersigned as Master 0£.. .............................. Lodge No.............,
and which are hereby served upon you.
Unless a written request for a hearing of the matter alleged against
you in the charges and specifications is delivered or mailed to the Master
within fifteen ( 15 ) days after your receipt of this notice by mail or
service, no further proceedings in the way of trial shall be had, and the
Master and Wardens will summarily hear the matter and fix the penalty
against you.
The request for a trial may be made by signing, delivering or mailing
to the undersigned as Master, the enclosed form entitled "Notice of
Defense" or a letter stating that you desire a trial as provided by Masonic Law. If you request such a trial, proceedings will be commenced
for the election of trial commissioners and you will be served with
summons advising you as to the date of trial.
Dated:
Worshipful Master

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Insurance Program is pleased to submit the
following report:
PUBLIC LIABILITY COVERAGE

In the event the accused files the Notice of Defense or requests a
trial by letter or otherwise, the Master shall call a special meeting of
his Lodge, as soon as practicable for the election of Commissioners and
the conduct of the trial as provided in Sections 296-339.
If the accused does not request a trial, the Master and Wardens
shall interview the accuser and such other witnesses as they deem necessary, fix and determine the guilt of the accused and the nenalty, and at
the next stated meeting of the Lodge, the Master shall announce the
penalty and the Secretary shall record the same as the judgment of the
Lodge. The Secretary shall immediately after said stated meeting notify
the accused of the penalty fixed by the Master. The record shall be
prepared by the Secretary and shall consist of evidence that the accused
was duly served with copy of charges and notice, a summary of evidence
and the facts to support the charges, the penalty fixed and determined
by the Master and Wardens and a copy of the minutes of the Lodge
as to the announceme nt of the penalty in the Lodge. The Secretary
shall transmit the original of the record to the Grand Secretary, and
file a copy thereof in the archives of the Lodge. The record shall be
referred to the Grievance Committee for report and action at the next
Annual Commuication of Grand Lodge in accordance with the regular
procedure prescribed in the Ordinances for trails.
If the Master is disqualified to hear and determine the matter for
any reason, the Grand Master may appoint any Past Master of the
jurisdiction to hear and determine it with the same power and authority
as the Master whose place he takes.
Respectfully submitted,
HARRY

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Grievances.

Your special committee on insurance reviewed and investigated the
effectiveness and adequacy of Public Liability Coverage of the Grand
Lodge and constituent lodges and believe the plan of General Liability
insurance, dated September 24, 1953; as developed by Thompkins &
Company as brokers with the Seaboard Surety Company, is well developed and equitably marketed. The limits of liability quoted are
certainly not excessive. In the absence of information as to the exact
specifications furnished the broker by the officers of the Grand Lodge.
for their guidance in the development of the recommended program,
it is considered advisable to touch upon all matters from the standpoint
of their consideration in long-term planning and not with any idea of
criticizing the preparation of the submittal as now constituted.
Your committee feels that in order to provide the proper coverage
at the most economical rate, the plan should be broadened to include
Grand Lodge, the constituent lodges and their so-called "Temple Associations." While it is appreciated that the Grand Lodge does' not have
jurisdiction over so-called "Temple Association s" it is regarded by the
Committee that the interests of the lodges and associations are so closely
connected that exposure to loss cannot properly be segregated between
them. Accordingly, it is recommended that this program be expanded
to include the liability of such "Temple Association s" for the ownership
and maintenance of such real property in addition to the contemplated
protection of the active lodges for the occupancy and ownership. The
inclusion of the "Temple Association s" will eliminate overlapping coverage at a very nominal additional cost.
It is further recommended that all constituent lodges be included in
the program to provide uniformity of coverage for the adequate protection of Grand Lodge as well as the constituent lodges. In order to accomplish this, it will be necessary to make the program mandatory by
Grand Lodge and it would probably necessitate the cost being covered
by a per capita tax, as mentioned in the proposal submitted by Thompkins & Company.
On the assumption that the officers of the Grand Lodge may have
occasion to travel well beyond the confines of the State of California,
and even the territorial boundaries of the United States, it is recommened that the coverage, in the present policy, be extended with ref-

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Berkeley respectfully submits its report covering the year
1952-1953.
The Board considers it to be one of its important duties to maintain
the physical properties of the Club in flrst class condition. To that end,
we provide in our budget items to care for certain replacements and repairs. During the past year, a material improvement was the replacement
of the cement sidewalk on the Bowditch Street frontage of the property.
This was an item in a former budget, but because of the delay by the
contractor it was not undertaken and completed until this year. The original contract called for the repair of the existing sidewalk. However, due
to the poor condition of the existing walk, it was decided to install a new
walk which would be extended to the street curbline. This has not only
greatly improved the appearance of the property, but also has removed
a great possibility of damage suits because of the faulty condition of the
old walk. The total cost was $446.40.
Some of the other more important improvements are: Repair of the
linoleum in the billiard room, and recovering of the pool table; an additional letter flle: three pianos completely reconditioned; window shades
replaced: several pieces of furniture recovered: purchase of two reconditioned typewriters.
An expenditure that has greatly added to the enjoyment of the students was the purchase of a large television set. Through the courtesy of
one of our members, we were able to buy this at quite a saving.
During this summer, the annual cleaning, painting, floor waxing, etc.,
has been carried out.
There are three principal improvement items listed in the 1953-54
budget. One is the replacement of the large reception room rug. This
was planned for this year, but the Board decided it could be made to last
another year---especially as prices of rugs were on the decline. This replacement is carried over in the new budget. Another large item is the
replacement of the window drapes. The present drapes are about twenty
years oia, and in very poor condition. The third is for necessary repairs
to the cornice and the roof. This must be done before winter.

In addition to its responsibility for the care of the club property, your
Board of Directors has endeavored to promote the most effective use of
the club by the students, and has participated in the various student activities. For a report of student activities, we respectfully refer you to
the attached reports of student Presidents Paul R. Merritt and Miss
Joanne D. Anderson. While there is always room for improvement, we
feel that the club is well managed, and successful efforts to increase the
enrollment have been made during the year.
One of the most enjoyable social events of the year was the visit of
our Grand Master, M.W, Arthur M. Warren, and his family. This is
an event eagerly looked forward to by the students, and they truly enjoyed meeting him and his family.
Another important affair was the visit of the Grand Master and some
450 Masons during Grand Lodge Week. The Board sincerely appreciates the interest of the Grand Master and his fellow officers in the club.
While we regretted that both Brother Earl Warren and Brother Frank
R. Killinger felt it necessary to resign from the Board because of inability
to attend, it api>reciates the appointment of Brother Angus Holden of
Mt. Davidson Lodge No. 481 and Brother Gene Otwell of El Cerrito
Lodge No. 705 to fill the vacancies. These two brothers have proven to
be very helpful and cooperative.
During the year your Board has given much consideration to means
for promoting interest in and knowledge of the Masonic Club House.
h would like to see the Masters of Lodges of the state as fully interested
in the Masonic Clubs as in the Masonic Homes. The following is an
exact quote from a letter recently received from the Master of a California Lodge:
"Dear Sir:
"I am interested in having information on the Masonic Club
House for the students of the University of California. Please
send me the details such as the requirements, cost and purpose of
the dub. Can members take friends such as roommates? And any
other information you have on it."
(Signed by the Master.)

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of the President
University Masonic Club
Spring 1953
I. Membership:
During the spring semester, the membership reached approximately
200 people. There was a slight drop from the preceding semester, probably due to the decrease in registration at the University.
We tried several new ways to increase membership. We kept members at the booth in registration line to bring prospective members over
to the club as they came out of registration. This seemed to help in making the Club known better. New folders advertising the Club were also
printed in time for passing out in the line.
II. Open House:
The first two weeks of the spring semester were turned over to open
h'ouse activities at the Club. We secured a permit to operate a public
address system, and music and announcements of the Club facilities were
broadcast to the passing public during the hours the Club was open. We
also had record dances on Friday and Saturday nights with free admission and refreshments. These were attended by 100 to" 150 new people.
This gave us a good chance to show off the Club to new people.
III. Social Activities:
We s~arted Coffee Hours this semester, with faculty members from
the University coming over to the Club and just chatting with the members. Many of us cleared up many things had been bothering us this way.
Our Sunday Suppers were held every month. Heads of Job's Daugh. ters, DeMolay, and Rainbow Girls were invited to these to look the Club
over and go back to their groups with the information as to what the
Club offered and what the members did. Our Faculty Representative,
Dr. Stohler, also went around to these organizations with the same purpose. 'f.his should help membership.
The Board of Trustees also helped in this line. We decided to open
our Initiation Dance to high school seniors in the above mentioned organizations and invite them to witness our Initiation Ceremony itself.
Many of them came and stayed to dance. The evening was one of the
best events of the semester. A midnight dinner climaxed the affair.
The dinner and dance honoring t•e Grand Master wa! probably the
best remembered event of the semester. All of us enjoyed meeting the
Grand Master and his family, and the members of Grand Lodge who
were able to attend. The whole idea and spirit of Masonry was brought
a lot closer to us through their appearance.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

256-i

A women's tea and fashion show was put on by the female members
of the Club in March. This was a success, as it always is. Clothes were
modeled by the Club members from the various women's stores around
Berkeley. All of the mothers of the members were invited.
We had a picnic at Adobe Creek Lodge, outside of San Jose. Despite
the fac~ tha.t we were rained out, everyone had a lot of fun playing ball
and swimming. The Club furnished some of the lunch, and the members
brought the rest. This furnished a needed relief from studying for midterms.
The Club also sponsored Bowling and Skating Parties during the
semester at local places. These events were also successful due to a large
turnout and lots of spirit on the part of the members.
Our p~e~ges rece~ved the benefit of a system doing away with pledge
~ours. This 1~ea was tried last semester, and shows signs of being a good
idea for g_ettmg new people into Club affairs. It's basically a committee
system with the plan of getting all members on committees under the
leadership of Council members. The committees were all set up this semester, and turned in good results. The pledges also formed theii: own
group under the leadership of the Membership Secretary, and had a lot
of fun putting on a dance for the members. It was well planned by them
and showed a lot of work.
IV. Snack Bar:
The Snack Bar showed a profit this year, by selling sandwiches and
hot dogs at noon in addition to their soup and milk. Coffee and donuts
were a strong favorite in the morning.
V. Miscellaneous:
The new television set occupies a place of honor in the main room
and is probably the most used of all of our facilities. It runs most of th~
day and a good part of the evening, giving the members a much needed
break from studying.

256-j

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Recovering of the pool tables gave the men a much better place to
give to some extra energy also. Their use has 'picked up considerably
since.
The Photography Darkroom received its share of use, too. Many of
the people used it to save themselves some money on pictures. and it was
also used to prepare pictures from our dances.
Two of the items needed at the Club seem to be hard to come by.
One is a tape recorder. With it, the members could practice speeches,
and other things necessary to school. The Club itself could record music
for dances. and interesting things that happen around here. It could be
substituted for the second necessity. which is a three speed record changer and new records. Maybe one or both of these will be forthcoming soon
if some Lodge is lookins:i for an idea on something we could really use.
In conclusion, I'd like to thank Mrs. Morton, the Board of Trustees,
representatives of Henry Morse Stephens Lodge. and Faculty Representative Dr. Stohler for making my job as President easier for me, and
above all. I think the members will join me in thanking the Masons of
California for providing the Masonic Club for our use as a home away
from home.
Respectfully submitted.
PAUL

President, University Masonic Club
Spring 1953
Report of the President
Fall 1952
I. Organization:
Council members were elected at res:iular1y scheduled elections. Office
hours were held twice weekly by each council member. In accordance
with the Club Constitution council meetings were held bi-weekly. A new
committee system was introduced and proved to be of great value after
certain necessary improvements were made. This system equalized the
duties of the council members.
II. Membership:
Membership was approximately 225 for the fall semester. Further
opportunity for increased membership was made possible by gaining
University recognition. This gives us permission to advertise on campus.
Our University sponsor under the terms of the recognition is Dr. Rudolf
J. Stohler.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

256-k

III. Snack Bar:
The Snack Bar proved profitable by serving sandwiches and coffee
throughout the semester. It is a favorite gathering place for that between-classes cup of coffee.
IV. Activities-Recreational & Social:
Our Open House activities proved to be very successful. They were
well attended and with the new charter we hope that they will be even
more successful in the future.
General business meetings were held the first Sunday of every month
and as usual a supper preceded the meetings. After the meetings we had
movies and/or dancing. These meetings are enjoyed by everyone; especially those members preparing the supper.
The annual All-U weekend was held on the Berkeley campus this
year. Our sister club from the U.C.L.A. campus was our guest. Brunch
was served before the game as is customary.
A wood-gathering party in November brought in a comfortable supply of wood besides giving the members attending a chance to enjoy a
nice weekend at Redding. Our thanks to Marcie Micheal for her hospitality and generosity in making the party possible.
Our pledge class gave a very successful dance with a South Seas
theme. The ballroom was changed into a tropic isle for the evening and
the "islanders" had a very good time.
The members had an old-fashioned tree-decorating party that was a
treat for all. The pie and ice cream were especially enjoyed. Members of
the Henry Morse Stephens Lodge joined us and were responsible for
the wonderful.refreshments.
.
·
Initiation this semester was highlighted by a candle-light procession
in the ballroom. Dr. Stohler was the speaker for the occasion and his
wit and humor made the perfect welcome for our new members.
Our annual children's party was held after school had recessed for
vacation at Christmas time. However, the party was well attended by
the members as our guests were teen-agers affiicted with cerebral palsy.
We have had these children to the Club before and they have become
very dear to all who have met them. The big question is who enjoyed the
party more, the hosts or the guests?
Despite a very limited budget our semester was a success on the
whole. Our activities did not reach the splendid heights of former years,
but they were enjoyed immensely by the participants.
V. Visitors:
We were honored by the annual visit of the Grand Lodge this year
when almost 450 visitors toured the club.
VI. Publicity:
Our advertising scope was greatly increased by on-campus publicity.
We feel that by closer relations to the University our membership will
increase quite noticeably.
·

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

256-1

VII. Conclusion:
This semester has been one of readjustment and great change. We
feel that the following semester will bear the fruit of our work this Fall.
I should like to thank Mrs. Edna M. Morton and Marcie Micheal for
their help over the All-U weekend and in emergencies. Deepest thanks
to Dr. Stohler for his support and help in setting the club on its way to
better relations with the University; to Mr. Marvin Martin and Mr. C.
Melvin Davis, the representatives from Henry Morse Stephens Lodge
for their kind support and counsel over a hectic semester; to Lee Vellom,
Social Chairman, who was my right hand and best help with Council
affairs, to the Executive Council. and the members of the Club for making everything worthwhile.
Respectfully submitted,
JOANNE D. ANDERSON

President, Fall 1952

of California is assuming a contingent liability which should be insured.
Your committee concurs with the previous recommendation of the
Grand Secretary to have the Grand Lodge of California negotiate
blanket workmen's compensation coverage to include all subordinate
lodges as well as the Grand Lodge of California. Such a policy will
furnish adequate coverage and result in a considerable reduction in
total premium.
It is estimated that the total premium to insure all 621 lodges will
be approximately $5,000.00 annually. In view of the nominal premium
it will probably be to the advantage of the Grand Lodge of California
to assume the cost and thereby eliminate the clerical work necessary to
determine and collect pro rata amounts from the respective lodges.
It is suggested that due consideration be given to place the policy
with a substantial carrier who writes on a participating basis in order
to obtain the best coverage at the lowest cost.
Respectfully submitted,
HERBERT NELSON

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF THE
MASONIC CLUB HOUSE, LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In our reports for the last three communications, we have given you
information regarding the redecoration of the club house which you
maintain adjacent to the U.C.L.A. campus. We are pleased to report that
throughout the club house, new rugs have been laid, furniture either replaced or refinished, and new drapes installed. The whole redecorating
scheme provides a beautiful, luxurious interior for the use of our members.
It is also gratifying to report that, although the final cost for the complete refurnishing was approximately $23,000.00, nevertheless it was
necessary to sell only $5,500.00 bonds from our reserve fund. We were
able to absorb the entire cost without asking Grand Lodge for additional
assistance.
One new member of the board was nominated and elected during the
year, Brother A. H. Nicoll, a Past Master of Mt. Davidson Lodge, a
pr_ominent business man, and one who has served Grand Lodge this year
as Grand Sword Bearer.

AMENDMENT SECTION 150 (a}
Since Research Lodges pay no per capita taxes and are not responsible for the relief of their members or dependents because members of
these Lodges belong to and pay their taxes and liabilities through other
California Lodges, they should not be required to charge their members
the minimum annual dues. Therefore, Section 150 (a) of Ordinances
should be amended by adding the following:

SPANI SH LANGU AGE LODGES
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge of California:
. There was referred to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes a resolution authorizi ng the dispensa ting and charterin g of Lodges
to work in the Spanish language . Your Committee has studied this resolution on previous occasions, and this Grand Lodge has, at previous
Communications, voted against this proposal.
We find that there are several very serious problems in this proposal.
1st. There is the questio n as to whether or not these Lodges, if
formed, would continue. We now have two French language Lodges.
One had a membership of 117 in 1943 and now has a membership of 125,
a gain of 8 members in ten years. The other had a membership of 130 in
1943 and now has a membership of 118, a net loss of 12 members in ten
years.
We now have two German language Lodges. One had a membership
of 61 in 1943 and now has a membership of 55, a net loss of 6 members
in ten years. T~e other had a membership of 191 in 1943 and now has
a membership of 209, a net gain of 18 members in ten years.
We now have one Italian language Lodge. It had a membership of
356 in 1943 and now has a membership of 311, a net loss of 45 in ten
years.
These Lodges are all located in Los Angeles or San Francisco, where
the larger groups of these nationalities are located and where you would
expect them to draw the most new members, yet with two exceptions,
they have dropped in membership.
During this same period the membership in our English speaking
Lodges has increased from 129,511 in 1943, to 213,639 now. Your Committee wonders whether these foreign language Lodges will be able to
continue with this record of steadily falling membership in most instances.
Would not the same history follow a Spanish language Lodge? It has
been said that they would fare better because there are more Spanish
speaking people in Californ ia than there are of the other language s, but
how many would or could join our Lodges? Your Committee does not
· believe the story would be any different and believes that the difficulties
do not make the gamble worth while.

262

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

263

2nd If Spanish language Lodges were formed it would require the

SPECIAL COMMUN ICATION CALL

number of Inspectors, sufficiently conversant with both langua~esf to ~
able to instruct in Spanish. Such men are not easy to find, or if oun •
are not easily kept working. Look at the turnover in our Inspectors. 't
3rd. Masonry attempts to unite men. not to set them apart. W.o~ld 1
not be better if Spanish speaking people who could and would J 01 ~ us
joined our English speaking Lodges. as they do now, rather than wor ng
with their own language group?
For these reasons your Committees on Ritual a~d Policy and General
Purposes are unanimous in their disapproval of this proposal.
We. therefore. recommend that this resolution be not adopted.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
recommendation of the Grand Master to amend Section 11 of the Constitution to provide that a special Communication of the Grand Lodge shall
be called upon the petition of twenty per cent of the Masters of our
chartered Lodges, instead of the request of fifteen Masters as the law
now reads.
A resolution signed by three Masters and making the same recommendation is also before the committee. The resolution reads as follows:
Resolved, that that portion of Article 1, Section 32, Ordinances of
the Grand Lodge of California, reading "and signed by the Masters of
at least fifteen chartered lodges" be changed to read "and signed by the
Masters of at least tw~nty per cent of the chartered lodges."
Under the present law it would be possible for the Masters of one
of our larger cities to request a special Communication for some reason
that could be purely local in nature and of no particular interest to the
Craft in general. whereas if the reason was of sufficient importance no
difficulty would be experienced in obtaining the signatures of twenty
per cent of the Masters of the chartered Lodges of the jurisdiction.
Your Committee concurs with the recommendation of the Grand
Master and also the resolution dealing with the same subject and recomJ
mends their approval by Grand Lodge.
The policy was adopted.

consideration to the proposal of Crocker Lodge No. 454 which seeks to
amend Section 126 of Ordinances to permit solicitations and lodge donations for statewide issues involving the protection and improvement of
our Public Schools System.

of this or other jurisdictions, without the permission of the Grand Master. Nor shall any Mason circulate here a petition asking financial aid
for any matter whatever, not Masonic, however worthy it may be."

·
"with the exception of our Public Schools System.
"Public Schools welfare is MASONIC and a proper subject for discussion. Solicitation for individual donations and Lodge donations in any
Statewide issue involving the protection or improvement of our Public
Schools System, may be made."

SOJOURNING MASONS
The Committee on Sojourners ( whfch term is used relative.to .M~s~ns
residing in California but whose membership is in anoth~r 1unsdict10~
and has nothing to do with the organization of Masons m the Arme
Forces using the same name) has recommended:
( 1 ) That the Committee be continued; ( 2) That copies of what t~~
Committee calls "assists" be forwarded to the Masters of Lodges wit
a letter from the Grand Master, requesting a written annual ~eport on
sojourners' activities in their lodges, and ( 3) That a lettMer be issuefd ~
aste~s o .t e
the Grand Master giving "his encouragement to the
Lodges" and expressing hi.s desire ~.hat they se~ as.ide ~?e meeting mght
during the year to be designated as Sojourners Night.
your Committee is heartily in favor of every legitimate phase of a
eneral program to interest Masons of other jurisdictions who have
~aken up residence in California to become affiliated with our Lodges.
The Grand Master in 1950 initiated efforts on this matter by a. lett~
to the Masters calling attention to the large number of non-California
Masons residing in our midst and also to the possibilities of dual membership. Grand Masters Paulsen and Dr~peau further advanced the
cause. Our efforts in this field should be continued.
However, we believe th~t enough annual reports are prese~tl.y reuired from our Lodges. We are opposed to further paper work if it can
~ avoided. We recognize that there might be a Master her~ or there
who will do nothing if he does not have to report, but who might mak~
some effort if he was required to report, but we do not feel that a
Lodges should be compelled to report to overcome the letharg~ of a few·
Efforts given because of such leverage would probably be frmtless ,any.
,
way.
Similarly. we do not believe that the holding ~fa Sojourners Night
should carry the mandate implicating a request fro~ the Grand Master
that it be held. We have several other mandatory mghts now.
There is always the risk that a mandate for observ~?~e m~y res~lt ·
in a program that is merely perfunctory. We believe that nights sho~ d
be left to the discretion and ingenuity of the Master. After all, thd affibad
tion of sojourning Masons is of primary benefit to the l.ocal. ~ ge an
if it wishes to overlook this legitimate means of advancing its interests.
that is a concern of its membership.
We therefore move: That the Committee on Sojourners b~ con~inued
for the ensuing year. that said Committee be directed to continue its efforts on the basis of voluntary cooperation from our Lodges, that no
mandatory reports be required from the Lodges and that no mandatory
sojourners' night be required.

GRAND LODGE REPRESENTATIVES
The Grand Master requested that the Committee on Policy and General Purposes study the matter of appointing and receiving representatives to, and from other Grand Lodges.
Probably but a small percentage of our membership had any idea
that there were such representatives, so inactive has been the system in
this jurisdiction. The Chairman of this Committee happens to be the
official representative of the Grand Lodge of Egypt. We would have to
search our archives to ascertain whether there are still representatives of
other jurisdictions in our midst.
The situation is slightly more active in other jurisdictions. When
some of our sister jurisdictions open their annual communications there
is a roll call of jurisdictions. Each representative answers and steps to
the altar and when the call is completed the Grand Master speaks words
of greeting and compliment and one of the representatives replies for the
group. It is a brotherly affair and kindly gesture. It is worthy of the
effort of the Grand Master of this jurisdiction in complying with the request of another jurisdiction for such an appointment, when a vacancy
occurs.
As we read Section 14 of our Constitution, the appointment of representatives by the Grand Master is not required, it is discretionary. The
section states that among the powers of the Grand Master, he is granted
the authority to appoint and receive representatives. Probably the system of representatives is on the way out, but there are some Grand
Lodges which desire such designations. If we can comply with their requests, it is W'ell and no harm is done. If we must say we have discontinued our former policy in that regard they may not understand.
We recommend therefore, that it be the policy of this Grand Lodge
to designate, upon request, and to receive, upon request, representatives
to, and of other jurisdictions.
Adopted.

CONTRIBU TIONS TO LOCAL CHARITIES
Tuolumne Lodge No. 8 presents a Resolution to amend Sec. 159 of
Ordinances by adding thereto, after the words "fraternal intercourse"
the following:
"and in its discretion, may expend a portion of said monies authorized by this Section, to make contributions to various local organizations
soliciting for charitable, general health and community welfare purposes."
From time immemorial. it has been the law of the various Masonic
Jurisdictions that Masonic charity be confined to strictly Masonic purposes, that is, for the relief of Masons and their families.
The proposal to expand the scope of our charity work and take the
monies for such purposes only from the entertainment funds of the
lodge adds nothing to the basic principle involved. Such a change in
our Ordinances would open the door for solicitations from every quarter.
The lodge would have no control over the final disposition of the monies
so allocated, and it might find that such funds were ultimately being
channeled to purposes contrary t~ our Masonic interest, or to the interests of some of the members of the lodge. Further, the lodge would
become the target for each member's particular non-Masonic pet charity.
This would probably result in conflicts and internal strivings for the
limited lodge funds which might be available for such outside charities.
On the other hand, we take the view that so far as the worthy nonMasonic charities are concerned, the proposed amendment might work
adversely to their interests. Presently there is nothing to prevent such
charities from soliciting individually those who are members of the
lodge for personal donations from them in their personal capacities as
members of the community. The effect of the proposed amendment
would be to present a situation where a hesitant solicited citizen might
avoid making such personal donation by saying. "I am making my donation to you through my lodge." This result is not theoretical. for those
familiar with community welfare work have frequently met similar
replies from members of other organizations which do make organiza..
tional donations.
The fundamental basis of the entire Masonic organization of the
world is fraternal intercourse and fraternal charity, which means limiting
the charity to members of the Craft and their families. The individual
member of the fraternity has joined Masonry on the basis of this historical record. He is subject to the duties and responsibilities, and in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

270

271

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

time of need, he is entitled to the benefits and privileges of such a
philisophy of charity. The individual Mason has a real interest in the
funds of the lodge, whether those funds happen to be General or Refreshment monies. All are subject to the demands of Masonic charity.
He has a right to have those funds expended only upon the basis of
historical Masonic law and custom, rather than upon the basis of the
majority vote of a small portion of the lodge membership who happen
to be in attendance at a particular stated meeting.
We believe, therefore, that departure from our ancient law and custom would be a serious error. and therefore recommend that the Resolution be not adopted.
A motion to adopt the resolution was defeated.

HAWAIIAN LODGES AND THEIR SUPERVISION
The Grand Master has made certain recommendations in relation
to the administration and supervision of lodges located in the Territory
of Hawaii. While these recommendations are severally presented in
his message, they are all related and are therefore here being discussed
collectively in the report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The over-all picture of Masonry in the Hawaiian Islands is of great
satisfaction to the Grand Lodge of California. There Masonry flourished, even before the establishment of Masonic lodges within the
continental border of our California Jurisdiction. The initial spirit and
enthusiasm of those early Masons in the Sandwich Islands has continued uninterrupted and undiminished through the years and Masonry
is not only on a very high plane, but the fraternity as such has an important and proper place in the general culture of the community, and
among the profane is deservedly highly regarded as a noble fraternal
and charitable organization.
For more than one hundred years the proper administration of
Masonic affairs in the Islands has been generally satisfactory. The
flexibility of our Masonic laws, and the authority these laws grant to
our Grand 'Master has permitted the succeeding Grand Masters to
adjust and re-adjust the mode of conducting the relationship of these
constituent lodges to the Grand Lodge of California. Despite the overwater distance between the Territory and the Mainland and the emergencies arising directly from two all encompassing world-wide wars the
relationship has been maintained on a most creditable basis.
It is admitted that th~re have occasionally been difficulties of communication, delays in contact and instances of inefficiency during period.
of conflicts. For short periods thereafter there have been some instances
where the technical administration of a lodge and proficiency in Ritual
has in some measure deteriorated, but it has never been critical and we

the resolution and its codification is before this Communication for our
action.
Before us at this Communication there is also a resolution similar in
purpose but proposing to accomplish that purpose in a different manner.
That resolution amending application question 13 is ineptly drawn
and has in it some typographical errors as well, but the substance of it
is to provide that a Candidate promise that he will pass a satisfactory examination in the Candidates Lecture of the Third Degree before applying
for any degree in a body or Order, the prerequisite of which is that the
person be a Master Mason.
Your Committee is in accord with the policy and method of accomplishing the purpose, as presented by this resolution. It should be pointed
out that the "sanctions" for failure to learn the Third Degree Lecture
are far less severe than those proposed by the 1952 resolution. It is to be
noted that if the 1952 resolution became our law, the newly created
Master Mason could not get a receipt for dues until he had passed his
examination in the Third Degree. Until that time he could not visit
other lodges nor in emergencies unquestionably establish that he was a
Master Mason, . In this day when many young men are compelled to
travel in foreign countries, under circumstances over which they have no
, control. the penalty of the proposed 1952 resolution is an exceedingly
severe one and is in our humble opinion still undesirable, even though the
Grand Lodge in 1952 voted a contrary policy.
The theory of the present resolution accomplishes the purpose without inflicting a severe penalty for failure to learn the Third Degree Lecture.
It should ·be pointed out that while the 1953 resolution refers to taking
degrees in the "collateral Masonic bodies" it is not directed toward them
nor will it, except under very rare circumstances, effect the disqualification of their prospective Candidate.
· If a Master Mason has been able to learn the Candidates Lecture of
the First and Second Degrees (and he has proven himself in that respect) • he will have no difficulty completing his proficiency in the Third
Degree Lecture in the one year's time. If he is traveling in foreign countries and is so located that he is able to petition for degrees in one of the
collateral bodies he can arrange under the usual procedure for his coaching and examination in the Third Degree work. On the other hand, if
he is in our outposts his possibility of getting either instructions or further
additional degrees of Masonry are nil. But in any event, during all the
time the Brother is a Master Mason in good standing and entitled to
visit any Masonic Lodge because he has his dues card and is proficient
in sufficient of the work to identify himself.
For these reasons we support the principal of the 1953 resolution and ·
still stand opposed to the policy of the 1952 resolution.

SUBVERSIVES INELIGIBLE
Under Deci~ion No. 14, the Grand Master held that membership in
the Communist Party constituted unMasonic conduct and that such a
person could "be tried therefor if the Lodge membership was obtained
after his Communistic membership had ceased."
Past Masters Burch, Helbach, Swank and Visger offer a Resolution
which makes one who has ever been a Communist ineligible to receive
the degrees of Masonry, or retain his Masonic membership if already a
Mason.
Inasmuch as the Resolution and the Decision apply to the same subject, we choose to consider them together. It is the recommendation of
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes that the policy behind
the Grand Master's Decision and that behind the Resolution should both
be approved. The language of the Resolution is broader than the limited
field covered by the Grand Master's Decision.
· There is no place in Masonry for persons who have a general philosophy of changing the form of our government by other than constitutional
methods, and that should be applied whether the individual be classed as
a Communist, Fascist or any other name. We. therefore, recommend that
the proposed Sec. 210.01 of Edicts and Ordinances be adopted.
Referred to Committee on Jurisprudence.

The. Committee on Masonic Information submits its 1953 Report and
presents for consideration a document of 99 pages, the document being
entitled "707Questions and Answers about Freemasonry."
The majority of the members of that Committee recommend that the
document be printed, that three copies be distributed to each Lodge, that
the balance of the editions be sold at cost to members of lodges and that
$5,000.00 be added to the Grand Secretary's printing appropriation for
this purpose.
The preparation of this document has been primarily the work of
Brother Henry Coil, Chairman of the Committee on Masonic Information. It represents a tremendous amount of research and a judicious selection of subjects that are very interesting to the members of our fraternity. From a superficial examination of this lengthy document we marvel
that any brother in these days has the time, the energy and the tenacity
to do all things necessary to presenting the material in its present form
and we do compliment and commend him for this work.
.Two things stand out in this matter: ( 1 ) that the document is presented at Grand Lodge and referred to your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes only after the opening of this Annual Communication
and at a time when your now reporting Committee is burdened with the
all time consuming problems of considering almost every proposal and
recommendation presented to Grand Lodge: ( 2) The recommendations
of the Committee on Masonic Information are supported by the signatures of two of its members and formally disapproved by the third member of that Committee.
Certainly the importance of the document requires under these circumstances, the studious consideration of at least every member of the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and obviously that has not
been possible.
Several weeks prior to the 1952 Communication of this Grand Lodge.
a similar document, identically entitled, was informally submitted to the
then members of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. At
that time, in our limited time and our admittedly limited knowledge of
Masonic history and custom, as related to the subjects covered in the
documents, we found material which to us appeared to be in error and
many matters upon which we knew Masonic History disagreed, sometimes quite heatedly. While our knowledge was not sufficient to cover
the scope of all the material presented it was sufficient that we determined
that it was not proper for the Grand Lodge of California to put the stamp
of official authenticity on the document in that form.
The majority of the Committee on Masonic Information say that our
notations as to the 1952 proposed publication have been corrected and
that it is now ready for printing, but brethren, not doubting their word,

276

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

we have not had the time to consider other parts of the material within
that document.
Aside from this and as a matter of fundamenta l policy we seriously
doubt the wisdom of putting the stamp of official authenticity upon any
document dealing with matters of this kind, especially where none of us,
including even Brother Coil. have access to the original source materials
that are essential to the proper conclusions as to Masonic customs, history, etc. '.fhough we did sponsor and publish "100 Years of Freemasonry in California," we are not and should not become publishers.
This particular document, "707 Questions and Answers about Freemasonry," has apparent value. It has a monetary value to Brother Coil,
if he desires to avail himself of it outside the scope of a formal Grand
Lodge Publication: on the other hand. it has a value as a basis of research
by those members of the fraternity who have the time and interest to review and search out and probably confirm the conclusion of the majority
of the Committee on Masonic Information.
With this thought in mind and with further compliments to Brother
Coil we recommend that the Grand Lodge of California do not publish
the document. Further, that if Brother Coil approves. we would recommend to him and our Research Lodges that this document be made available to them for use in their activities. For them it will be of great value;
it will not only furnish for them avenues of study but also act as a guide
to those matters which are of a general interest to the individual member
of the Craft.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ing that only certain individuals may apply is unwise in that an applicant
should be allowed to pick a lodge of his own choice without limitation
except to be able to qualify, and your committee therefore disapproves
suggestion "A".
Paragraphs "B" through "F" read as follows:
" ( B) Provide that no lodge shall confer the Second or Third Degrees
upon the same applicant at an interval less than four weeks from the time
of conferring the preceding degree.
" ( C) Provide that no lodge shall confer the Third Degree upon more
than one applicant at any one meeting, nor confer the first Degree or
the Second Degree upon more than three applicants at any one meeting.
" ( D) Provide that no lodge shall confer any Degrees upon more
than three applicants at any one meeting.
" ( E) Provide that no lodge shall confer the Third Degree upon more
than one applicant at any one meeting.
" ( F) Provide that no lodge shall engage in the conferring of Degrees
oftener than once every two weeks."
Sub-paragraphs "B" through "F" all deal with placing legislative
road block by further limiting the number of degrees conferred at a single
meeting, fixing a time limit between degrees for each applicant and limiting the conferring of the Third Degree to one Degree per meeting.
Your committee maintains that to do all this is now within the power
of the Master of a lodge, and we subscribe to the idea that the lodge
should be run by the officers and members. The suggested legislation,
in our opinion, would possibly retard the natural growth of some small
lodges, and would certainly complicate the work of record keeping by
the Secretary. We therefore disapprove the preceding suggestions.
Paragraph "G" reads as follows:
" ( G) Provide that lodges hereafter instituted shall be limited to a
membership of five hundred, except that applications may be received at
any time from the sons, brothers, sons-in-law or nephews of the members."
The same comment given under" A" applies to "G".
Your committee concludes that the most effective and practical way
to control the "Degree Mill" or oversized lodges is through the officers
and members themselves. This can be accomplished by encouraging the
formation of new lodges. Brethren who have moved to rural areas, and
who are members of oversize lodges, should be encouraged to dimit to a
neighborhood lodge. The construction of new lodge halls should be encouraged. Experience indicates that where meeting places are made
available, the formation of new lodges will follow, especially in metropolitan areas.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes suggests that this
special committee be discharged as recommended in this item ( 4): that
legislation suggested therein be not adopted, but that the report be rec-

ommended for study by the officers of the so-called oversize lodges, with
the suggestion that they bring the content of the report to the attention
of their members, thus informing them of the attitude of this Grand
Lodge.
We move that the report ~e not adopted.
A motion to adopt the recommendation presented by the Special Committee was defeated.

ADVERTISING IN LODGE BULLETINS
One of the recommendations of the Committee on Publications was
referred to this Committee, namely, that Section 127 be amended by adding thereto the following language:
"This Section does not apply to the official bulletin or trestleboard of a Lodge or any appendant body in which advertising
space is sold to cover _cost of printing and circulating provided
that the nature and contents of advertising be not offensive to
Grand Lodge regulations."
We approve the policy of permitting the sale of advertising space
in the official bulletin or trestleboard of a lodge to the extent of covering
the cost of printing and circulating such bulletin or trestleboard, if a
lodge so desires. We understand such to be one of the purposes of the
proposed amendment.
we understand another purpose of the proposed amendment to be to
similarly raise the presently asserted prohibition on official bulletins of
other Orders and groups having as a requisite to membership .Masonic
affiliation.
If this Grand Lodge has the power to tell the Eastern Star, Knights
Templar, Scottish Rite and other groups that they cannot carry any advertising in their official bulletins, we do not believe that it should be our
policy to assert that power as to advertising which is not offensive to
Grand Lodge regulations.
We, therefore, also approve as a matter of policy this phase of the
proposed amendment.
A motion to adopt the above was defeated.

WHITE HOUSE STONE
The Grand Secretary read the f91lowing letter as received from the
Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia, and presented to this Grand
Lodge the stone referred to ther~in:
"Most Worshipful Sir:
"Through the good offices of an ambassador from the Grand
Lodge of the District of Columbia, which is Masonically supreme
in the Capital of the Nation, I place in your hands a stone taken
from the walls of the White House during its just-completed rebuilding.
"A sufficient number of these stones, each with a Masonic
symbol upon it, was discovered to give one to each Grand Lodge
in the United States.
"These evidences of the number of members of the Craft who
built the President's official residence so intimately aligns Freemasonry with the formation and the founding of our Government
that I believe your Grand Lodge will cherish this link between the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Fraternity and the Government of the Nation, of which the
White House is a symbol.

if the criminal act was not a felony, but a misdemeanor, or where it was
a felony, and after receiving notice for automatic expulsion, the accused
demands a masonic trial, the act or acts committed by the accused should
be charged, rather than the fact that he was convicted of the offense
charged. It is the conduct indulged in by the accused which may constitute unmasonic conduct, not the fact that he has been convicted on a
criminal charge. To charge the conviction, rather than the ates of misconduct, is to char$le the consequence of the misconduct rather than the
misconduct itself. For example, a specification charging as follows:
"That on or about the 2nd day of June, 1953, the said
John Jones struck and beat George Black with a
club.",
would be a proper specification, because it charges what Jones did, but
to word the specification as follows: ·
"That on or about the 2nd day of June, 1953, the said
John Jones was convicted of the offense of battery in
the Municipal Court of the City of Los Angeles.",
does not charge a masonic offense. The reason for this is obvious. If
charged with having been convicted, the accused brother can neither
deny nor disprove such conviction; but if charged with the conduct
which resulted in the conviction, he might be able to show, and in all
events should be given the right to show, that in spite of the conviction
in court, he was not, in fact, guilty of the misconduct charged.
Your committee notes that trial commissioners sometimes fail to
vote separately on each of the specifications, and separately on the
charqe of unmasonic conduct. Some trial commissions have not voted
at all on the specifications, but have proceeded at the conclusion of the
taking of evidence, to vote only on the charge of unmason{c conduct:
this failure to vote separately is in violation of the plain provisions, stated
in the plainest language, in Section 322, Constitution and Ordinances.
In one of the cases which we are reporting in this omnibus report for
approval by Grand Lodge, the Lodge, after election of trial commissioners, proceeded to elect two alternate trial commissioners. While the
election of alternate trial commissioners might be desirable, it is not provided for by the controlling sections, which are Sections 299 and 311,
Constitution and Ordinances, the latter of which provides that should
vacancies occur on the Trial Commission, the Commissioners may, subject to the approval of the Master, choose properly qualified members of
the Lodge to fill such vacancies. However, in the case reported herein
. for approval. since neither of the alternates actually served as trial
commissioners, we are of the opinion that the election of alternates was
a mere irregularity which resulted in no prejudice to the accused. An
approval of the result in this particular case is not to be interpreted as
approving the election of alternates, since to do so would be in conflict
with the provisions of Section 311.

Sincerely and fraternally yours,
Harry S Truman"
The Grand Master directed the Grand Secretary to send acknowledgment covering receipt of the above to Brother Harry S Truman and
to the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON GRIEVANC ES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances is not unmindful of the serious consequences of remanding the matter of a masonic trial to the Lodge for
retrial. Such action results in additional expense to the Lodge. We
therefore attempt to explore every possibility of amending the trial record by resolution of Grand Lodge, but in many instances such action
cannot be taken by Grand Lodge because of jurisdictional defects or failure of proof.
We urge that the elective officers of the Lodges make careful study
of the trial provisions of our Constitution and Ordinances, and that
when doubt arises as to their meaning or application, advice be asked
from those well-informed in masonic law.
We urge that especial notice be taken of the fact that under our
masonic law, there are two distinct methods of disciplinary procedure:
FIRST: The procedure for so-called automatic expulsion under Section 332, Constitution and Ordinances, which procedure is available and
should be used where a mason has been convicted of a felony by the
courts, and has been imprisoned therefor, and, SECOND: The procedure for trial provided for in Sections 287 to 331, inclusive. We urge
the use of the forms prescribed by Grand Lodge, and believe that if such
sections be studied and followed, and such forms used, there will not be
frequent occasion for reversal by Grand Lodge.
In proceedings for automatic expulsion we emphasize the necessity of
mailing the required notice to the proper address of the accused, which
proper address, if he still be confined, is the prison or institution in
which he is held in custody, not his address before being so confined.
We must again make mention of the frequency with which we find
that charges of unmasonic conduct are filed upon a specification that
the accused was convicted of, or arrested for a criminal offense, rather
than the proper specification that he did the acts constituting the criminal offense. Where the charge of unmasonic conduct arises out of a
matter which has been the subject of criminal proceedings in the courts,

284

285

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We are aware of the addition~} burden placed upon the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master by the 1951 amendment to Section 301,
providing for the appointment by the Grand Master of a Trial Master
in .each case of a masonic trial. Some Masters of Lodges regard it as their
prerogative to preside over such a trial in their Lodge; and perhaps resent the appointment of a Trial Master. Such Masters should not regard such appointment of a Trial Master as an usurpation of the Master's traditional rights. We believe that many reversals and retrials,
and much expense, can be saved our lodges by the appointment of Trial
Masters skilled in masonic law, and we suggest that every Master of a
Lodge might well survey the list of Past Masters of his Lodge, in order
that he might recommend the best qualified Past Master for appointment as Trial Master.

the fact that they involve appeals, petitions for restoration, or some other
situation ~hich, in the opinion of your committee, requires them to be
separately considered:

It is the duty of the Inspector to require attendance of officers at meetings of the Officers' Associations; likewise, it is part of the duties of the
officers to attend. (Sec. 53, 865 R.D.) If the offending officer is one who
requires a certificate of advancement, then the Inspector may withhold
such certificate. If such officer is one who does not require a certificate
for advancement, the Inspector should request the Master to remove the
offending officer and appoint another in his place. Failure of a Master
to accede to such request of the Inspector, or if the Master be the offender, would subject the Master to suspension by the Grand Master. See
Sec. 34, Para. 8, 856, 857, 858 R.D.
Similar action may be taken in respect to any officers who for any
reason fail or refuse to perform any of the duties of their respective offices
as imposed by the Constitution and Ordinances of Grand Lodge. See
Sec. 34, Para. 8, and Sec. 856 R.D.

The Grand Master was asked the following question:
"May an Entered Apprentice, in the company with a Master
Mason who witnessed his initiation, visit another Lodge on the
First Degree?"
The Grand Master replied, "The answer is YES. provided, however,
that the other lodge may refuse admission if it so desires, since admission
would be as a courtesy only. The Entered Apprentice would not have
a right, albeit itself qualified, of a Master Mason. Moreover, if the other
lodge permits the Entered Apprentice to visit, this is done without examination and 'as a courtesy shown to the lodge in which he received the
Degree, or to the Master Mason accompanying him." (Sec. 173, 1046
R.D.)
This ruling is approved, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes concurring. Your Committee recommei:ids that when a Master
grants admission to a visiting Entered Apprentice to his lodge, he should
have the visiting Entered Apprentice introduced as such to the lodge in
order that the Brethren may be advised, in the event of any discussion of
matters concerning only Master Masons.
Adopted.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the

ances providing
for plural membership and also neces sary amendments
to other Sections
of Ross Diges t to make them comply with the propo

proposed amen dments to Sections 163, 250, 251, 101 and 175 of Ordin ances
.
Sectio n 163 is amen ded to read as follows:
This Grand Lodge recognizes and authorizes membership
in more
than one Lodge under the following conditions:
1. A member of a Lodge of this jurisdiction residing
in.the jurisdiction of anoth er Gran d Lodge which allows dual membership
may affiliate
with one or more Lodges in that jurisdiction while retain
ing his membership in this jurisdiction. He becomes a dual member.
2. A member of a Lodge of any other Grand Jurisdiction
which allows
dual membership may, if residing in this jurisdiction, affilia
te with one or
more Lodges under this Gran d Lodge while retain ing his
membership in
such other jurisdiction. He becomes a dual member.
3. A member, in good stand ing, of a Lodge in this jurisd
iction may
retain such membership and affiliate with any one or more
Lodges under
this Grand Lodge or join in the petition for a Dispe nsatio
n for a new
Lodge and may prese nt a paid up dues receipt in lieu of
a dimit or dema nd
for dimit. Such a member becomes a plural member.
4. Upon the election of a plural member or the forma
tion of a new
Lodge containing one or more plural members, the Secre
tary shall immediately notify the Gran d Secre tary and also every
other Lodge in
which the plural member holds membership.
5. A plural member shall pay all dues required by each Lodge
wherein
membership is held and shall have all the rights and privil
eges of membership in each of the Lodges excep t that he shall not be
Maste r, Ward en
or Secre tary of more' than one of such Lodges at the same
time and except
that the burde n of the relief of a plural member, his wife,
widow and orphans shall rest on the Lodges in which he holds memb
ership in propo r- ·

6. Suspension for non-p ayme nt of dues or otherwise, or

295

Whereas by the provisions of Sections 79 and 80 of the Ordinances
of Grand Lodge, the Trustees of that corporation are declared to be the
successors of the Trustees originally appointed under the resolutions
adopted in 1892, and subsequently thereto: and there is vested in that
corporation the title to all property, real and personal, and all rights of
action belonging to said charity, or to which it may in any way become
entitled: and
Whereas the Grand Treasurer of Grand Lodge by virtue of his office
is also the treasurer of Masonic Homes of California, a Corporation, and
as such has the custody of the Endowment Fund and all funds of Ma~
sonic Homes of California: and
Whereas an Endowment Board of Grand Lodge was established in
1933 consisting of 15 members representing the various Masonic districts
in California who are charged with the duty, among others, of issuing
appeals to the lodges and to Masons for contributions to the Endowment
Fund for the Masonic Homes of California: and that in issuing these ap~
peals, the Endowment Board recommends certain forms for gifts and
bequests, and that in all of them it is suggested that the gift or bequest
be made to "Masonic Homes of California, a California corporation, to
become a part of its Endowment Fund" and gifts and bequests have been
made directly to the Corporation, all of which has resulted in unnecessary
confusion as to the ownership of such funds: and
Whereas during the current year a bequest to "Masonic Endowment
Fund of the Grand Lodge of California" was reported by an Inheritance
Tax Appraiser as taxable, as was also, in another case, a bequest to
"Masonic Homes Endowment Board of the State of California": and in
each case, the bequest was exempted only after objection interposed by
the Trustees of Masonic Homes of California, and the presentation, by
affidavit, of facts showing the creation, organization and purpose of the
fund, and that the sole beneficiary is the Masonic Homes of California,
a charitable corporation, with the requisite provision in its Articles of
Incorporation with respect to the ultimate disposition of the funds to a
similar type fund in the event of the liquidation, dissolution, or abandon~
ment of the corporation: and
Whereas said Endowment Fund was accumulated solely for the pur~
pose of the support and maintenance of the Homes conducted by said
Masonic Homes Corporation and the entire income is used by the said
Corporation for said purpose: now therefore,
Be It Resolved:
That Grand Lodge does hereby formally and specifically, in accord~
ance with the provisions of Sections 79 and 80 of the Ordinances of
Grand Lodge, confirm the legal title in and to the Permanent Endowment
Fund of the Masonic Homes of California in the Masonic Homes of
California, a corporation, and declares that t~e said legal title be and it
hereby is, vested in said corporation subject only to the trusts attaching

CALL FOR SPECIAL COMMUNICATION
Be It Enacted, That Section 32 of Article 1, Ordinances of the Grand
Lodge of California, be amended to read as follows:
"Special communications may be ordered by the Grand Master whenever, in his opinion, the welfare of the fraternity shall
require it, and shall be ordered by the Grand Master upon application therefor in writing, setting forth the causes which demand
it, and sign~d by the Masters of at least 2(} per cent of the chartered Lodges. Every order for a Special communication shall designate the object thereof. so far as is proper to be written, and,
unless such communication be called merely for the performance
of some Masonic ceremony, shall be issued to each Lodge and
Grand Officer at least thirty days before the day named for meeting: and no business shall be transacted thereat other than that for
which the Grand Lodge was especially convened."
Adopted by 5/6 vote.

APPRECIATION FROM GRAND LODGE OF CHINA
Worshipful Eugene E. Dong, .Master of Confidence Lodge No. 203
of this jurisdiction, addressed Grand Lodge as follows:
"I have the honor to bring to you a message from the representatives of the Grand Lodge of China. At the Wednesday
session of this Grand Lodge, by your very charitable action, recognition was extended to the Grand Lodge of China. This recognition has brought joy to all Masonic brethren of that Grand
Lodge who were sojourning within your jurisdiction, yet not legally recognized. Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master H. C.
Mei, who had the privilege of being received at several communications of this Grand Lodge had expressed his hope of recognition many times. He was cherishing this hope at the time of his
death in March of this year. Brother Mei was Masonically active
for 40 years in China. He became District Deputy Grand Master
of the Philippine Islands. During the course of World War II
a price was placed upon his head by the Japanese. He went into
the jungle in the Philippines, and for 4 years subsisted on what
he could obtain from nature. He was given up for dead by his
family who had, in the meanwhile, moved to San Francisco.
When he got back, emaciated and sick, his first concern was for
Masonry in China. He worked diligently for the recognition of
that Grand Lodge, but the Supreme Grand Master summoned
him to his reward before this hope was realized. We know that

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

301

he would have been overjoyed at the action taken at this Communication of the Grand Lodge of California.
"The local members of the Grand Lodge of China have asked
me to present the following message from them:
. " 'We, the members of the Grand Lodge of China residing
m the Ba~ A~ea, r~ceived the good news of your recognition of
our Constitution with deep appreciation. This news we have already cabled to our Grand Officers in Hongkong. No doubt ·
due ti~e: th~y will ~end their fraternal greetings and thanks. y~~~

to you our most sincere fraternal greetings.' "

Your Committee has had under consideratio n the resolution by
Crocker Lodge respecting Section 126 of Ross Digest, and reports as
follows:
"Resolved that the provisions of Section 126 of Ross Digest
be repealed and the following inserted:
"A Lodge shall not, by circular or otherwise, solicit pecuniary
assistance from Lodges or Masons of this or other jurisdictions,
without the permission of the Grand Master. Nor shall any Mason circulate on Lodge premises a petition asking ·financial aid
for any matter or thing whatever, not Masonic, however worthy
it ·may be except for statewide public school purposes. and then
only as a duly appointed member of an authorized Lodge Committee.
"Statewide public schools welfare is a proper subject for discussion in Lodges. Solicitation of individual donations for any
statewide purpose concerning the protection or improvement of
the public schools system may be made on Lodge premises but not
in a tiled Lodge. Such solicitation may be made by First Class
mail in a sealed envelope by a duly authorized Lodge Committee.
which committee may use the Lodge membership list for such purpose."
We move the adoption of the resolution.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON DeMOLAY
AMENDM ENT OF SECTION .100
Your Committee on Jurispruden ce has had under consideration the
proposed amendment of Section 100 of the Ordinances and recommends
that the third paragraph of that section be amended to read as follows:
"If an applicant shall die before being raised or be elected to
membership in another Lodge beyond this jurisdiction under a
dimit issued by his Lodge, or shall be denied advancemen t by action 0 £ the Lodge, or shall suffer forfeiture of his fees as provided
for in Section 241 the fact shall be certified to the Grand Secretary
by the Secretary of the Lodge ~nd the Grand Secretary shall
thereupon cause the contribution to be returned to the Lodge,
which shall thereupon refund the payment to the widow or representative of the deceased applicant, or to the applicant himself as
the case may be."
Adopted by 5/6 vote.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The special committee on DeMolay is pleased to report that the
order of DeMolay is in good condition in this jurisdiction. A steady
increase in interest is being evidenced in several sections of the state.
There has been numerically a growth in admissions of younger boys
into the order. A great many of the older boys have been called into
military service. Th-is change in age ratio, although not too drastic, has
called for some revamping of social and financial programming.
