Gillespie, attorney and trustee for the Masonic Lodge, who proceeded
to erect a two-story, brick building on the site. Although Gillespie was
the actual owner of the property. it was intended that the upper portion of the structure be used as the Masonic Hall. The Columbia Lodge
of Masons had been chartered on May 5, 1853. Owning and occupying
the upper floor of the Methodist Church, South (which later became the
Presbyterian Church), as early as March 1853, the Masons continued
to meet in the cht1:rch hall until Gillespie's building was completed. As
early as December 1853, they had intended to build a large hall of
brick. but nothing materialized immediately. The church, including the
Masonic hall, being one of the major buildings of the town not burned
in the 1854 fire, was thrown open to those who had lost their homes in
the fire, along with the halls of the Odd Fellows and Sons of Temperance.
Desiring to build. after finding a suitable lot, the Masons' opportunity came when Gillespie decided to build his two story brick building on the corner of Washington and Broadway. Undoubtedly, his
decision to build had been influenced by the need for a new Masonic
Hall. In any event, the proceeds from the performance of Lee and
Marshall's circus, which was held in September on the lot adjoining the
Columbia Exchange. were don!lted for the new Masonic Hall. which was
proposed for the second story of Gillespie's building. With the commencement of the structure on October 2. 1854, and the laying of the
cornerstone by the Masons on October 18, the structure, measuring 30
feet on Broadway and 60 feet on Washington, rose rapidly. The laying of the cQrnerstone was an impressive one. In addition to band music,
the Hon. J. W. Coffroth delivered the dedicatory oration. The ·box
deposited in the cornerstone contained various gold and silver coins, a
Mormon coin, and several documents.
The Gillespie Building, one of the town's large~t. having fireproof
doors and windows, was partially constructed by November. In addition to the Masonic HaU on the second floor. the first floor was to contain one long room, and was to be occupied by a wholesale or retail
commission house. By early November, the timbers for the floor of the
second story were being laid by the contractors, Wall & Stout. Completed on November 31, 1854, so far as the bricklayers were concerned,
Gillespie intended to have it ready for lodge meetings within two weeks.
By January 1855 it was completely finished, and regular meetings were
being held by the Masons in their new hall: and on February 9, 1855,
Gillespie deeded the second floor to them, together with a 14 foot entrance on Broadway and a 9 foot wide stairway.
The Gillespie Building in 1855 is shown in the Huckel and Dresel
Lithograph of 1855. As portrayed. the brick structure was flat-roofed
with two stores. A door and two windows are to be seen on the ground
floor on Washington Street. Three windows facing Washington were
on the second floo~. This side was the entrance for the store under-

EXHIBIT A

The Gillespie Block (Including the Masonic Hall)
One of the outstanding buildings of old Columbia was the Masonic
Hall, which was constructed by Col. C. E. Gillespie on the northeast
comer of Broadway and Washington Street~ after the. fire. of 185~.
Occupying what is now lot No. 5, Block 17, its destruct~on m 1891 is
typical of many of the fine brick structures of the town being t~rn down
for the pittance of gold which was to be found beneath their rugged
d fil d
walls.
According to what title records are available, D. E. Alexan er e
a claim to this property on December 18, 1850: and on Decem?er 9,
1852, M. Courtright filed a claim for the same property, upon which he
had previously built a house and stable. In January 1853 the house ~nd
lot on the northeast corner of Broadway and Washington, measuring
40 feet on Broadway and 52 feet on Washington, then owned b_Y 0. W.
Howell, was sold in a sheriff's sale to B. Stacy & Co. In April 1853 a
judgment against HoweJl's partner, Courtright, was secured for property
adjacent to HowelJ's. Stacy & Co. in turn sold the corner lot to C. Cardinell on August 6, 1853, for $1000. On the first floor of the three-story
frame building, which existed on the lot at that time, the St. Charles
Restaurant was opened in October 1853. The remainder of the structure, operated as the St. Charles Hotel by Cardinell, was the scene of
various of the town gatherings, induding a masquerade ball on December 25, 1853. given under the direction of Cardinell in the saloon.
In February 1854. J.. A. Cardinell & Co. became the operators of the
·
restaurant and hotel.
The St. Charles was destroyed in the fire of 1854 with a loss of
$7,000. Shortly afterward~. in September, the lot was sold to Col.

neath. On the Broadway side were a door and window on the first
~oor and two windows on the second. Pavement, curbing. and hitching
posts complete the scene.
Although desiring to sell his building in March 1855, Gillespie continued as the owner until April 1857. On June 25, 1855, St. John's Day,
the Masonic Hall was dedicated with impressive ceremonies. In addition to the dedication, at which Col. Whitmann was the speaker, dinner
and supper were served at the American Hotel. and a ball was held at
Ferguson's Saloon. In August 1855, the Columbia Flour and Feed
Store was being operated by D. S. Baldwin under the Masonic Hall.
. Gillesp~e. by ?ctober 1855, had almost completed another two-story
bnck building adJacent to the Masonic Hall on Broadway. With its completion by Blake & Co., contractors, the overall dimensions of the Gillespie Block were 60 feet on Washington and 80 feet on Broadway. As
stated in an advertisement in March 1856. the two two-story brick
buildings included three storerooms on the ground floor. The comer
store occupied a space of 30 by 60 feet, and the other two were 25 by 50
feet each. The hall in the second story of the new building measured 50
feet square, as compared with the 30 by 60 feet dimensions of the
Masonic Hall.
In March 1856, the Gillespie Block was fully rented. In addition to
the offices of Gillespie and Dr. J. S. Davis, M. D., a confectionery and
ice cream saloon was to be put in the hall above the two stores on Broadway. In April 1856 Gillespie, in partnership with A. Allen, established
a real estate, land and loan agency. This firm was dissolved in August,
however. Another who occupied a portion prior to the 1857 fire included
F. Cooper. who operated a grocery, drygoods, and hardware store in the
comer first occupied by Baldwin. Dr. S. Wales & Co. established the
Broadway Drug Store in the store northward in June 1856. This latter
firm, operated by S. Wales and W. P. Gibbons, was dissolved in the
latter part of July, when Gibbons became the sole owner. Wales then
started ~ doc~or's office in the second floor over the drugstore. In April
1857, G1llesp1e was succeeded ·b y T. Caldwell as the owner of the structures, with the .exception of the Masonic Hall. G. W. Spalding, attorney, also occupied an office in the Gillespie Block in April 1857.
The fire of 1857, although destroying nearby structures, failed to
damage the Gillespie Block to any extent, largely through the efforts
of several of the local citizens. After placing a pole against the Masonic
Hall, they ascended then to the roof, "closed the, hatches-fought the
flames and saved the property from destruction." A well on the property.
as well as private flumes and ditches, helped to put out the fire west of
Broadway. New tenants after the fire included the county surveyor in
the office of Dr. Gibbons, the dancing academy of A. Silversmith in 1859,
and Co. A. of the Tuolumne Home Guards in l 86J. The fire of 1861

resulted only in minor damage to the roof of the Masonic Hall, although
frame buildings nearby were destroyed. ·.
On January 13, 1863, Caldwell sold the lower floor of the comer
building to the Masons. Columbia Lodge No. 28, F. & A. M., continued
to hold its meetings in its hall. About 1860 M. Brady occupied the lower
floor, where he conducted a general merchandise store for many years.
Finally, in 1890, the Columbia Masons joined with the Sonora lodge,
and the property was sold to G. L. Mead. who tore the building down
and mined the property. The adjacent brick structure built by Gillespie
on Broadway had been demolished earlier. No evidence remains today
of the Gillespie block. Stone walls on this and adjacent lots are retaining
walls erected at the time these properties were mined.
Although the Columbia Lodge of Masons became extinct on October
15, 1891, with their consolidation with the Sonora lodge, it has been
proposed that the old Columbia lodge be revived. In so doing, the
Masonic Hall would be rebuilt on its old site, and authentic materials,
dimensions, and structural details would be followed as closely as
possible.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Without change in its membership, your Committee on Taxation
has operated during the years 1952-53. It has answered many queries
on taxation problems from officers of Grand Lodge, constituent lodges
·
and affiliated bodies.
Of unusual importance has been the query from the Committee on the
Grand Lodge Memorial Temple of the tax problems involved in the
operation of such a temple, and a special report has been made to that
committee for its use.
The resolutions proposed by Ionic Lodge No. 520, to be found on
page 66 of the Transactions of Grand Lodge for 1952 were also considered, and a special report is presented to Grand Lodge on that
problem.
This Committee has also given its attention to the present tax exempt
status of the Endowment Fund, and to potential changes in such status.
It appears to your Committee that it is of great importance that steps
be taken by this Communication of Grand Lodge to preserve the present
exempt status of the Fund. The Endowment Fund was established
originally, and has since been enlarged, as a trust fund, for the use and
benefit of the Masonic Homes. Subsequently, Grand Lodge caused the
establishment of Masonic Homes of California, a corporation, for the
primary purposes of acquiring and holding title to real and personal
property, and administering the funds belonging to it for charitable
purposes. To better effectuate this plan, your committee has prepared

Of interest both to Grand Lodge and the constituen t lodges is the
change in status of ritualistic officers. We have heretofore advised you
that all employees, except ritualistic employees, who are receiving $50.00
or more per calendar quarter should be reported. Because the exemption
of ritualistic officers has been omitted from the new draft of the Internal
Revenue Code, the exemption can no longer be claimed. The organist
or other ritualistic officers therefore should hereafter be included if they
are paid $50.00 or more per calendar quarter. ( 26 U.S.C.A. [b) [11) ) .

Special Report on Exemption From Income Tax of
Donations to Masonic Temple Association
Your Committee on Taxation has given attention to the Resolution
introduced at the 103rd Communication on behalf of Ionic Lodge No.
520 to procure from the Federal Treasury Departme nt a ruling that
would allow deductions from Federal income tax for contributions made
for the building of Masonic Temples, either for Grand l.Bdge or con~
stituent lodges. Primarily. may we state that any exemption from the
payment of Federal taxes is given only by an Act of Congress. The
exemptions are very specifically stated in the Internal Revenue Act and
have ·b een strictly construed for many years. not only by the Treasury
Departme nt, but by the courts.
Your Committee is firmly convinced that there is no provision in
the Internal Revenue Code that would grant the special exemption from
income tax and which is the object of the resolution introduced. Grand
Lodge and the constituen t lodges are at the present given an exemption
for income tax as a Fraternal Association, under Section 101 ( 3) of the
Internal Revenue Act. Donations to Grand Lodge or to constituen t
lodges are deductible from income tax only if such funds are to be used
exclusively for religious. charitable. scientific, literary or educational
purposes, or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals. Deci~
sions of the courts sustain the Internal Revenue Departme nt in holding
tha_t the Masonic Order is not operated exclusively for any of those
purposes.
We believe. therefore, that it would be fruitless to petition for such
a ruling by the Treasury Departme nt.
On the question of policy involved, we of course are sympathet ic
to the object to be obtained and realize that from a practical standpoin t
it would be of great benefit to those lodges that are dependen t upon
contributions for the building of their temples. To secure such an exemp~
tion however. would necessitat e the promotion of a bill before Congress
giving special exemption for such contributions. It would seem unwiseto mention the Masonic Order as such, and any general exemption
would probably be effective in allowing many organizati ons of doubtful

as of August 1, 1953. The cost of this insurance is approximately

GEORGE WASHINGTON MASONIC NATIONAL MEMORIAL

Your Committee has reviewed with interest the report of the committee of this great project. We note that over the period of years, this

CALIFOR NIA MASONIC MEMORI AL TEMPLE.

Your Committee has reviewed that part of the Californ ia Masonic
Memoria l Temple Committee report with reference to the recommendation of the $1.00 per annum per capita tax. We have considered the proposal that this $1.00 per capita tax be made a constitutional provision.
We note that this suggesti on is made for the purpose of giving adequate
assuranc e to the Masons of Californ ia that there is no idea of levying in
the future, assessments or per capita of a larger amount. The point also
is made that should it be made a part of the constitution, it would take
a 5/6 vote to change it, and also that such fixed requirem ents in the constitution might be helpful in arrangin g long-term financing. Your Committee on Finance concurs that this proposal was well worth considering,
however, we feel also that there are sufficiently good reasons for not
making this $1.00 per capita tax a part of the constitution, but to leave
it to the sound discretion of each Annual Commun ication to fix its own
per capita tax. If the matter were left to each Annual Communication,
there would not, of course, be the assuranc e that the per capita tax would
be kept at $1.00, and it might be possible that it may be higher or it may
be lower, but we are firmly of the conviction that if our project for a new
Memorial Temple is to be a success, it must be as a result of a continuing
effort and that each year the members of Grand Lodge should be asked
to renew their confidence in the project by renewing such per capita tax
for building purposes as may be necessary. We, therefore , recommend,
with the concurrence of the Jurisprudence Committee to which this part
of the report was referred, that the per capita tax of $1.00 per member
for Memoria l Building Funds be continued during the coming year, and
propose the following resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved: That a per capita tax of $1.00 be levied during the coming
year and the proceeds be paid into the Californ ia Masonic Memoria l
Temple Fund.

316

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

TRAVEL EXPENSES
In discussing with the auditor the details of the travel expenses, we
have come to the conclusion that a misapprehension exists as to the use
of travel expenses. Without any sense of criticism, and without reflection
on any individual, we feel that there should be one standard for payment
of expenses in connection with travel, and we believe that this can be
divided into two categories:
1. Expenses for the attendance at Grand Lodge.
2. Expenses incurred by individuals while traveling on Grand Lodge
business during the recess of Grand Lodge.
So far as expenses for the attendance at Grand Lodge are concerned,
the method of payment is provided for in Section 66 of our Ordinances,
and we are of the opinion that no person should receive any greater sum
than that provided for in that Section, unless such expenditure is de8nitely authorized by the Grand Master or by our ordinances, regardless of
the fact that certain meetings may be held to coincide with the annual
Communication.
So far as other traveling expenses during the recess of the Grand
Lodge are concerned, we believe that each person traveling on Grand
Lodge business should receive his necessary traveling expenses, including
mileage, hotel. meals and incidentals, upon presenting to the Grand Secretary a proper voucher for such expenses; that at each meeting of every
Board and Committee held in the interests of Grand Lodge, that the
Chairman or Secretary of such Committee or Board shall certify to the
Grand Secretary the list of those persons attending such meeting entitled
to travel allowances; that this shall apply to all traveling expenses whether paid out of appropriations approved by Grand Lodge or whether paid
out of other Grand Lodge funds. If this meets the approval of the Grand
Lodge, we request that this information be communicated by the Grand
Secretary to all Boards and Committees affected.
MASONIC HOMES
Your Committee has reviewed with interest the report of the Trustees
of the Masonic Homes, and have consulted with them as to their needs
for the coming year. Last year on the recommendation of this Committee,
a per capita tax of 75c was levied by Grand Lodge for the beneflt of the
Masonic Homes. This year it is felt that a per capita tax of 50c will be
sufficient, although it should be borne in mind that the proper maintenance of our Homes is our major responsibility and that this per capita tax
may require adjustment in f~ture years. We, therefore, propose the following resolution and move its adoption:
R~solved: That the sum of 50c per capita be levied for the present
fiscal year, the proceeds to be paid to the Trustees of the Masonic Homes.

317

BUDGET
Your Committee has had considerable difficulty in arriving at a budget which we believed was reasonable to present to the Grand Lodge. The
total of all the requests for appropriations and estimates for the expenses
for the coming year total a sum which we felt to be considerably out of
line with that which we should recommend to you for your consideration.
Consequently, we have made a considerable effort to reduce the total to
be somewhat in line with that of the expenses for the past year. In doing
this we have made certain changes in appropriations bringing the totals
to less than the amount requested, but we feel that with care, the appropriations can be made to cover the purposes needed. Previously, we referred to the committment of $10,000.00 for the Maricopa Temple and
we are not including that in the present budget, feeling that for the present, when required, it should be a surplus expenditure.
The estimated budget follows:

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT FUND AUDIT
Grand Lodge F. & A M. of California
San Francisco, California
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts and records of the MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT FUND for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1953 and present the following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of Assets, July 31, 1953.
Schedule 1: Endowment Fund Securities owned, July 31, 1953.
Exhibit B: Statement of Cash Receipts and Disbursements, August 1,
. ~· ·~·-~ "'
1952 to July 31, 1953.
Schedule 2: Securities redeemed and sold during the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1953.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach Fund, July 31, 1953.
Exhibit D: Statement of Income and Capital Accounts for the fiscal year
ended July 31, 1953.

COMMENTS
Cub:
The bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries.
All interest and dividends due from investments and savings bank accounts
were received and deposited in the bank accounts of the Masonic Homes.
The total income received by the Homes from the Endowment Fund amounted to $155,052.86 as compared to $125,715.87 for last year.
Securities:
Securities owned on July 31, 1953 are listed on Schedule 1. Securities
redeemed and sold during the current year are listed on Schedule 2.
Stocks and bonds purchased are listed at cost. Donated securities are
listed at market value when received, or at a nominal value of $1.00 if the
actual value is unknown.
Certified lists of securities held for the account of the Endowment and
Luckenbach Funds were received from the Anglo California National Bank
which has custody of the securities. The records were checked to these lists
and the securities not listed were inspected by us at the oftice of the Grand

Secretary.

lncreue In Fund:
The combined assets of the Endowment Fund and the Luckenbach Fund
show the following increase for the current year:

The books of the Masonic Homes carry the record of the Harriet C. Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund. After the death of the beneficiaries of this
fun~, the remainder will be transferred to the Endowment Fund. The Masonic Homes report shows that this fund had a balance of $19,311.65 as at
.
July 31, 1953.
The Masonic Homes also hold several pieces of real estate for the account of the Endowment Fund. Whenever a sale is made the proceeds will
be deposited to the account of the Endowment Fund.
Accountants' Opinion:
In our opinion, the accompanying statements present fairly the financial
position of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund at July 31 1953 in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles applied' on a basis consistent with that of the preceding year.
Respectfully submitted,
BURROWS & PARKER
Certified Public Accountants

MASONIC HOMES AUDIT

Statement of Inc:ome and Capital Ac:c:ounts

Masonic Homes of California

Gentlemen:
We have audited the books of account and records of the MASONIC
